2015.Q2:
### Financial Insights

1. **Southwest Airlines reported record second quarter 2015 net income of \$691 million excluding special items, a 44% increase over Q2 2014**  
   The company achieved \$691 million in net income excluding special items, or \$1.03 per diluted share, up \$206 million from \$485 million (non-GAAP) in Q2 2014, surpassing consensus estimates of \$1.02 per share. GAAP net income was \$608 million, or \$0.90 per diluted share. Operating income reached a record \$1.1 billion with a 22.5% operating margin, up 40% from \$775 million in Q2 2014 [8-K 2015-07-23; 10-Q 2015-07-31].

2. **Operating revenues rose 2.0% year-over-year to \$5.1 billion despite a 4.6% decline in passenger unit revenues (PRASM)**  
   Passenger revenues increased \$100 million to \$4.85 billion, driven by a 7.0% capacity increase (ASMs) and strong demand reflected in a record 84.6% load factor. However, PRASM declined 4.6%, mainly due to a 5.4% drop in passenger revenue yield and a \$47 million favorable revenue adjustment in Q2 2014 that distorted year-over-year comparisons. Additional 2-3% PRASM decline was attributed to a 4.6% increase in average aircraft stage length and a 2.4% increase in seats per trip (gauge), reflecting fleet modernization and longer average flights [10-Q 2015-07-31; 8-K 2015-07-23].

3. **Operating expenses fell 5.0% year-over-year to \$4.03 billion, driven mainly by a 29.5% reduction in fuel costs**  
   Fuel and oil expense dropped \$420 million to \$1.005 billion, a 34.1% decrease per ASM, driven by a 33.1% decline in average economic jet fuel cost per gallon from \$3.02 to \$2.02. Fuel gallons consumed rose 5.1%, but capacity grew 7.0%, improving fuel efficiency slightly. Other expense categories showed mixed changes: salaries, wages, and benefits rose 14.3% (\$201 million), driven by higher profitsharing expense (\$182 million record in Q2 2015), while aircraft rentals fell 21.3% and acquisition/integration costs declined 92.1%. Operating expenses per ASM declined 11.1% to 11.04 cents, and excluding fuel and profitsharing, unit costs fell 1.8% [10-Q 2015-07-31].

4. **Return on invested capital (ROIC) before taxes and special items improved sharply to 28.2% for the 12 months ended June 30, 2015**  
   This compares to 17.1% for the prior 12 months ended June 30, 2014, reflecting the company’s improved profitability and capital efficiency. The calculation adjusts for aircraft leases by assuming ownership and excludes special items [8-K 2015-07-23].

5. **Strong free cash flow of \$1.0 billion in first half 2015 supported \$811 million returned to shareholders via dividends and share repurchases**  
   In Q2 2015, Southwest repurchased approximately 10 million shares totaling \$380 million, including accelerated share repurchase (ASR) programs, and paid \$50 million in dividends. The company announced a new \$1.5 billion share repurchase authorization and increased its quarterly dividend by 25%. An additional \$500 million of ASR purchases was planned for 2015, bringing total repurchases to nearly \$1.2 billion for the year [8-K 2015-07-23].

### Operations Insights

6. **Capacity grew 7.0% in Q2 2015 with RPMs up 7.9%, yielding a record load factor of 84.6%**  
   Available seat miles (ASMs) increased from 34.1 billion to 36.5 billion. Revenue passenger miles (RPMs) rose from 28.6 billion to 30.9 billion. Load factor improved by 0.7 points from 83.9% in Q2 2014. Average length of passenger haul increased 2.1% to 1,002 miles, and average aircraft stage length rose 4.6%, reflecting longer routes and fleet modernization. Trips flown slightly declined 0.3%, while seats per trip increased 2.4% to 145.9 seats, consistent with a larger gauge [8-K 2015-07-08; 10-Q 2015-07-31].

7. **Fleet grew modestly to 689 aircraft at June 30, 2015, with deliveries and retirements reflecting ongoing modernization**  
   Southwest took delivery of 11 aircraft in Q2 (six Boeing 737-800s and five pre-owned 737-700s) and retired one Boeing 737-300. The company planned additional deliveries of six 737-800s and eight pre-owned 737-700s for the remainder of 2015. The fleet modernization supports increased seats per trip and longer stage lengths [10-Q 2015-07-31].

8. **Southwest continued network expansion, particularly at Dallas Love Field and internationally**  
   The company increased daily nonstop flights from Dallas Love Field to 166 in April 2015, with plans to operate 180 weekday departures to 50 nonstop destinations by August 2015. International expansion included new service to Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, and plans for eight international destinations from Houston Hobby, including Belize City and Liberia, Costa Rica, pending government approvals [8-K 2015-07-23; 10-Q 2015-07-31].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

9. **Passenger unit revenues declined due to yield softness, longer average stage length, and increased seat gauge**  
   The 4.6% decline in PRASM was attributed to a 5.4% decline in passenger revenue yield, a 4.6% increase in average aircraft stage length, and a 2.4% increase in seats per trip. Management noted challenging year-over-year comparisons including a \$47 million revenue adjustment in Q2 2014 and expected PRASM declines in the 4-5% range for Q2 2015. Despite this, demand remained strong, demonstrated by record load factors [10-Q 2015-07-31; 8-K 2015-07-23].

10. **Ancillary revenues were stable despite AirTran service termination, supported by growth in EarlyBird Check-in and gate boarding position sales**  
    Other revenues declined 0.9% year-over-year primarily due to AirTran service ending but were nearly offset by increased ancillary fees from Southwest-branded services. Freight revenues increased 4.5% in Q2 2015 due to higher volume shipped [10-Q 2015-07-31].

11. **Southwest amended and extended its co-branded credit card agreement with Chase, expecting significant revenue enhancements starting Q3 2015**  
    The agreement involves selling loyalty points and other items to Chase, with an expected one-time non-cash revenue increase of approximately \$150 million in Q3 2015 due to a change in accounting methodology accelerating revenue recognition. The company anticipates this will increase other revenues significantly in Q3 2015 and beyond [10-Q 2015-07-31].

### Labor Insights

12. **Salaries, wages, and benefits increased 14.3% year-over-year, reflecting record profitsharing and workforce growth**  
    Salaries, wages, and benefits rose by \$201 million to \$1.607 billion in Q2 2015. Profitsharing expense was a record \$182 million, contributing significantly to the increase. The active full-time equivalent employee count grew 4.7% to 47,645 [10-Q 2015-07-31].

13. **Dispatchers represented by Transport Workers Union ratified a new four-year contract during Q2 2015**  
    This labor agreement was disclosed but without specific financial or operational impact details [10-Q 2015-07-31].

### Wrap Up

Southwest Airlines’ second quarter 2015 results featured record profitability driven principally by sharply lower fuel costs and strong operational efficiency amid a 7% capacity increase and record load factors. Passenger unit revenues declined due to longer average flights, larger aircraft gauge, and softer yields, partially offset by ancillary revenue growth and co-branded credit card agreement enhancements. Operating expenses fell 5%, led by a 30% fuel expense drop, though salaries and benefits rose due to profitsharing and workforce expansion. The company continued fleet modernization and network growth, especially at Dallas Love Field and in international markets, while maintaining strong cash flow that supported nearly \$1.2 billion in share repurchases and dividends in 2015.

For the third quarter of 2015, Southwest guided for a roughly 1% decline in unit revenues compared with 2014, with economic fuel costs expected around \$2.20 per gallon versus \$2.94 in Q3 2014, supporting continued fuel cost savings. Capacity growth was expected near 8%, with ongoing network optimization including new markets and pruning less profitable flights. The company anticipated a one-time \$150 million non-cash revenue boost in Q3 from the amended credit card agreement and related accounting changes. No material operational disruptions or litigation were disclosed for the period.

The revised aircraft delivery schedule raised firm capital commitments by \$400 million beyond 2015. The fleet ended 2015 with 704 Boeing 737 aircraft. Southwest also issued \$500 million of 2.65% senior unsecured notes due 2020 in Q4 2015, maintaining a strong investment-grade balance sheet [8-K 2016-01-21; 10-K 2016-02-03].

5. **Strong cash flow supported \$1.4 billion returned to shareholders in 2015 via \$180 million dividends and \$1.2 billion in share repurchases, with an additional \$500 million accelerated share repurchase planned.**  
   Southwest generated significant free cash flow in 2015, enabling shareholder returns that exceeded 2014 levels. During Q4 2015, the company completed an accelerated share repurchase (ASR) program totaling \$500 million and intends to launch another \$500 million ASR program. After this, \$200 million remains under the existing \$1.5 billion share repurchase authorization from May 2015 [8-K 2016-01-21; 10-K 2016-02-03].

### Operations Insights

6. **Capacity grew 8.4% in Q4 2015, with traffic rising 11.1%, lifting load factor to a Q4 record of 84.0%, driven by network expansion and increased gauge.**  
   Southwest flew 29.7 billion RPMs in Q4 2015, up from 26.8 billion in Q4 2014, while ASMs rose 8.4% to 35.4 billion. The load factor increased 2.0 points to 84.0%, a Q4 record. The average stage length increased 2.0% to 979 miles. The company flew 319,178 trips in Q4 2015, a 3.2% increase year-over-year. The company attributed growth to new service from Dallas Love Field and expansion of international routes, including new destinations in Central America and Mexico [8-K 2016-01-11; 10-K 2016-02-03].

7. **Southwest’s network continued to evolve with 20 new domestic nonstop destinations added at Dallas Love Field and expansion into Central America and Mexico.**  
   The company offered 180 daily departures to 50 nonstop destinations from Dallas Love Field by year-end 2015, enabled by the repeal of federal flight restrictions in late 2014. Southwest expanded international service to 11 destinations by end-2015, including new service to Liberia and San Jose in Costa Rica and Belize City, Belize. The opening of a new five-gate international terminal at Houston Hobby Airport supported this expansion [10-K 2016-02-03; 8-K 2015-10-22].

8. **Operational reliability improved with on-time performance increasing approximately 7 points to around 80% through November 2015 compared to 2014.**  
   Post-AirTran integration, Southwest invested in flight schedule improvements to enhance reliability, contributing to better on-time performance metrics during 2015 [10-K 2016-02-03].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

9. **Southwest’s revenue mix shifted with a \$172 million non-cash special revenue adjustment in Q3 2015 due to a change in accounting for co-branded credit card agreements, boosting “Other” revenues by 119.1% in Q4 2015.**  
   The company changed its accounting methodology effective July 1, 2015, for the sale of frequent flyer points and related items to Chase Bank under an amended co-branded credit card agreement. This accelerated revenue recognition for non-transportation elements and resulted in a \$172 million special revenue adjustment in Q3 2015 and increased other revenues by \$379 million in Q4 2015, a 119.1% increase year-over-year [8-K 2015-10-22; 10-K 2016-02-03].

10. **Load factor records in Q4 and throughout 2015 reflect strong demand for Southwest’s low-fare, customer-friendly product, including no change fees and two free checked bags.**  
    The company maintained a simple fare structure with three main fare categories and emphasized customer-friendly policies such as free checked bags and no change fees, which it believes contributed to increased market share and revenue. Marketing campaigns in 2015 reinforced these points of differentiation [10-K 2016-02-03].

### Labor Insights

11. **Profitsharing payouts surged 74.6% to a record \$620 million in 2015, reflecting strong financial performance and impacting labor costs.**  
    Salaries, wages, and benefits increased 19.4% in Q4 2015 to \$1.66 billion, driven in part by the record profitsharing payout. Labor agreements remained under negotiation with pilots and flight attendants, with ratification votes pending or ongoing into 2016 [8-K 2016-01-21; 10-K 2016-02-03].

### Wrap Up

Southwest Airlines’ fourth quarter and full-year 2015 results showed record profitability driven primarily by strong demand growth, capacity expansion, and sharply lower fuel costs. Despite a softer yield environment and flat to slightly down unit revenues, the company’s load factors hit record levels, supported by network growth including new domestic and international destinations. Operating expenses declined slightly on a unit basis excluding fuel and profitsharing, aided by fleet modernization and cost control. Profitsharing payments reached unprecedented levels, reflecting strong earnings. The company’s balance sheet remained strong with continued debt issuance and robust cash flow supporting significant shareholder returns through dividends and share repurchases. A notable accounting change in co-branded credit card revenue recognition increased other revenues and produced a special revenue adjustment in Q3 2015.

Looking ahead, Southwest expected first quarter 2016 operating unit revenues to approximate 2015 levels amid continued strong demand but softer yields. Capacity growth was projected at 5-6% for 2016, with ongoing fleet modernization and network optimization efforts. Fuel costs were expected to remain favorable assuming current market prices, although the company remained largely unhedged for Q1 2016. Labor negotiations with pilots and flight attendants continued into early 2016, representing a potential operational and cost risk. No material operational disruptions or litigation were disclosed for the period.
2015.FY:
### Financial Insights

1. **Southwest reported record annual net income of \$2.18 billion in 2015, nearly doubling 2014’s \$1.14 billion, driven by a 6.5% increase in operating revenues and a 4.1% decrease in operating expenses.** Operating revenues rose to \$19.82 billion from \$18.61 billion in 2014, with passenger revenues increasing \$641 million (3.6%) primarily due to a 7.2% capacity increase and a record annual load factor of 83.6%. Operating expenses fell to \$15.7 billion from \$16.38 billion, led by a 31.7% decline in fuel and oil costs to \$3.62 billion, partially offset by a 17.5% rise in salaries, wages, and benefits to \$6.38 billion. Operating income more than doubled to \$4.12 billion from \$2.23 billion [10-K filed 2016-02-03].

2. **Unit revenues declined in 2015 despite volume growth, with passenger revenue yield down 4.7% and passenger revenue per available seat mile (PRASM) down 2.4%, reflecting a softer yield environment.** Southwest’s passenger revenue yield per revenue passenger mile (RPM) decreased from 16.47 cents in 2014 to 15.92 cents in 2015, and PRASM fell to 13.13 cents from 13.45 cents. Meanwhile, available seat miles (ASMs) increased 7.3% to 140.5 billion and RPMs grew 8.8% to 117.5 billion, resulting in a record load factor of 83.6%, up 1.1 points from 2014 [10-K filed 2016-02-03].

3. **Fuel costs declined sharply due to lower prices and effective hedging, reducing fuel and oil expense by 31.7% year-over-year despite capacity growth.** Fuel and oil expense fell from \$5.29 billion in 2014 to \$3.62 billion in 2015. The company’s fuel efficiency improved, with available seat miles per fuel gallon consumed rising to 73.9 in 2015 from 72.8 in 2014. Fuel hedge gains and mark-to-market adjustments contributed to volatility but overall supported cost reductions [10-K filed 2016-02-03; 8-K filed 2016-01-21].

4. **Labor costs increased significantly by 17.5%, reflecting wage growth and profit-sharing payments, which rose 74.6% to \$620 million in 2015.** Salaries, wages, and benefits increased to \$6.38 billion from \$5.43 billion in 2014. The company reported record profit-sharing contributions due to exceptional financial results, paid to employees in early 2016 [8-K filed 2016-01-21; 10-K filed 2016-02-03].

5. **Southwest returned \$1.4 billion to shareholders in 2015 through \$180 million in dividends and \$1.2 billion in share repurchases, including accelerated share repurchase (ASR) programs.** The company completed a \$500 million ASR during the third quarter and planned an additional \$500 million ASR in early 2016. At year-end, \$200 million remained under the existing \$1.5 billion repurchase authorization [8-K filed 2016-01-21].

### Operations Insights

6. **Capacity grew 7.3% in 2015 with ASMs rising to 140.5 billion, supporting an 8.8% increase in RPMs to 117.5 billion and a record annual load factor of 83.6%.** The average length of haul rose 1.6% to 994 miles. Trips flown increased 0.9% to 1.27 million, and average seats per trip (gauge) increased due to slimline seat retrofits and use of larger aircraft [10-K filed 2016-02-03; 8-K monthly traffic releases].

7. **Monthly and quarterly traffic data show consistent year-over-year RPM growth ranging from 6.9% to 13.9% and ASM growth of approximately 6.7% to 9.7%, with record load factors in most months.** For example, July 2015 RPMs increased 8.2% to 11.5 billion with a load factor of 87.7%, an all-time record for July. Fourth quarter 2015 RPMs rose 11.1% with an 84.0% load factor, a quarterly record [8-K filings from May 2015 through January 2016].

8. **Southwest’s point-to-point route structure continued to expand, highlighted by new service from Dallas Love Field to eight cities starting in third quarter 2015 and international service from Houston Hobby to Mexico and Central America launched in October 2015.** The company operated 704 aircraft at year-end 2015 and planned to replace older 737-300 and 737-500 aircraft with more efficient models, expected to increase aircraft capital commitments by \$400 million beyond 2015 [10-K filed 2016-02-03; 8-K filed 2015-10-29].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

9. **Revenues benefited from an amended co-branded credit card agreement with Chase effective July 1, 2015, which changed accounting for frequent flyer points and increased operating revenues by approximately \$255 million for 2015.** The company recorded a one-time special revenue adjustment of \$172 million in the third quarter related to this change. The loyalty program continued to estimate spoilage rates based on customer behavior to recognize revenue appropriately [10-Q filed 2015-10-29; 10-K filed 2016-02-03].

10. **Southwest maintained its simple fare structure with three main fare categories and continued marketing its “Bags Fly Free®” policy and no change fees, which management attributed to increased market share and revenue.** Approximately 79.4% of 2015 passenger revenues were generated through the company’s website, reflecting a focus on direct distribution channels [10-K filed 2016-02-03].

### Labor Insights

11. **Labor negotiations showed mixed progress in 2015: the company reached tentative agreements with pilots and ramp/operations employees, but ratification failed for pilots and flight attendants, with negotiations ongoing into 2016.** Profit-sharing payments increased substantially due to record profits, reflecting strong employee financial participation [10-K filed 2016-02-03; 8-K filed 2015-07-23; 8-K filed 2016-01-21].

### Wrap Up

In 2015, Southwest Airlines achieved record profitability supported by strong capacity growth, high load factors, and notably lower fuel costs, which more than offset rising labor expenses. The company’s revenue growth was tempered by declining unit revenues, reflecting a softer pricing environment despite higher traffic. Capacity expansion included new domestic and international routes, and the fleet modernization plan increased capital commitments. Operational efficiency gains and a favorable fuel environment drove margin improvements and strong cash flow, enabling substantial shareholder returns through dividends and share repurchases. Labor negotiations remained unsettled for some groups, posing ongoing operational and labor relations considerations.

Guidance issued late in 2015 and early 2016 indicated expectations for flat to slightly down operating revenue per ASM (RASM) in the fourth quarter of 2015 and the first quarter of 2016, reflecting management’s caution amid softer yields despite continued demand growth. The company planned further share repurchases and anticipated a return to normalized market development levels in 2016 following the integration-related expansions of 2015. No material litigation, accidents, or regulatory actions were disclosed that materially affected the 2015 results.

2016.Q1:
### Financial Insights

Operating income reached a record \$944 million GAAP and \$952 million excluding special items, yielding a strong operating margin of 19.7%, up from 17.7% in 2015Q1 (calculated from \$780 million operating income on revenues of \$4,414 million) [8-K 2016-04-21; 10-Q 2016-04-29].

   Total operating revenues rose to \$4.826 billion from \$4.414 billion in 2015Q1. Passenger revenue increased to \$4.398 billion, up 5.3% from \$4.178 billion, while "Other" revenue (which includes loyalty-related and ancillary revenues) surged 101% to \$386 million from \$192 million. Freight revenue declined 4.5% to \$42 million [10-Q 2016-04-29].  

3. **Operating expenses excluding fuel and special items were essentially flat on a unit basis, while total operating expenses increased 6.8% due to volume growth and higher non-fuel costs.**

Excluding fuel and special items, operating expenses per available seat mile (ASM) increased slightly by 0.1% to 8.59 cents from 8.58 cents. Including profitsharing expense, unit costs excluding fuel and special items decreased 0.5% [10-Q 2016-04-29]. The increase in maintenance materials and repairs (+14.4%) and depreciation and amortization (+18.9%) contributed to cost growth [10-Q 2016-04-29].

   The company reported a fuel and oil expense (economic) of \$844 million, down 3.3% from \$873 million in 2015Q1, reflecting lower fuel prices despite an 8.8% increase in gallons consumed to 472 million gallons. Southwest was effectively unhedged for 2016Q1 at current price levels [10-Q 2016-04-29; 8-K 2016-01-21]. Fuel derivative contracts covered approximately 20% of 2016 fuel consumption, increasing to 62% in 2017 and 35% in 2018 [10-Q 2016-04-29]. Unrealized gains on fuel derivatives contributed \$88 million to operating cash flow in 2016Q1 [10-Q 2016-04-29].  

5. **Free cash flow was robust at \$1.2 billion in 2016Q1, supporting \$596 million returned to shareholders via dividends and share repurchases.**

The company returned \$596 million to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases, including \$500 million via an accelerated share repurchase (ASR) program launched in January 2016 [8-K 2016-04-21; 10-Q 2016-04-29].  

6. **Southwest’s balance sheet showed increased liquidity with cash and equivalents rising to \$2.388 billion and total stockholders’ equity of \$7.496 billion at quarter-end.**

### Operations Insights

   The fleet grew 5.2% from 679 aircraft at March 31, 2015. The company noted accelerated retirement of Boeing 737-300 and 737-500 models, expected to increase depreciation expense by approximately \$88 million for the remainder of 2016 [10-Q 2016-04-29]. Southwest planned modest fleet growth through 2018, not exceeding 2% annually [8-K 2016-03-08].

Management attributed flat unit revenues to softer yields despite strong demand [8-K 2016-02-05; 8-K 2016-03-08].

12. **The workforce grew 8.3% to 50,911 full-time equivalent employees, reflecting network expansion and integration activities.**  
    Employee count increased from 47,005 in 2015Q1 [10-Q 2016-04-29]. Profitsharing expense increased to \$136 million in 2015Q4 from \$100 million in 2014Q4, reflecting strong financial results [8-K 2016-01-21]. The company continued negotiations with unions, including unresolved pilot and flight attendant contracts as of early 2016 [10-K 2016-02-03].  

### Wrap Up

Southwest Airlines’ 2016 first quarter results reflected record profitability with net income rising 12.8% on a GAAP basis and 25.7% excluding special items, supported by 9.3% revenue growth and disciplined cost control. Capacity and traffic expanded by approximately 9%, with a slight load factor improvement and modest unit cost increases excluding fuel. Fuel costs declined due to lower prices despite increased consumption, although the company was effectively unhedged in the quarter, exposing it to market price volatility. The fleet grew modestly with continued modernization, and network expansion included new slots and applications for Cuba service. Revenue per ASM remained flat amid softer yields and lower average fares, with loyalty program changes contributing significantly to other revenue growth and accounting adjustments. Southwest maintained strong cash generation, returning substantial capital to shareholders. Labor headcount increased in line with growth, with ongoing labor negotiations unresolved.

**Guidance:** Management reiterated expectations that first quarter 2016 operating revenue per ASM (RASM) would be in line with first quarter 2015, reflecting stable unit revenue despite capacity growth and softer yields [8-K 2016-02-05; 8-K 2016-03-08; 8-K 2016-04-07]. The company anticipated 2016 capacity growth of 5-6% with modest fleet growth and capital expenditures around \$2.0 billion [8-K 2016-03-08]. Fuel cost savings of over \$300 million versus 2015 were forecast based on current market prices and hedging [8-K 2016-03-08]. There were no disclosed major operational disruptions, litigation, or labor strikes affecting 2016Q1 results.

The Company had \$1.97 billion in cash and equivalents as of September 30, 2016, up from \$1.58 billion at year-end 2015, and no borrowings on its new \$1 billion revolving credit facility established in August 2016 [8-K 2016-10-26; 10-Q 2016-10-31].

### Operations Insights

Lauderdale.** The Company plans to slow 2017 ASM growth to under 4.0%, with 2.0 points from domestic and 1.0-2.0 points from international growth, reflecting strategic prudence given the revenue environment and fuel cost pressures [8-K 2016-07-21; 8-K 2016-10-26].

### Route Network Insights

### Wrap Up

Southwest Airlines' third quarter 2016 results show a meaningful earnings contraction driven by a 4.1% decline in operating unit revenues and a 4.2% rise in unit costs, with a notable impact from a July technology outage that disrupted over 2,000 flights and reduced revenues by about \$55 million. Despite strong passenger demand and record load factors, average fares and yields declined nearly 5%, pressured by competitive pricing and softer close-in yields. Operating expenses rose substantially, reflecting higher labor costs including \$356 million in proposed union signing bonuses, and increased depreciation from fleet acquisitions. The Company continued its fleet modernization and network expansion, including new international routes, while moderating capacity growth to under 4% for 2017. Cash flow remained positive with solid free cash flow generation supporting shareholder returns and liquidity.

Guidance for the third quarter 2016 RASM decline remains in the 3.5%-4.5% range, with about 0.5 points attributable to the technology outage. The Company projects third quarter operating expense per ASM (excluding fuel, special items, and profitsharing) to increase 3.0%-4.0%. Fuel costs are expected near \$2.05 per gallon for 2016Q3, supported by hedges. Southwest plans to slow capacity growth in 2017, balancing growth opportunities against a soft revenue yield environment and rising fuel prices. No major operational disruptions, litigation, or regulatory actions beyond those disclosed were reported.

### Financial Insights

   Operating income for 2016 was \$3.76 billion, down 8.6% from \$4.12 billion in 2015 [8-K 2017-01-26]. The decline in Q4 operating income (down 17.5% year-over-year to \$846 million) contributed to this [8-K 2017-01-26].  
   The company returned \$1.67 billion to shareholders in 2016 through dividends and share repurchases, including \$312 million in Q3 and \$763 million in Q2 [8-K 2016-10-26; 8-K 2016-07-21].

2. **Operating revenues grew 3.1% to \$20.4 billion in 2016, driven by passenger revenue growth of 1.6%, but the revenue per available seat mile (RASM) declined in the second half of the year due to a technology outage and softer yields.**  
   Passenger revenues increased to \$18.6 billion in 2016 from \$18.3 billion in 2015, a 1.6% rise [8-K 2017-01-26]. Other operating revenues (including ancillary and cargo) grew 41.9% to \$1.66 billion, reflecting a continued focus on non-passenger revenue streams [8-K 2017-01-26].  
   Despite traffic growth, the company revised downward its RASM expectations for Q3 and Q4 2016. For Q3 2016, RASM was expected to decline 3.5-4.5% year-over-year, worsened by a 0.5 point decline due to a July 2016 technology outage causing over 2,000 flight cancellations and delays [8-K 2016-08-10; 8-K 2016-10-11].    The technology outage also increased operating expenses, with third quarter 2016 operating expenses per ASM (CASM) excluding fuel and special items estimated to rise 3.0-4.0% [8-K 2016-08-10].

3. **Operating expenses increased 6.1% to \$16.7 billion in 2016, with notable increases in salaries and benefits (+6.5%) and depreciation (+20.3%), while fuel costs were stable year-over-year.**  
   Salaries, wages, and benefits rose to \$6.8 billion from \$6.4 billion in 2015, reflecting higher staffing and profitsharing costs [8-K 2017-01-26]. Depreciation and amortization increased to \$1.22 billion, up 20.3%, consistent with investments in new aircraft and technology [8-K 2017-01-26].  
   Fuel and oil expense was \$3.65 billion, a slight increase of 0.9% over 2015, despite lower jet fuel prices, reflecting increased capacity and consumption [8-K 2017-01-26]. Southwest’s fuel hedging program contributed to volatility, with net fuel contract impacts reducing net income by \$113 million in 2016 [8-K 2017-01-26].

   Operating cash flow totaled \$4.29 billion in 2016, up from \$3.24 billion in 2015, driven by record net income [8-K 2017-01-26]. Free cash flow was \$1.2 billion in Q1 2016 alone and \$649 million in Q2 2016 [8-K 2016-04-21; 8-K 2016-07-21].  
   The company returned substantial capital to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases, including a \$500 million accelerated share repurchase program launched in 2016 [8-K 2016-01-21].  
   Capital expenditures for 2017 were expected at approximately \$2.3 billion, down from 2016 levels, reflecting deferred aircraft deliveries and a focus on fleet modernization [8-K 2017-02-15].

### Operations Insights

5. **Capacity (available seat miles) grew 5.7% in 2016 to 148.5 billion, with passenger traffic (revenue passenger miles) increasing 6.2%, leading to a load factor improvement to 84.0%.**  
   Southwest increased ASMs to 148.5 billion from 140.5 billion in 2015, driven by a 5.5% increase in revenue passengers carried to 124.7 million [8-K 2017-01-26].    Monthly load factors set records in May (85.8%), June (87.4%), September (84.2%), and November (85.1%) 2016, indicating strong operational efficiency [8-K 2016-06-08; 8-K 2016-05-09; 8-K 2016-09-07; 8-K 2016-12-07].

6. **Southwest experienced a significant operational disruption in July 2016 due to a technology outage, causing over 2,000 flight cancellations and delays, negatively impacting revenue and unit revenue metrics.**

July 2016 load factor declined slightly to 86.9% from 87.7% in July 2015, with RPM growth of only 1.4% despite a 2.3% capacity increase [8-K 2016-08-10].  
   Trips flown in July 2016 fell marginally (-0.3%) compared to July 2015 [8-K 2016-08-10]. This disruption constrained revenue growth and increased costs in Q3 2016.

8. **Southwest maintained a simple fare structure emphasizing low fares, no change fees, and free checked bags, with marketing campaigns reinforcing these points of differentiation to support market share gains.**

Southwest’s fare categories include “Wanna Get Away®,” “AnytimeSM,” and “Business Select®” to simplify customer choices [10-K 2016-02-03].  
   Other operating revenues increased 41.9% in 2016, reflecting ancillary services and cargo [8-K 2017-01-26]. The Rapid Rewards frequent flyer program received industry recognition, supporting customer loyalty [8-K 2016-07-21].

### Route Network Insights

9. **Southwest’s point-to-point route network continued to expand prudently with focus on domestic markets and select near-international destinations, including new service from Long Beach, CA, and incremental international expansion into Mexico and the Caribbean.**  
   Capacity growth in 2016 was 5-6%, with plans to slow growth in 2017 and 2018 to maintain strong margins [8-K 2016-06-23]. The company opened its 98th city, Long Beach, California, in Q2 2016 [8-K 2016-07-21].  
   Southwest expanded in U.S.-Mexico markets and sought additional international authority, including to Cuba and Canada [8-K 2016-06-23]. The fleet’s 737 range supports these near-international markets [8-K 2016-06-23].  
   Southwest’s point-to-point strategy contrasts with hub-and-spoke models, allowing more nonstop routing and operational flexibility [10-K 2016-02-03].

### Labor Insights

    No labor disputes, strikes, or contract renegotiations materially affecting 2016 results were disclosed.

### Wrap Up

Southwest Airlines’ 2016 fiscal year was marked by record annual profitability of \$2.24 billion on a 3.1% revenue increase and 5.7% capacity growth. The company balanced rising operating costs, particularly labor and depreciation, against stable fuel expenses and strong cash flow generation. Operationally, Southwest’s point-to-point network and fleet modernization contributed to improved load factors and passenger growth, although a July technology outage disrupted Q3 results and pressured unit revenues. The airline moderated capacity growth for 2017 and deferred capital spending, reflecting a cautious stance amid softer yields and revenue per ASM declines in the latter half of 2016. Marketing efforts emphasized Southwest’s low-fare, no-fee value proposition, supporting market share gains and ancillary revenue growth. Labor costs rose in line with expansion and profitsharing, but no material labor disruptions were reported.

Guidance for early 2017 projected a slight decline in RASM (flat to down 1% in Q1 2017) and capacity growth of about 3.5%, with capital expenditures expected to fall below 2016 levels around \$2.3 billion [8-K 2017-02-15]. The company flagged ongoing risks from demand variability, competitive pressures, and technology reliability, underscoring the operational challenges behind its financial results. No material accidents, regulatory actions, or litigation developments affecting 2016 were disclosed.

Southwest Airlines’ first quarter 2017 results reflect a complex interplay of modest revenue growth in absolute terms but declining unit revenues amid a competitive fare environment and higher fuel and labor costs. Fleet modernization continued with new 737 deliveries and accelerated retirements of older aircraft, supporting efficiency gains. The launch of a new reservation system and network expansions, including new international destinations, underscore strategic investments to support longer-term growth. Labor cost increases from recently ratified contracts contributed to expense inflation but are expected to moderate later in the year. 2. **Operating expenses rose 9.4%, driven by higher labor and fuel costs.** Salaries, wages, and benefits increased 13.9% to \$1.87 billion; fuel and oil expense rose 9.6% to \$990 million; maintenance materials and repairs declined 10.4% to \$251 million; aircraft rentals decreased 10.2% to \$53 million; landing fees and other rentals increased 7.4% to \$332 million; depreciation and amortization grew 6.7% to \$319 million; other operating expenses were up 10.2% to \$682 million [10-Q 2017-05-03, 8-K 2017-07-27].

3. **Excluding fuel, special items, and profitsharing, unit costs increased 5.3% year-over-year, mostly due to wage rate increases from new labor agreements.** The company reported that approximately two-thirds of the unit cost increase was attributable to wage rate increases effective in Q4 2016 from amended collective bargaining agreements with Flight Attendants and Pilots [8-K 2017-07-27].

4. **Fuel costs per gallon increased to an estimated \$1.95-\$2.00 in Q2 2017, up from \$1.78 in Q2 2016, reflecting market prices and hedging effects.** Economic fuel costs (including fuel derivative settlements) were \$1.96 per gallon in Q1 2017, with Q2 2017 expected in the \$1.95-\$2.00 range [8-K 2017-06-07, 8-K 2017-04-27].

5. **Operating cash flow for Q2 2017 was \$746 million, with free cash flow of \$195 million, returning \$476 million to shareholders via dividends and share repurchases.** Year-to-date free cash flow was strong, though cash and cash equivalents declined to \$1.54 billion at June 30, 2017, from \$1.85 billion at March 31, 2017, reflecting capital expenditures and shareholder returns [8-K 2017-07-27].

6. **Return on invested capital (ROIC) for the 12 months ended June 30, 2017, was 27.5%, slightly below 27.7% for the 12 months ended March 31, 2017.** This indicates a modest decline in capital efficiency year-over-year [8-K 2017-07-27, 8-K 2017-04-27].

7. **The company expects 2017 capital expenditures of approximately \$2.3 billion and ASM growth of about 3.5% year-over-year with domestic growth accounting for 2.5 points.** For 2018, ASM growth is expected to be below 5.7% (2016 growth rate) and below 4% in the first half [8-K 2017-06-07].

### Operations Insights

8. **Capacity and traffic grew about 5.1% year-over-year in Q2 2017, with load factor stable at 85.6%.** Available seat miles (ASMs) increased from 38.2 billion to 40.2 billion; revenue passenger miles (RPMs) rose from 32.7 billion to 34.4 billion; trips flown grew 4.0% to 347,827; and seats per trip (gauge) increased 1.1% to 148.53. Average length of haul remained steady at 1,011 miles [8-K 2017-07-10, 8-K 2017-07-27].

9. **Load factor remained flat at 85.6% year-over-year for Q2 2017, reflecting balanced demand and capacity growth.** This was a quarterly record load factor for the company [8-K 2017-07-27].

10. **Fuel consumption increased 3.2% to 487 million gallons in Q1 2017, consistent with capacity growth and higher fuel prices.** Economic fuel cost per gallon rose 10.1% year-over-year in Q1 2017 to \$1.96 [10-Q 2017-05-03].

11. **Fleet size increased modestly to 727 aircraft at quarter-end, up 1.8% from 714 at June 30, 2016.** The company took delivery of nine new Boeing 737-800s and three pre-owned 737-700s during Q1 2017, with firm orders and options for additional 737 MAX and 737-800 aircraft scheduled for delivery through 2027 [8-K 2017-07-27, 8-K 2017-04-27].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

12. **Passenger revenue yield increased 1.5% year-over-year in Q2 2017, reversing prior declines and contributing to 1.5% RASM growth despite competitive fare environment and a transition to a new reservation system.** The reservation system transition caused less than one point of temporary unit revenue pressure, with adjustments expected by year-end [8-K 2017-07-27].

13. **Passenger revenue per ASM (PRASM) and operating revenue per ASM (RASM) increased about 1.5% in Q2 2017, following a 2.8% unit revenue decline in Q1 2017.** The improvement was attributed to stronger bookings and yield trends [8-K 2017-07-27, 8-K 2017-04-27].

14. **Southwest expanded international service with filings for new routes and launched service to Mexico and the Caribbean, including plans to serve Providenciales, Turks & Caicos, and Grand Cayman.** The company also consolidated Ohio operations and launched service to Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport in June 2017 [8-K 2017-04-27].

### Labor Insights

15. **Labor costs increased notably, with wage rate increases from amended collective bargaining agreements becoming effective in Q4 2016 driving about two-thirds of the 5.3% unit cost increase excluding fuel and special items.** Profitsharing expense was \$202 million in Q2 2017, slightly below the \$206 million record in Q2 2016 [8-K 2017-07-27].

16. **Active full-time equivalent employees increased 7.3% year-over-year to 54,652 at March 31, 2017, supporting network and capacity growth.** This reflects ongoing hiring aligned with operational expansion [10-Q 2017-05-03].

### Route Network Insights

17. **Southwest grew capacity approximately 5.1% in Q2 2017 and continued network optimization by adding new markets and pruning less profitable flights.** The company planned to grow ASMs about 3.5% for full-year 2017, with less aggressive growth expected in 2018 [8-K 2017-06-07, 8-K 2017-04-27].

18. **The airline pursued international expansion with new gateways in California and the Caribbean, including four gateways in California and new service to San Jose del Cabo/Los Cabos, Mexico.** The company filed for authority to serve Providenciales, Turks & Caicos from Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport starting in Q4 2017 [8-K 2017-04-27].

### Wrap Up

Southwest Airlines' second quarter 2017 performance showed revenue growth driven by higher passenger volumes and improving yields, with unit revenue growth reversing earlier declines despite a challenging fare environment and a new reservation system rollout. Capacity expansion of roughly 5% was matched by stable load factors, while labor cost increases from recent collective bargaining agreements contributed to rising unit costs excluding fuel. Fuel costs were elevated compared to prior year, consistent with market prices and hedging outcomes. The company generated positive free cash flow and returned \$476 million to shareholders in the quarter, while maintaining a strong ROIC above 27%. Network expansion continued with targeted international growth and domestic optimization, while fleet additions supported capacity increases.

Guidance for full-year 2017 included approximately 3.5% ASM growth, capital expenditures near \$2.3 billion, and expected unit cost increases of about 6% in Q2 (excluding fuel, profitsharing, and special items), with cost inflation anticipated to moderate in the second half of the year. Fuel economic costs were forecast in the \$1.95-\$2.00 per gallon range for Q2 and full year 2017 based on derivative contracts and market prices as of early June. No material operational disruptions, labor disputes, or regulatory issues were disclosed for the quarter.

### Financial Insights

1. **Third quarter 2017 operating income rose 20% year-over-year to \$834 million, but operating margin declined to 15.8% from 18.1% in 2016 due to revenue pressures and cost increases.**  
   Southwest reported third quarter 2017 operating income of \$834 million, up from \$695 million in Q3 2016, representing a 20% increase. However, operating margin fell to 15.8% from 21.8% in the prior year quarter when excluding special items. Net income attributable to shareholders was \$503 million, up 29.6% from \$388 million in Q3 2016, with diluted EPS of \$0.84 compared to \$0.62. Excluding special items, net income was \$528 million and diluted EPS was \$0.88, down 9.3% from \$0.93 in 2016 Q3 [8-K filed 2017-10-26].

2. **Operating revenues increased modestly by 2.6% year-over-year to \$5.27 billion, driven by a 1.6% rise in passenger revenue, but unit revenues (RASM) declined 0.5%.**  
   Passenger operating revenues grew to \$4.75 billion from \$4.67 billion in Q3 2016, a 1.6% increase. Other operating revenues increased 13.1%, partly offsetting weaker passenger unit revenues. Operating revenue per available seat mile (RASM) decreased 0.5% compared to the prior year. The revenue yield per revenue passenger mile (RPM) fell 0.9% to 14.32 cents [8-K filed 2017-10-26].

3. **Operating expenses were essentially flat (-0.2%) year-over-year at \$4.44 billion, but unit costs (CASM) declined 3.2%, reflecting capacity growth.**  
   Total operating expenses of \$4.44 billion were stable versus \$4.44 billion in Q3 2016. On a per available seat mile (ASM) basis, CASM declined 3.2% due to a 3.1% increase in ASMs. Fuel and oil expenses increased 6.6% to \$1.0 billion, driven by higher fuel prices and consumption, while salaries, wages, and benefits fell 6.0% to \$1.80 billion [8-K filed 2017-10-26].

4. **Fuel costs per gallon increased 6.6% to \$1.93 (economic cost including hedges), with fuel consumption up 4.3%, partially offset by fuel hedging gains.**  
   Economic fuel costs per gallon rose to \$1.93 from \$1.81 in Q3 2016. Fuel consumption increased 4.3% due to capacity growth. The company’s fuel hedging program generated gains that partially mitigated price increases, but the net impact on fuel expense was still a 6.6% increase [8-K filed 2017-10-26; 10-Q filed 2017-08-01].

5. **Cash flow from operations remained strong, supporting capital expenditures of approximately \$1.6 billion year-to-date and enabling \$1.5 billion returned to shareholders via dividends and share repurchases.**  
   Through 9 months 2017, operating cash flow was about \$3.4 billion, capital expenditures were \$1.6 billion, and free cash flow was \$1.8 billion. The company returned \$274 million in dividends and repurchased approximately \$1.25 billion in stock during the period, indicating significant cash generation capacity [8-K filed 2017-10-26].

### Operations Insights

6. **Third quarter 2017 capacity (ASMs) increased 3.1% year-over-year, while traffic (RPMs) grew 2.5%, causing a 0.5 point decline in load factor to 84.8%.**  
   The airline operated 39.1 billion ASMs in Q3 2017, up from 37.9 billion in Q3 2016. Revenue passenger miles rose 2.5% to 33.1 billion. Load factor decreased slightly to 84.8% from 85.3%, reflecting capacity growth outpacing demand. Average length of haul shortened 1.4% to 1,003 miles [8-K filed 2017-10-26].

7. **September 2017 alone saw a 1.6% decrease in ASMs and a 4.5% decrease in RPMs versus September 2016, with load factor falling 2.5 points to 81.7%, primarily due to Hurricane Harvey disruptions.**  
   Southwest canceled approximately 2,800 flights in Q3 and about 5,000 flights through September 27 due to Hurricane Harvey and other natural disasters. The company estimated a \$100 million negative impact on operating revenues for Q3 2017 from these events. The disruptions contributed to a September load factor decline and lower yields [8-K filed 2017-09-06; 8-K filed 2017-10-06].

8. **Fleet grew modestly to 687 aircraft by end of Q3 2017, including deliveries of 6 new Boeing 737-800s, 6 pre-owned 737-700s, and 9 new 737 MAX 8s; retirement of the 737-300 Classic fleet was completed.**  
   The company planned to end 2017 with 707 aircraft and 2018 with 750. The introduction of the 737 MAX 8 supports network expansion, including new routes and international gateways starting in 2018, and the planned launch of service to Hawaii [8-K filed 2017-10-26].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

9. **Unit revenue (RASM) declined 0.5% in Q3 2017, including a headwind from the new reservation system and competitive pressures exacerbated by natural disasters.**  
   Management attributed the slight decline in RASM partly to a less than one-point temporary impact from the transition to a new reservation system, which is expected to be largely resolved by end of 2017. Additionally, weakness in passenger revenue yields was driven by the industry revenue environment and Hurricane Harvey's effects [8-K filed 2017-09-06; 8-K filed 2017-10-26].

10. **Southwest continued investing in network expansion with nearly 20 new nonstop routes and increased frequencies on 27 routes in California, plus plans to sell tickets for Hawaii service in 2018.**  
    These network initiatives indicate a strategic focus on growth in key markets and new international gateways, supported by the new 737 MAX 8 aircraft. The company also announced plans to pursue ETOPS certification, which allows extended overwater flights, required for Hawaii service [8-K filed 2017-10-26].

### Labor Insights

11. **Salaries, wages, and benefits expense decreased 6.0% in Q3 2017 despite a 5.8% increase in full-time equivalent employees year-over-year, reflecting timing of profitsharing and contract bonuses.**  
    The decline in labor expense contrasts with prior quarters where wage increases from amended collective bargaining agreements drove costs higher. The company recorded \$63 million in aircraft grounding charges related to operational disruptions, which may have influenced labor cost patterns [8-K filed 2017-10-26; 10-Q filed 2017-08-01].

### Route Network Insights

12. **Capacity growth moderated in Q3 2017 to 3.1%, down from 5.1% in Q2, with management projecting 1-2% growth for Q4 and less than 5.7% growth for full-year 2018 capacity.**  
    The company’s cautious capacity expansion reflects adjustments to market conditions and operational disruptions. The addition of new routes and aircraft deliveries aligns with this measured growth strategy [8-K filed 2017-09-06; 8-K filed 2017-10-26].

### Wrap Up

Southwest Airlines’ third quarter 2017 results show a mixed operational and financial picture influenced by natural disasters, a new reservation system rollout, and competitive pressures on unit revenues. While operating income grew 20% year-over-year, operating margin declined due to flat revenue per ASM and rising fuel costs. Capacity increased moderately, but Hurricane Harvey caused significant flight cancellations and revenue losses estimated at \$100 million for Q3, contributing to a September load factor decline. The company continued fleet modernization with new Boeing 737 MAX 8 deliveries and completed retirement of older aircraft, supporting network expansion initiatives, including planned Hawaii service.

Management’s outlook reflects cautious revenue expectations with RASM flat to down 1% in Q3 and a modest capacity increase forecast for Q4 and 2018. The company maintained strong cash flow generation, enabling substantial shareholder returns through dividends and share repurchases. Labor costs showed signs of moderation after prior contract-driven increases, though operational disruption expenses appeared. Southwest’s fuel hedging program partially offset rising fuel prices, which remain a key cost factor. No material litigation, accidents, or labor disputes were disclosed impacting the quarter. The company’s financial and operational disclosures highlight the balancing act between growth investments, operational challenges, and a competitive revenue environment in late 2017.
2017.Q4:
### Financial Insights

1. **Southwest reported record fourth quarter and annual 2017 net income, driven by strong revenue growth and solid operating margins.**  
   For Q4 2017, Southwest reported net income of \$1.9 billion and diluted EPS of \$3.18, with net income excluding special items of \$459 million or \$0.77 per share [8-K 2018-01-25]. For the full year 2017, net income was \$3.5 billion, or \$5.79 per diluted share, with net income excluding special items at \$2.1 billion, or \$3.50 per diluted share [8-K 2018-01-25]. Operating income for 2017 was \$3.5 billion, yielding an operating margin of 16.6% (16.3% excluding special items). Annual operating revenues increased 3.7% year-over-year to a record \$21.2 billion, supported by a 0.1% increase in operating revenue per available seat mile (RASM) [8-K 2018-01-25].  

2. **Operating expenses rose 6.4% in Q4 2017, with unit costs increasing 4.3%, largely due to higher fuel and labor costs, partially offset by efficiency gains.**  
   Total operating expenses in Q4 2017 were \$4.5 billion, up 6.4% from Q4 2016, and operating expenses per available seat mile (CASM) increased 4.3% [8-K 2018-01-25]. Excluding special items related to fuel hedge derivative contracts, expenses increased 5.1% and unit costs rose 3.0% year-over-year. Economic fuel cost was \$2.09 per gallon in Q4 2017, slightly higher than \$2.07 in Q4 2016, including unfavorable cash settlements from fuel derivatives of \$0.19 per gallon versus \$0.50 in Q4 2016 [8-K 2018-01-25]. Salaries, wages, and benefits increased due to a \$1,000 cash bonus to employees related to tax reform and ongoing labor negotiations, which added approximately \$70 million in Q4 expenses [8-K 2018-01-02].  

3. **Free cash flow remained strong at \$1.8 billion for 2017, supporting \$1.9 billion returned to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases.**  
   Operating cash flow for 2017 was \$3.9 billion, with free cash flow of \$1.8 billion [8-K 2018-01-25]. The company returned \$274 million in dividends and \$1.6 billion in share repurchases during the year [8-K 2018-01-25]. As of December 31, 2017, cash and cash equivalents stood at \$1.5 billion [10-K 2018-02-07].  

4. **The adoption of new accounting standards in 2018 led to a \$1.4 billion reduction in deferred tax liabilities and a significant increase in loyalty program liabilities by \$1.1 billion.**  
   The company adopted ASU 2014-09 (Revenue from Contracts with Customers), ASU 2017-07 (Compensation—Retirement Benefits), and ASU 2017-12 (Derivatives and Hedging) effective January 1, 2018, which required restatement of 2017 and 2016 financials [8-K 2018-03-21]. The new revenue standard caused a \$1.1 billion increase in loyalty program liabilities due to a change to the relative fair value approach for customer flight points [8-K 2018-03-21]. The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act enacted in December 2017 led to a \$1.4 billion deferred tax liability reduction and a \$1.27 billion tax expense reduction for 2017 [8-K 2018-01-25].  

### Operations Insights

5. **Capacity grew modestly in Q4 2017 with a 2.0% increase in available seat miles (ASMs), while load factor reached a record 85.0% for the quarter.**  
   Q4 2017 ASMs increased 2.0% to 37.9 billion from 37.1 billion in Q4 2016. Revenue passenger miles (RPMs) rose 2.6% to 32.2 billion, and load factor improved by 0.6 points to 85.0% [8-K 2018-01-25]. Despite a 2.6% decrease in average length of haul to 955 miles, trips flown increased 2.3% to 337,190 [8-K 2018-01-25].  

6. **Monthly traffic data in Q4 showed steady growth in RPMs and load factors, with December 2017 load factor at 83.3%, a record for the month.**  
   December 2017 RPMs were 10.7 billion, up 2.6% from December 2016, with ASMs up 1.8% to 12.9 billion and load factor increasing 0.7 points to 83.3% [8-K 2018-01-09]. November and October 2017 also showed year-over-year RPM increases of 3.4% and 1.9%, respectively, with load factors at record highs for November (85.8%) and stable for October (85.8%) [8-K 2017-12-07, 8-K 2017-11-08].  

7. **Fleet modernization advanced with retirement of Boeing 737-300 aircraft and introduction of Boeing 737 MAX 8, contributing to expected fuel efficiency gains.**  
   In 2017, Southwest retired all Boeing 737-300 Classic aircraft and became the first North American airline to operate scheduled service with the Boeing 737 MAX 8 [10-K 2018-02-07]. The company expects 2018 available seat mile growth in the low 5% range, with fuel efficiency improvements of 2-3% driven by the newer, more fuel-efficient aircraft and retirement of older models [8-K 2018-01-25].  

### Commercial Strategy Insights

8. **Passenger revenue per ASM (PRASM) declined slightly in Q4 2017, reflecting competitive pricing and yield pressure despite higher load factors.**  
   Passenger revenue yield per revenue passenger mile (RPM) decreased 0.9% year-over-year in Q3 2017 and Q4 was expected to see a 0.1% decrease in passenger revenue yield despite record load factors [10-Q 2017-11-01, 8-K 2018-01-25]. Management attributed the modest yield pressure to competitive fare environment and transitional impacts from the new reservation system implemented in 2017 [8-K 2017-10-26].  

9. **Southwest continued to differentiate itself by maintaining a no-fee policy on checked bags, flight changes, and seat selection, though facing increased competition from ultra-low-cost carriers (ULCCs).**  
   The company highlighted its competitive positioning through its policy of no fees for first and second checked bags, flight changes, seat selection, snacks, and other services, which it believes differentiates it from competitors, including ULCCs [10-K 2018-02-07]. However, ULCCs have surpassed Southwest’s cost advantage with larger gauge aircraft, increased seat density, and lower wages, making it increasingly difficult for Southwest to improve its cost position [10-K 2018-02-07].  

10. **The company invested in technology with the deployment of a new single reservation system in 2017, expected to yield approximately \$200 million in incremental pre-tax benefits in 2018.**  
    The new reservation system was the largest technology project in company history, designed to improve scheduling, inventory management, revenue enhancements, and support international growth [10-K 2018-02-07]. The system caused some headwinds to unit revenues in Q3 2017 but is expected to improve financial results going forward [8-K 2017-10-26].  

### Labor Insights

11. **Labor costs increased in Q4 2017 due in part to a \$1,000 cash bonus to employees celebrating tax reform and additional costs from ongoing labor negotiations.**  
    The company recorded approximately \$70 million in incremental salaries, wages, and benefits expense in Q4 2017 related to the \$1,000 cash bonus approved in December 2017 and paid in January 2018 [8-K 2018-01-02]. Additional unplanned labor costs related to ongoing negotiations also contributed to higher expenses [8-K 2018-01-02].  

### Route Network Insights

12. **Southwest expanded its international footprint in 2017, adding service to Grand Cayman and Turks and Caicos, and planned further international growth in 2018.**  
    The airline operated 706 Boeing 737s serving 100 destinations including 14 international destinations through 16 gateway cities in the continental U.S. [10-K 2018-02-07]. It opened a new five-gate international concourse at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport to support near-international operations [10-K 2018-02-07]. The company announced plans to begin selling tickets in 2018 for service to Hawaii and to apply for FAA authorization for Extended Operations (ETOPS), enabling longer overwater flights [8-K 2017-10-26, 8-K 2018-01-25]. Southwest’s point-to-point route structure served 675 nonstop city pairs as of December 31, 2017 [10-K 2018-02-07].  

### Wrap Up

Southwest Airlines’ 2017 fourth quarter and full-year results reflect record profitability supported by modest capacity growth, strong load factors, and disciplined cost control despite higher fuel and labor expenses. The company’s operating margin remained robust at about 16.6%, while unit revenues faced modest pressure from competitive pricing and a new reservation system transition. Fleet modernization through retirement of older aircraft and introduction of the 737 MAX 8 contributes to incremental fuel efficiency gains expected in 2018. Southwest’s labor costs rose due to a one-time employee bonus and ongoing negotiations. Commercially, the airline continued to emphasize its no-fee policy and expanded its international network, preparing for further growth including service to Hawaii pending regulatory approval.  

Management’s adoption of new accounting standards and the impact of U.S. tax reform materially affected reported tax liabilities and loyalty program accounting in the quarter. Strong cash flow generation enabled substantial shareholder returns through dividends and stock buybacks. The company guided to modest RASM growth and stable ex-fuel unit costs for Q1 2018 but noted some near-term pressure from fleet retirements and competitive fare environments. No material operational disruptions or litigation developments were disclosed for the period.

In 2017, Southwest Airlines sustained its 45th consecutive year of profitability with record net income of \$3.5 billion despite margin pressures from rising fuel costs and wage inflation. Southwest Airlines’ 2018 second quarter results featured record net income and strong operating cash flow generation despite unit revenue pressures linked to the April Flight 1380 accident and a suboptimal schedule following accelerated retirement of older aircraft. Capacity grew modestly, but load factors and yields declined, pressing unit revenues down about 3%. Operating costs rose notably due to higher fuel prices and wage inflation, lifting unit costs by over 2%. The company continued fleet modernization with deliveries of newer, more efficient 737-800 and 737 MAX 8 aircraft, supporting fuel efficiency gains. Management lowered 2018 capacity growth guidance to the low 4% range and expects revenue unit trends to improve in the second half. ### Wrap Up

Southwest Airlines’ 2018 fourth quarter and full year results showed a notable earnings decline versus strong 2017 comparables, primarily due to the absence of one-time tax benefits and higher fuel costs. Despite this, the company delivered record operating cash flow and free cash flow, supporting substantial shareholder returns through share buybacks and dividends. Revenue growth was driven by capacity increases and yield improvements but was partly offset by declining load factors amid aggressive capacity growth. Fuel cost increases materially pressured operating expenses, though fleet modernization contributed to modest fuel efficiency gains.

Operationally, Southwest continued expanding its network with new international gateways and planned Hawaiian service, maintaining its point-to-point model with high-frequency short-haul routes complemented by longer nonstop flights. The company’s commercial strategy emphasized revenue management improvements and loyalty program growth, alongside its longstanding no bag fees and no change fees policies. Labor costs rose with profitsharing reflecting strong employee participation in profits. The company maintained a strong liquidity position and an investment-grade balance sheet heading into 2019.

**Guidance overview:** For the fourth quarter 2018, Southwest expected RASM growth of 1-2% year-over-year and CASM (excluding fuel and profitsharing) to be flat to up 1%. Fuel costs were guided in the range of \$2.25 to \$2.30 per gallon. For 2019, the company planned capacity growth of no more than 5%, with first quarter capacity growth guidance at 3.5-4%. Subsequent 2019 guidance (post-2018) noted disruptions and capacity growth revisions due to labor negotiations and Boeing 737 MAX groundings [8-K filed 2018-12-12; 8-K filed 2019-01-24; 8-K filed 2019-03-27].

For the full year 2019, total operating revenues increased 2.1% to \$22.43 billion on 1.6% lower available seat miles (ASMs) due to the MAX grounding [8-K 2020-01-23; 10-K 2020-02-04].

3. **Operating expenses rose 3.7% in Q4 2019 to \$5.06 billion, driven by a 12.9% increase in salaries, wages, and benefits, partially offset by a 7.3% decrease in fuel and oil costs.**  
   Salaries, wages, and benefits increased to \$2.25 billion from \$1.99 billion, reflecting wage inflation and profitsharing expenses. Fuel and oil expense decreased to \$1.11 billion from \$1.19 billion, helped by lower market jet fuel prices and fuel hedging [8-K 2020-01-23]. Maintenance materials and repairs rose 5.1% to \$307 million. Total operating expenses per ASM (CASM) increased 4.6% in Q4 2019 compared with Q4 2018 [8-K 2019-12-17].

4. **Operating income declined 18.9% in Q4 2019 to \$665 million due to higher unit costs and capacity reductions from MAX groundings.**  
   Operating income fell from \$820 million in Q4 2018 to \$665 million in Q4 2019. The capacity decline and associated fixed costs contributed to unit cost pressures, with CASM excluding fuel and profitsharing expected to increase 6-8% year-over-year in Q1 2020 [8-K 2020-01-23; 8-K 2019-12-17].

5. **Southwest returned \$596 million to shareholders in Q3 2019 through dividends and share repurchases and repurchased \$2 billion of stock during 2019.**  
   The company completed \$2 billion in share repurchases authorized in 2019 and paid \$377 million in dividends for the year. Treasury stock cost increased from \$8.45 billion at year-end 2018 to \$10.44 billion at year-end 2019, reflecting repurchases [8-K 2019-10-24; 10-K 2020-02-04].

6. **Liquidity improved with cash and equivalents rising to \$2.55 billion at year-end 2019, up from \$1.85 billion at the end of 2018, despite \$2.99 billion used in financing activities for share repurchases and debt repayments.**  
   Operating cash flow for 2019 was \$2.96 billion, down from \$3.16 billion in 2018, while capital expenditures were \$1.22 billion [10-K 2020-02-04; 8-K 2019-10-24].

### Operations Insights

7. **Capacity (ASMs) declined 0.9% in Q4 2019 and 1.6% for the full year due to Boeing 737 MAX groundings, reducing the fleet’s most fuel-efficient aircraft availability.**  
   Southwest flew 40.0 billion ASMs in Q4 2019 versus 40.4 billion in Q4 2018. For 2019, ASMs decreased to 157.3 billion from 159.8 billion in 2018. The MAX grounding forced removal of 34 MAX aircraft from schedules and delayed 41 MAX deliveries originally planned for 2019 [10-K 2020-02-04; 10-Q 2019-11-08].

8. **Revenue passenger miles (RPMs) decreased 1.5% year-over-year in Q4 2019 and for the full year, reflecting lower capacity and a slight load factor decline.**  
   Q4 2019 RPMs were 33.2 billion compared to 33.7 billion in Q4 2018; annual RPMs were 131.3 billion versus 133.3 billion in 2018. Load factor fell 0.4 points in Q4 to 83.1% but was flat year-over-year at 83.5% for 2019 [8-K 2020-01-23; 10-K 2020-02-04].

9. **Average stage length decreased slightly to 755 miles in Q4 2019 from 754 miles in Q4 2018, consistent with Southwest’s point-to-point network and recent expansion into Hawaii.**  
   The Company began service to five Hawaiian airports in 2019-2020, starting with four in 2019 after receiving FAA ETOPS approval, adding Honolulu, Kahului, Kona, and Lihue, with Hilo service beginning January 2020 [10-K 2020-02-04].

10. **Fleet size remained steady at 747 Boeing 737 aircraft at year-end 2019, comprising 506 737-700s, 207 737-800s, and 34 grounded 737 MAX 8s.**  
    The average age was 12 years. Owned aircraft totaled 625, with 122 leased (52 operating leases and 70 finance leases) [10-K 2020-02-04].

11. **Fuel efficiency declined 1-2% in Q4 2019 due to the removal of MAX aircraft, with fuel costs per gallon averaging \$2.09 compared to \$2.20 in Q4 2018.**  
    Fuel consumption was 2.08 billion gallons for Q4 2019. Fuel derivative contracts helped reduce volatility, with premiums of about \$0.04 per gallon and no cash settlements in the quarter [8-K 2019-12-17; 10-K 2020-02-04].

### Labor Insights

12. **Salaries, wages, and benefits increased 12.9% in Q4 2019 and 8.4% for the full year, reflecting wage inflation, profitsharing awards, and investments in technology and facilities.**  
    The company employed approximately 60,767 full-time equivalent employees at year-end 2019, up from 58,803 at the end of 2018 [10-K 2020-02-04; 8-K 2020-01-23].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

13. **Passenger revenue yield increased 3.1% in 2019, driven by higher average fares and modest load factor gains, supporting a 3.7% increase in unit revenues (RASM).**  
    The Company’s 2019 RASM reached a record 14.26 cents, helped by capacity discipline from the MAX groundings and revenue management improvements implemented in 2018. Q4 2019 RASM benefited from the removal of MAX flights but was offset by schedule adjustments for uniformity during the peak holiday period [10-K 2020-02-04; 8-K 2020-01-23].

14. **Southwest expanded its corporate travel business through agreements with Amadeus and Travelport global distribution systems to increase booking access for corporate customers and travel managers.**  
    The Company also enhanced its SWABIZ online booking tool for business customers and improved digital platforms including Southwest.com and mobile apps to facilitate management of travel funds and reservations [10-K 2020-02-04].

15. **Loyalty program revenues increased, with approximately 10.4 million flight awards redeemed in 2019, representing 13.8% of revenue passenger miles flown.**  
    The Company recognized \$2.49 billion in passenger loyalty air transportation revenues in 2019, up from \$2.31 billion in 2018 [10-K 2020-02-04].

### Route Network Insights

16. **Southwest served 101 destinations as of December 31, 2019, including 25 international gateway cities and 13 international destinations in Mexico, the Caribbean, Central America, and the Bahamas.**  
    The Company’s point-to-point network supported 720 nonstop city pairs in 2019, with 77% of customers flying nonstop. The addition of Hawaii service marked a notable network expansion [10-K 2020-02-04].

17. **The MAX grounding disrupted fleet deployment and capacity plans, resulting in a 1.6% capacity reduction in 2019 and removal of MAX flights through at least June 6, 2020.**  
    Southwest canceled approximately 3,000 flights in Q4 2019 due primarily to winter weather, with the MAX grounding being the primary driver of capacity shortfall and associated revenue loss [10-K 2020-02-04; 8-K 2019-12-17].

### Wrap Up

For the fourth quarter and full year 2019, Southwest Airlines reported continued profitability with record revenues but faced headwinds from the Boeing 737 MAX groundings that constrained capacity by about 1.6% annually. This capacity reduction contributed to lower total passenger miles flown and pressured unit costs, which rose sharply despite lower fuel prices. Revenue per available seat mile (RASM) increased modestly due to higher fares and disciplined capacity management, but operating income and net income declined year-over-year, impacted by profitsharing payments related to the Boeing compensation and the operational challenges of the MAX grounding.

Southwest maintained a stable fleet of 747 Boeing 737 aircraft, including 34 grounded MAX 8s, and expanded its network notably into Hawaii and near-international markets. The company continued to invest in its corporate travel business and digital platforms, while labor costs increased in line with wage inflation and profitsharing. Liquidity improved, with cash balances rising despite significant share repurchases totaling \$2 billion in 2019. The MAX grounding remained the principal operational and financial risk, with removal of MAX flights scheduled through at least mid-2020, constraining capacity and pressuring unit costs.

**Guidance and Outlook:**  
Southwest expected first quarter 2020 RASM growth in the range of 3.5% to 5.5%, including a capacity-related benefit from the MAX groundings, but also anticipated a 6% to 8% increase in CASM (excluding fuel and profitsharing), reflecting ongoing unit cost pressures from lower capacity and inflationary factors [8-K 2020-01-23]. The timing of the MAX return to service remained uncertain, subject to FAA regulatory approvals and Boeing’s progress, with potential for further schedule adjustments and financial impacts.
2019.FY:
### Financial Insights

1. **Southwest Airlines reported a modest 2019 revenue increase but a decline in net income and operating margin due to multiple operational headwinds.**  
   For the full year ended December 31, 2019, operating revenues rose 2.1% to \$22.4 billion from \$22.0 billion in 2018, driven by a 1.6% increase in passenger revenues to \$20.8 billion. However, net income declined 6.7% to \$2.3 billion from \$2.5 billion in 2018, and operating income fell 7.8% to \$3.0 billion from \$3.2 billion, resulting in a reduced operating margin of approximately 13.2% (calculated from \$2.957B operating income on \$22.428B revenues) compared to 14.6% in 2018. Management attributed this margin compression primarily to unit cost pressures following the Boeing 737 MAX groundings and other disruptions [10-K filed 2020-02-04; 8-K filed 2019-10-24].

2. **Earnings per share declined 0.5% to \$4.27 diluted in 2019 from \$4.29 in 2018, influenced by lower net income and share repurchases reducing share count.**  
   Diluted shares outstanding decreased by approximately 6.1%, from 574 million in 2018 to 539 million in 2019, reflecting ongoing share repurchases [10-K filed 2020-02-04; 8-K filed 2019-04-25].

3. **Operating expenses increased by 3.8% year-over-year, with notable rises in salaries, wages, and benefits and maintenance costs, partially offset by lower fuel expenses.**  
   Salaries, wages, and benefits increased 8.4% to \$8.3 billion, reflecting wage inflation and profitsharing accruals, including a record \$667 million profitsharing expense in 2019 with a \$124 million special discretionary contribution related to Boeing compensation [10-K filed 2020-02-04; 8-K filed 2020-01-23].  
   Fuel and oil expenses declined 5.8% to \$4.3 billion, helped by favorable fuel prices and hedging, despite increased economic fuel costs [10-K filed 2020-02-04; 8-K filed 2019-10-24].  
   Maintenance materials and repairs rose 10.5% to \$1.2 billion, attributed to increased unscheduled maintenance disruptions [10-K filed 2020-02-04].

4. **The Boeing 737 MAX grounding materially impacted 2019 financials, reducing operating income by an estimated \$210 million in Q3 alone and causing schedule adjustments through at least mid-2020.**  
   Southwest grounded all 34 MAX aircraft following the FAA emergency order on March 13, 2019, removing MAX flights through at least March 6, 2020, and delaying 41 additional MAX aircraft deliveries originally scheduled for 2019 into 2020 [8-K filed 2019-09-18; 8-K filed 2019-10-24; 10-Q filed 2019-11-08].  
   The grounding led to a 1.6% reduction in capacity (Available Seat Miles) in 2019 versus 2018, with the company adjusting capacity growth guidance downward from an expected 3.5-4% in Q1 to approximately 1% due to cancellations related to MAX, labor contract negotiations, weather, and government shutdown effects [8-K filed 2019-03-27; 8-K filed 2019-01-24].

5. **Southwest generated strong operating cash flow of approximately \$5.1 billion in 2019, enabling \$1.4 billion in share repurchases and \$372 million in dividends, while maintaining a stable balance sheet.**  
   Cash and cash equivalents increased modestly to about \$2.5 billion at year-end 2019 from \$1.9 billion in 2018. Total stockholders’ equity remained stable at approximately \$9.8 billion [10-K filed 2020-02-04; 10-Q filed 2019-11-08].  
   The company repaid some long-term debt, with current maturities of long-term debt rising to \$637 million at year-end from \$606 million in 2018, and long-term debt less current maturities decreasing to \$2.4 billion from \$2.8 billion [10-K filed 2020-02-04].

6. **Revenue composition in 2019 showed a slight rise in loyalty program and ancillary revenues, reflecting ongoing growth in these segments.**  
   Passenger loyalty revenue increased to \$2.49 billion from \$2.31 billion in 2018, while ancillary revenues sold separately grew to \$711 million from \$642 million. Non-loyalty passenger revenues remained relatively flat at \$17.6 billion [10-K filed 2020-02-04; 10-Q filed 2019-11-08].

### Operations Insights

7. **Capacity (ASM) contracted 1.6% in 2019 due to the Boeing 737 MAX grounding and related operational disruptions, leading to a 1.5% decline in Revenue Passenger Miles (RPMs).**  
   Available Seat Miles fell from 159.8 billion in 2018 to 157.3 billion in 2019, while RPMs declined from 133.3 billion to 131.3 billion. Load factor remained steady at 83.5%, a slight 0.1 point increase year-over-year, indicating stable seat utilization despite reduced capacity [10-K filed 2020-02-04; 8-K filed 2019-10-24].

8. **Southwest maintained its point-to-point route structure and fleet homogeneity with 747 Boeing 737 aircraft at year-end 2019, serving 101 destinations including new service to five Hawaiian cities enabled by FAA Extended Operations (ETOPS) approval.**  
   The Hawaiian expansion began in 2019 with service to Honolulu, Kahului, Kona, and Lihue; the fifth destination, Hilo, opened in January 2020. The fleet remained exclusively Boeing 737s, supporting operational efficiency through simplified scheduling, maintenance, and training [10-K filed 2020-02-04].

9. **Fleet growth was constrained by MAX delivery delays; seven MAX deliveries were targeted in Q4 2019, with 34 deliveries deferred to 2020 or later, pending FAA regulatory approval.**  
   The company’s 2019 capacity guidance was revised downward to no more than 5% growth, with actual capacity declining due to grounded MAX aircraft and operational disruptions [10-Q filed 2019-11-08].

### Labor Insights

10. **Labor costs rose significantly in 2019, with salaries, wages, and benefits increasing 8.4%, driven by wage inflation and record profitsharing accruals totaling \$667 million, including a \$124 million discretionary profitsharing contribution related to Boeing compensation.**  
    Labor disruptions contributed to operational challenges, including approximately 2,800 flight cancellations in Q1 2019 due to unscheduled maintenance linked to contract negotiations with the Aircraft Mechanics Fraternal Association (AMFA) [10-K filed 2020-02-04; 8-K filed 2019-03-27; 8-K filed 2020-01-23].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

11. **Southwest's loyalty program and ancillary revenues continued to grow, supported by partnerships such as with Chase and enhancements to booking platforms, including agreements with Amadeus and Travelport to improve corporate travel bookings.**  
    Rapid Rewards program revenues rose year-over-year, and ancillary revenues from fees such as EarlyBird Check-In and Upgraded Boarding increased, contributing to total passenger revenues [10-Q filed 2019-07-30; 10-K filed 2020-02-04].

12. **The company emphasized its "Transfarency" campaign, highlighting no change fees and no baggage fees, with approximately 80% of passenger revenues originating from the company’s website and SWABIZ platform, reflecting a direct distribution focus.**  
    Marketing efforts focused on Southwest’s differentiation from competitors through transparent pricing and customer-friendly policies [10-K filed 2020-02-04].

### Wrap Up

In 2019, Southwest Airlines experienced modest revenue growth but faced earnings and margin pressure primarily due to the grounding of its Boeing 737 MAX fleet and related operational disruptions, which constrained capacity and increased unit costs. Labor cost inflation and increased maintenance expenses further pressured profitability, despite lower fuel costs. The company maintained a stable balance sheet and generated strong operating cash flow, supporting shareholder returns via dividends and share repurchases. Operationally, Southwest preserved its fleet homogeneity and point-to-point network, expanding into Hawaii with new ETOPS approval.
