3. **Hawaiian converted higher revenue into improved margins, with operating revenue per ASM (RASM) rising 5.6% to 13.56¢ and CASM stable, expanding operating margin.** Load factor was stable at 81.5%, while passenger revenue per ASM (PRASM) increased 3.5% to 11.99¢, supported by a 3.4% yield increase to 14.70¢ [8-K 2015-01-29].

4. **Cash and liquidity strengthened, with unrestricted cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments of \$524 million at year-end 2014, up from \$423 million at year-end 2013.** Outstanding debt and capital lease obligations increased to approximately \$1.05 billion from \$806 million a year earlier, reflecting financing for new aircraft deliveries [8-K 2015-01-29; 8-K 2014-01-28].

5. **Capital expenditures included fleet investments with deliveries and financing of Airbus A330-200 aircraft and introduction of ATR42 turboprop aircraft for Neighbor Island service.** The fleet at December 31, 2014, consisted of 18 Boeing 717-200s for Neighbor Island routes, 10 Boeing 767-300s, 19 Airbus A330-200s for North America, International, and charter routes, and 3 ATR42 turboprops for the "'Ohana by Hawaiian" service launched in 2014 [10-K 2015-02-09; 8-K 2014-01-28].

### Operations Insights

6. **Capacity measured in available seat miles (ASM) grew 1.7% to 17.07 billion, while revenue passenger miles (RPM) increased 1.8% to 13.92 billion, resulting in a stable passenger load factor of 81.5%.** Fourth quarter ASM increased 2.0% year-over-year to 4.27 billion and RPM increased 3.8% to 3.51 billion, with load factor improving 1.4 points to 82.2% [8-K 2015-01-29].

7. **Fuel consumption rose modestly by 1.8% to 230.2 million gallons on a full-year basis, with fuel costs benefiting from a 3.8% decrease in economic fuel cost per gallon to \$3.03.** Fuel represented approximately 33% of operating expenses in 2014 [8-K 2015-01-29; 10-K 2015-02-09].

8. **Network and fleet utilization expanded with new and seasonal routes including launch of Beijing-Honolulu service, reintroduction of San Jose-Honolulu, and expanded service from Los Angeles and Oakland to Neighbor Island destinations Kona and Lihu‘e.** The "'Ohana by Hawaiian" turboprop operation began in March 2014, introducing ATR42 aircraft on Neighbor Island routes to Moloka‘i and Lana‘i, later expanding to Maui-Moloka‘i, Kona, and Hilo [8-K 2015-01-29; 8-K 2014-07-22; 8-K 2014-04-22].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

9. **Revenue per ASM growth was supported by higher yields and passenger revenue per ASM, reflecting improved pricing and network mix.** Passenger yield increased 3.4% to 14.70¢, while PRASM rose 3.5% to 11.99¢, indicating effective revenue management amid capacity growth [8-K 2015-01-29].

10. **Other operating revenue increased 26.7% to \$269.8 million, driven by cargo operations and ancillary services, enhancing total revenue diversification beyond passenger fares.** This other revenue component rose from \$213 million in 2013 [8-K 2015-01-29].

### Labor Insights

11. **Employee count increased slightly to 5,362 active employees as of June 30, 2014, supporting expanded operations and new service launches.** Wage and benefit costs rose 4.7% to \$447.4 million for the full year 2014, reflecting higher staffing levels and compensation [10-Q 2014-07-24; 8-K 2015-01-29].

### Route Network Insights

12. **Hawaiian’s route network remained focused on the Hawaiian Islands, U.S. mainland, and select international markets in the South Pacific, Asia, and Australia, with 73% of passenger revenue generated from routes between Hawai‘i and the U.S. mainland or inter-island flights.** The company acknowledged its exposure to demand and capacity changes on these concentrated routes, which differ from geographically diversified competitors [10-K 2015-02-09].

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines completed 2014 with revenue and profitability expansion driven by modest capacity growth, improved yields, and disciplined cost control, particularly in fuel expense. The airline maintained stable load factors while expanding its network with new and seasonal routes, including the launch of the "'Ohana by Hawaiian" turboprop service. Operating margins improved as RASM outpaced CASM, aided by lower fuel prices and increased ancillary revenue. Liquidity strengthened with cash balances rising alongside increased debt financing for fleet investments, including Airbus A330-200s and ATR42 turboprops.

The airline’s revenue remains concentrated on the Hawai‘i-U.S. mainland and inter-island markets, exposing it to risks from demand fluctuations and competitor capacity changes in these corridors. Labor costs increased with modest workforce growth to support expanded operations. Hawaiian’s 2015 outlook, as disclosed, anticipates further revenue per ASM improvement and cost control, with operational and financial performance sensitive to fuel prices, demand, and competitive dynamics in its core markets.

2015.Q1:
### Financial Insights

1. **Hawaiian Airlines returned to profitability in 2015Q1, reporting net income of \$25.9 million versus a net loss of \$5.1 million in 2014Q1.**  
   The airline’s GAAP net income was \$25.9 million or \$0.40 per diluted share, compared to a net loss of \$5.1 million or \$0.10 per diluted share in the prior year quarter [8-K 2015-04-23; 10-Q 2015-04-24]. Adjusted net income, excluding loss on extinguishment of debt and reflecting economic fuel expense, was \$24.7 million or \$0.38 per diluted share, improving by \$25.6 million year-over-year [8-K 2015-04-23]. The adjusted pre-tax margin rose to 7.4% from a negative 0.2% in 2014Q1, evidencing significant margin expansion [8-K 2015-04-23].

2. **Operating revenues increased modestly by 2.9% year-over-year to \$540.3 million, driven primarily by other revenue growth, while passenger revenue was flat.**  
   Passenger revenue was essentially flat at \$469.1 million (+0.2%), while other revenue rose 25.1% to \$71.1 million, contributing to the overall revenue growth [10-Q 2015-04-24]. The increase in other revenue was attributed to stronger cargo operations on North America and International routes [8-K 2015-03-24].

3. **Operating expenses declined 8.9% to \$469.1 million, largely due to a 34.9% fall in aircraft fuel expense, despite wage and benefit costs rising 11.6%.**  
   Aircraft fuel expense fell sharply to \$111.3 million from \$171.1 million in 2014Q1, reflecting a 28.7% reduction in economic fuel cost per gallon to \$2.21 and a modest 3.3% increase in gallons consumed [10-Q 2015-04-24]. In contrast, wages and benefits rose to \$120.0 million (+11.6%) due to increased pension and postretirement expenses and higher profit-sharing tied to improved financial results [10-Q 2015-04-24]. Other expense categories showed modest changes, with aircraft rent up 8.0% due to lease return costs, and maintenance expenses declining slightly [10-Q 2015-04-24].

4. **Unit cost per available seat mile (CASM) fell 13.0% to 11.09 cents, driven by lower fuel costs, while CASM excluding fuel was stable at 8.46 cents.**  
   The reduction in CASM was mostly fuel-driven, with fuel expense per ASM dropping 38.0% to 2.63 cents [8-K 2015-04-23]. CASM excluding fuel was essentially flat (-0.6%), indicating limited cost improvement outside of fuel [8-K 2015-04-23].

5. **Operating income surged 609% to \$71.2 million from \$10.0 million in 2014Q1, supported by lower fuel costs and modest revenue growth.**  
   The operating margin expansion was primarily driven by the fuel cost decline, which more than offset wage inflation and other expenses [10-Q 2015-04-24]. Operating revenue per ASM (RASM) declined slightly by 1.7% to 12.77 cents, reflecting yield pressure, but lower CASM enabled margin growth [8-K 2015-04-23].

6. **Cash flow from operations nearly doubled to \$161.7 million, supporting capital expenditures and debt repayments.**  
   Operating cash flow increased from \$89.5 million in 2014Q1 to \$161.7 million in 2015Q1, reflecting improved profitability [10-Q 2015-04-24]. Investing cash flow was negative \$13.4 million, primarily due to pre-delivery deposits for aircraft, partially offset by proceeds from an Airbus A330-200 sale-leaseback [10-Q 2015-04-24]. Financing cash flow used \$186.2 million, mainly for repurchasing convertible notes [10-Q 2015-04-24].

7. **Liquidity remained strong with \$488 million in unrestricted cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments, down from \$524 million at year-end 2014, while total debt and capital lease obligations were approximately \$962 million.**  
   Cash and short-term investments decreased by \$36 million since December 31, 2014, partly reflecting share repurchases and debt repayments [8-K 2015-04-23; 10-Q 2015-04-24]. The leverage ratio improved to 3.6x [8-K 2015-04-23].

8. **The Board authorized a \$100 million share repurchase program, signaling capital return to shareholders amid improved financial performance.**  
   The repurchase program was announced concurrent with the strong first quarter results [8-K 2015-04-23].

### Operations Insights

9. **Capacity (ASM) increased 4.7% year-over-year to 4.23 billion seat miles, with a 4.8% increase in revenue passengers flown, but load factor declined 0.9 points to 79.1%.**  
   The increase in capacity and traffic was driven by network and fleet expansion, including new and resumed routes [10-Q 2015-04-24; 8-K 2015-04-23]. The slight load factor decline reflected increased industry capacity and a 3.3% drop in passenger yield to 14.02 cents per RPM [10-Q 2015-04-24].

10. **Revenue passenger miles (RPM) rose 3.6% to 3.35 billion, indicating solid traffic growth but at lower yields and load factors.**  
    Passenger revenue per ASM (PRASM) declined 4.3% to 11.10 cents, reflecting competitive pressures and a stronger U.S. dollar [10-Q 2015-04-24; 8-K 2015-04-23].

11. **Fuel consumption increased 3.3% to 57.0 million gallons, but the average fuel price per gallon dropped 37.1% to \$1.95, driving significant fuel cost savings.**

Network changes included suspensions of some international routes (Fukuoka and Taipei) in 2014, partially offset by new Beijing and seasonal Neighbor Island services [10-Q 2015-04-24; 8-K 2015-01-29].

    North America revenue increased \$11.9 million year-over-year due to higher traffic but offset by yield declines from increased industry capacity [10-Q 2015-04-24]. Neighbor Island revenue grew \$6.6 million, aided by the turboprop launch and fare increases [10-Q 2015-04-24]. International revenue fell \$17.4 million due to capacity cuts and yield pressure [10-Q 2015-04-24].

14. **Passenger revenue remained steady despite a 3.3% yield decline, supported by increased traffic and a broader route network.**  
    The company attributed the yield decline to competitive capacity increases and currency effects [8-K 2015-04-23; 10-Q 2015-04-24].

### Labor Insights

15. **Wages and benefits increased 11.6% mainly from higher pension and postretirement expenses and increased profit-sharing tied to improved earnings.**  
    The increase was partially due to improved financial results leading to higher profit-sharing accruals [10-Q 2015-04-24].

16. **Headcount was 5,371 active employees as of March 31, 2015, with no disclosed labor disputes or contract changes in the period.**  
    No material labor events affecting operations or costs were disclosed [10-Q 2015-04-24].

### Route Network Insights

17. **The network continued to focus on Hawai‘i’s key markets: Neighbor Island, North America, and International routes, with capacity and frequency growth in North America and Neighbor Island offsetting International contractions.**  
    The airline operates from 11 U.S. gateway cities and international destinations in Asia, Australia, and the South Pacific [10-K 2015-02-09]. Recent route adjustments included suspensions of lower-performing international routes and launches of new Beijing service and seasonal Neighbor Island flights [10-Q 2015-04-24; 8-K 2015-01-29].

18. **Fleet composition supported network strategy with widebody Airbus A330-200s for long-haul, Boeing 717-200s for intra-island routes, and ATR42s for turboprop Neighbor Island service.**  
    The fleet was being modernized with new aircraft deliveries and lease returns, including lease return costs recognized in the quarter [10-K 2015-02-09; 10-Q 2015-04-24].

### Corporate Insights

19. **Fuel price volatility remains a key market risk; Hawaiian hedges approximately 50% of 2015 fuel requirements using heating oil puts and swaps, which are not designated for hedge accounting.**  
    Fuel derivatives contributed realized losses of \$14.6 million in 2015Q1 versus minimal impact in 2014Q1 [10-Q 2015-04-24]. The company recognizes changes in fair value of these derivatives in nonoperating income (expense) [10-K 2015-02-09].

20. **Foreign currency risk and competitive pressures from larger network carriers and potential new entrants, including low-cost carriers, are ongoing risks given Hawaiian’s concentrated market in Hawai‘i and reliance on tourism.**  
    The company emphasized exposure to U.S. dollar strength affecting international yields and noted competitive challenges from network carriers with broader geographic diversification [10-K 2015-02-09].

---

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ 2015 first quarter showed a marked financial turnaround from a loss to a \$25.9 million profit, driven primarily by sharply lower fuel prices that cut fuel expense nearly 35% year-over-year. Despite modest revenue growth of 2.9%, yields declined, and load factors fell slightly amid increased industry capacity and a stronger U.S. dollar. Operating expenses outside fuel rose, notably wages and benefits, reflecting higher pension costs and profit sharing. The airline increased capacity by 4.7%, expanding North America and Neighbor Island services while trimming some international routes. Liquidity remained solid with nearly \$488 million in cash and investments, and the company initiated a \$100 million share repurchase program. Fuel price hedging covered about half of 2015’s expected consumption but resulted in realized losses during the quarter. Risks remain from competitive pressures, currency fluctuations, and the airline’s geographic concentration in Hawai‘i’s tourism-dependent market.

**Guidance and Forward-Looking Commentary:**  
Hawaiian revised its 2015Q1 expectations upward for operating revenue per ASM due to better-than-expected passenger and cargo revenue on North America and International routes, and lowered cost per ASM excluding fuel due to improved cost performance and deferred maintenance expenses [8-K 2015-03-24]. The company expected continued capacity growth of 3.5% to 5.5% for 2015Q1, with operating revenue per ASM projected to decline 3.5% to 6.5% year-over-year due to currency and competitive factors, while operating cost per ASM excluding fuel was forecast to rise 1.5% to 4.5% [10-K 2015-02-09]. Economic fuel costs were expected to remain significantly lower than 2014 levels, based on forward curves [8-K 2015-04-23].

No material labor disputes, accidents, or regulatory actions were disclosed for the quarter. The company’s capital commitments included firm aircraft orders and purchase rights for new Airbus A330-800neo and A321neo aircraft to support future network development [10-K 2015-02-09].
2015.Q2:
### Financial Insights

1. **Net income more than doubled year-over-year to \$48.8 million in Q2 2015, driven by lower fuel costs and strong demand despite currency and capacity headwinds.** Hawaiian reported GAAP net income of \$48.8 million (\$0.79 diluted EPS) for Q2 2015, up from \$27.3 million (\$0.43 diluted EPS) in Q2 2014 [8-K 2015-07-28; 10-Q 2015-07-30]. Adjusted net income, which excludes loss on extinguishment of debt and reflects economic fuel expense, rose by \$15.1 million to \$37.5 million (\$0.61 per diluted share) compared to the prior year [8-K 2015-07-28]. Adjusted pre-tax margin improved to 10.7% from 6.4% in Q2 2014 [8-K 2015-07-28]. This earnings improvement was attributed by management to strong demand, low fuel prices, and despite adverse impacts from a strengthening US dollar, reduced fuel surcharges, and high industry capacity growth from North America [8-K 2015-07-28].

2. **Operating revenue was flat or slightly down, pressured by lower yields and international capacity reductions, while other revenue grew modestly.** Passenger revenue declined 1.5% to \$499.4 million in Q2 2015 from \$506.8 million in Q2 2014, while other operating revenue increased 4.3% to \$71.9 million, driven primarily by ancillary revenue growth from North America passengers [10-Q 2015-07-30; 8-K 2015-07-28]. Total operating revenue was \$571.3 million, a 0.8% decrease from \$575.7 million a year earlier [8-K 2015-07-28]. The yield (passenger revenue per revenue passenger mile) declined 6.8% to 13.92 cents [8-K 2015-07-28]. International revenue decreased by \$24.9 million due to reduced capacity from route suspensions (e.g., Honolulu to Fukuoka and Taipei) and lower fares caused by a stronger US dollar and reduced fuel surcharges [10-Q 2015-07-30].

3. **Operating costs fell 8.4% year-over-year, driven mainly by a 35.4% drop in aircraft fuel expense despite a 1.9% increase in fuel gallons consumed, offsetting wage and rent cost increases.** Total operating expenses declined to \$479.9 million from \$524.1 million in Q2 2014 [8-K 2015-07-28]. Aircraft fuel expense dropped sharply from \$174.1 million to \$112.5 million, reflecting a 36.6% decrease in average fuel cost per gallon to \$1.94 including taxes and fees, while gallons consumed increased slightly to 58.0 million [8-K 2015-07-28]. Economic fuel expense, which adjusts GAAP fuel expense for realized cash settlements on fuel hedges, fell 26.7% to \$129.1 million [8-K 2015-07-28]. Wages and benefits rose 10.2% to \$124.0 million, driven by higher pension and postretirement costs and increased profit-sharing expenses [8-K 2015-07-28; 10-Q 2015-04-24]. Aircraft rent increased 10.4% to \$28.8 million, partly due to lease return costs on Boeing 767-300s [8-K 2015-07-28; 10-Q 2015-04-24].

4. **Unit costs (CASM) declined 12.2% to 10.80 cents per available seat mile (ASM), mainly due to lower fuel costs, while CASM excluding fuel edged up 0.7% to 8.27 cents.** Operating cost per ASM (CASM) improved from 12.30 cents in Q2 2014 to 10.80 cents in Q2 2015 [8-K 2015-07-28]. When excluding aircraft fuel, CASM was essentially flat, indicating that controllable costs like labor and maintenance rose slightly despite overall cost reductions [8-K 2015-07-28]. Passenger revenue per ASM (PRASM) fell 5.5% to 11.25 cents, reflecting lower yields [8-K 2015-07-28].

5. **Strong operating cash flow of \$297.5 million in the first half of 2015 supported debt reduction and share repurchases, with liquidity reaching \$606 million at June 30, 2015.** Net cash from operations for the six months ended June 30, 2015 was \$297.5 million, up from \$204.0 million in the prior year, primarily due to improved profitability [10-Q 2015-07-30]. Financing activities used \$231.1 million, mainly for repurchasing convertible notes, repaying long-term debt, and buying back common stock under a \$100 million repurchase program authorized in Q1 2015 [10-Q 2015-07-30; 8-K 2015-04-23]. As of June 30, 2015, unrestricted cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments totaled \$606 million, up from \$488 million at March 31, 2015 [8-K 2015-07-28; 8-K 2015-04-23]. The company lowered its leverage ratio to 3.4x from 3.6x at March 31, 2015 [8-K 2015-07-28; 8-K 2015-04-23].

### Operations Insights

6. **Capacity grew modestly by 4.2% in Q2 2015 with a 5.8% increase in revenue passenger miles (RPM), leading to a 1.2 point improvement in load factor to 80.8%.** Available seat miles (ASM) increased from 4.26 billion to 4.44 billion, while RPM rose from 3.40 billion to 3.59 billion year-over-year [8-K 2015-07-28]. Passenger count increased 5.3% to 2.66 million [8-K 2015-07-28]. The load factor improvement reflects better seat utilization despite capacity growth [8-K 2015-07-28].

7. **Fuel consumption rose slightly by 1.9% to 58.0 million gallons in Q2 2015, while average fuel cost per gallon fell 36.6% to \$1.94, aiding cost reduction.** The increase in fuel gallons consumed corresponds with increased block hours operated (5.6% growth to 43,418 hours) and capacity [8-K 2015-07-28]. Economic fuel cost per gallon was \$2.23, down 27.8% from \$3.09 in Q2 2014 [8-K 2015-07-28]. Fuel costs represented 23% of operating expenses in Q2 2015, down from 33% in Q2 2014 [10-Q 2015-07-30].

8. **Fleet adjustments included adding an Airbus A330-200 under lease, retiring a Boeing 767-300, and accelerating retirement plans for certain 767-300s, smoothing capacity growth.** The company also continued retrofitting its Boeing 717 neighbor island fleet, with 12 of 18 completed as of Q2 2015 [8-K 2015-07-28]. Plans included a six-year lease for an additional A330-200 to be delivered in summer 2016 and purchase of three ATR 72 turboprops for cargo expansion [8-K 2015-07-28]. These moves indicate a gradual fleet modernization and capacity realignment [8-K 2015-07-28].

9. **Route network changes contributed to international capacity reductions and revenue declines, including suspensions of Honolulu-Fukuoka and Honolulu-Taipei routes.** These suspensions reduced international capacity and revenue, partially offset by new service to Beijing [10-Q 2015-07-30]. Seasonal service additions included summer routes from Los Angeles and Oakland to Kona and Lihu‘e, and a second daily seasonal Los Angeles-Maui flight [8-K 2015-07-28]. Year-round service from Los Angeles to Lihu‘e was announced starting January 2016 [8-K 2015-07-28].

### Labor Insights

10. **Wages and benefits increased 10.2% year-over-year in Q2 2015, driven by higher pension and postretirement expenses and increased profit-sharing tied to better financial results.** Wages and benefits rose to \$124.0 million from \$112.5 million in Q2 2014 [8-K 2015-07-28; 10-Q 2015-04-24]. The workforce totaled 5,439 active employees as of June 30, 2015 [10-Q 2015-07-30].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

11. **Yield compression and reduced fuel surcharges pressured passenger revenue per ASM, despite load factor gains and ancillary revenue growth.** Passenger yield declined 6.8% to 13.92 cents in Q2 2015 [8-K 2015-07-28]. The company noted that the strengthening US dollar and lower fuel surcharges reduced average fares, especially on international routes [10-Q 2015-07-30]. Ancillary revenue increased by \$2.5 million in Q2 2015, driven by a 15% increase in North America passengers [10-Q 2015-07-30].

### Route Network Insights

12. **Network capacity growth was moderate at 4.2% ASM increase in Q2 2015, with strategic seasonal and year-round route adjustments to align capacity with demand.** Seasonal services were reintroduced on several North America to Hawaii routes for summer 2015, including Los Angeles and Oakland to Kona and Lihu‘e [8-K 2015-07-28]. The company planned a year-round Los Angeles to Lihu‘e service starting January 2016 [8-K 2015-07-28]. International capacity was reduced due to 2014 route suspensions, impacting revenue [10-Q 2015-07-30].

---

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ Q2 2015 results showed a significant net income improvement driven primarily by sharply lower fuel costs and modest capacity growth that improved load factors. Despite a 5.5% decline in passenger revenue per available seat mile (PRASM) due to yield compression, the company’s strong cost control and fuel price environment led to a 12.2% reduction in unit costs (CASM) and a doubling of net income to \$48.8 million. Operating cash flow strengthened, enabling debt reduction and share repurchases, while liquidity rose to \$606 million at quarter-end. Capacity growth was moderate, with seasonal network adjustments and fleet modernization supporting operational efficiency. Labor costs increased moderately due to pension and profit-sharing impacts. International revenue declined due to capacity reductions and currency effects, partially offset by North America and neighbor island route gains.

For the third quarter and full year 2015, Hawaiian guided for a 3% to 5% ASM increase, a 2% to 7% decrease in operating revenue per ASM, and a 1.5% to 5.5% increase in cost per ASM excluding fuel. Economic fuel costs were expected to remain significantly lower than 2014 levels, with fuel cost per gallon guidance between \$2.00 and \$2.15 for Q3 2015 [8-K 2015-07-28]. No material labor disputes, accidents, or regulatory actions were disclosed that would materially affect the near-term outlook.
2015.Q3:
### Financial Insights

1. **Hawaiian Airlines reported strong net income growth in 2015Q3 driven by lower fuel costs despite a slight revenue decline.**  
   GAAP net income for Q3 2015 was \$70.0 million (\$1.15 per diluted share), nearly doubling the \$35.6 million (\$0.56 per diluted share) earned in Q3 2014. Adjusted net income was \$78.4 million (\$1.29 per diluted share), up \$28.9 million year-over-year. Operating revenue slightly declined by 1.2% to \$631.7 million from \$639.5 million in Q3 2014, with passenger revenue down 1.8% to \$556.9 million. The adjusted pre-tax margin improved to 20.0% from 12.6% in the prior year quarter. Lower fuel costs, which dropped 42.1% to \$105.5 million, were the primary driver of margin expansion despite a 1.6% increase in fuel consumption. Wages and benefits increased 10.0% to \$125.9 million, reflecting higher pension, postretirement, and profit-sharing expenses linked to improved financial performance [8-K 2015-10-19; 10-Q 2015-10-21].

2. **Operating cost per available seat mile (CASM) decreased significantly, mainly due to fuel price declines, while CASM excluding fuel rose slightly.**  
   Q3 2015 CASM was 10.23 cents, down 13.6% from 11.84 cents in Q3 2014. Excluding fuel, CASM increased 2.2% to 7.97 cents from 7.80 cents, indicating some upward pressure on controllable costs. Fuel expense per ASM fell sharply by 44.1% to 2.26 cents from 4.04 cents. The average fuel price per gallon fell 43.2% to \$1.72 from \$3.03, partially offset by a 1.6% increase in gallons consumed. This demonstrates that while fuel cost savings substantially improved unit costs, other operating expenses increased modestly [10-Q 2015-10-21; 8-K 2015-10-19].

3. **Passenger operating revenue per ASM (PRASM) and yield declined due to lower average fares and a stronger U.S. dollar, despite higher load factors.**  
   Scheduled operations PRASM fell 5.2% to 11.95 cents from 12.60 cents in Q3 2014, and yield dropped 4.4% to 14.34 cents per RPM. Load factor decreased slightly by 0.7 points to 83.3%. The revenue softness was attributed to a strengthening U.S. dollar and reduced fuel surcharges, particularly impacting international routes where revenue declined by \$22.9 million. North America and Neighbor Island segments saw revenue growth but with lower yields, partially due to increased industry capacity [10-Q 2015-10-21].

4. **Other operating revenue increased 3.2% in Q3 2015, driven by co-branded credit card agreements and ancillary services.**  
   Other operating revenue rose to \$74.8 million from \$72.5 million, with \$1.1 million attributed to increased co-branded credit card revenue and \$1.0 million to ancillary revenue growth linked to a 5% passenger increase on North America routes [10-Q 2015-10-21].

   As of September 30, 2015, Hawaiian held \$345.2 million in cash and cash equivalents plus \$265.4 million in short-term investments, up \$86.4 million from December 31, 2014. Debt and capital lease obligations totaled approximately \$914.4 million, with a secured revolving credit facility of \$175 million completely unused. The leverage ratio was lowered from 3.4x in Q2 2015 to 3.1x in Q3 2015 [8-K 2015-10-19; 10-Q 2015-10-21].

6. **Capital commitments included a six-year lease for an Airbus A330-200 scheduled for Q2 2016 delivery and purchase commitments for ATR 72 turboprop aircraft for cargo expansion.**  
   Hawaiian entered a six-year lease agreement for an A330-200 with delivery expected in summer 2016 and accelerated retirement of some Boeing 767-300s. The company also purchased three ATR 72 turboprops in all-cargo configuration to expand cargo services. The A330-200 lease carries minimum payments of \$2.2 million in late 2015 and \$8.4 million annually from 2016 to 2019 [8-K 2015-07-28; 10-Q 2015-10-21].

### Operations Insights

7. **Capacity grew modestly with ASM up 3.6% and RPM up 2.7% in Q3 2015, but load factor slightly declined.**  
   Scheduled operations ASM increased to 4.66 billion from 4.50 billion year-over-year, while RPM rose to 3.88 billion from 3.78 billion. Load factor decreased 0.7 points to 83.3%. Passenger traffic grew 4.5% to 2.83 million passengers. The modest capacity expansion was managed alongside a slight decline in yield, reflecting competitive and currency pressures [10-Q 2015-10-21].

8. **Fuel efficiency and consumption showed slight increases in gallons consumed but significant cost reductions due to lower fuel prices.**  
   Fuel gallons consumed rose 1.6% to 61.2 million in Q3 2015, consistent with capacity growth. However, the average fuel price per gallon fell 43.2%, leading to a 42.1% reduction in fuel expense. This dynamic underpinned the notable improvement in operating margins despite higher fuel burn [10-Q 2015-10-21].

9. **Operational challenges in summer 2015 included gate shortages at Honolulu and changed air traffic control procedures causing delays.**  
   Management disclosed that construction at Honolulu airport led to gate shortages, and abrupt changes in air traffic control extended flight times, resulting in operational delays during the summer peak. Employees worked to mitigate the impact on customers, but these external factors contributed to a "disappointing summer operationally" by the company's standards [8-K 2015-10-19].

10. **Fleet refurbishment and product enhancements continued, including the retrofit of 14 of 18 Boeing 717 aircraft and enhanced in-flight service on Japan-Hawai‘i routes.**  
    The interior retrofit of the neighbor island fleet was on track for completion by year-end 2015, improving passenger experience. The airline also launched a new onboard safety video and became the official airline of the Oakland Raiders for the 2015 NFL season. New seasonal and year-round service to Lihu‘e from Los Angeles was announced [8-K 2015-10-19].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

11. **Revenue growth was mixed by geography: North America and Neighbor Island segments increased revenue, while International segment declined due to currency and capacity changes.**  
    North America revenue increased by \$8.3 million in Q3 2015 compared to Q3 2014, driven by capacity additions, despite lower yields. Neighbor Island revenue grew by \$4.5 million, supported by fleet configuration changes and turboprop operations launched in 2014. International revenue fell by \$22.9 million due to a stronger U.S. dollar, reduced fuel surcharges, and capacity reductions, including route suspensions such as Honolulu-Fukuoka [10-Q 2015-10-21].

### Labor Insights

12. **Wages and benefits expenses rose 10% year-over-year, reflecting increased pension, postretirement, and profit-sharing expenses tied to improved earnings.**  
    The airline's wage and benefit costs increased by \$11.4 million in Q3 2015, attributed to higher pension and postretirement benefit expenses plus increased profit-sharing linked to financial performance gains. Employee headcount as of June 30, 2015 was 5,439 [10-Q 2015-10-21; 10-Q 2015-07-30].

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ 2015 third quarter was characterized by strong profitability gains driven mainly by sharply lower fuel costs, which more than offset a slight decline in passenger revenue and yield pressures from currency strength and competitive capacity growth. The airline expanded capacity modestly, maintaining solid load factors, while operational challenges at Honolulu due to airport construction and air traffic control changes caused delays during the summer. The company continued investing in fleet refurbishment and cargo expansion with new turboprops and A330-200 leases. Wage and benefit costs increased in line with improved earnings, and liquidity remained strong with a leverage ratio improved to 3.1x and over \$600 million in cash and short-term investments.

Management’s updated guidance for Q4 2015 and full year 2015 reflected expectations of cost per ASM excluding fuel up 2.5% to 5.5% and operating revenue per ASM down 4% to 7% for Q3, with fuel costs per gallon projected between \$2.00 and \$2.10. Capacity growth was forecasted at 3% to 5% for the year. The company noted no material risks or events beyond ongoing market and operational factors. The next material period for review will be the fourth quarter and full year 2015 results.

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines closed 2015 with improved profitability driven largely by sharply lower fuel costs that cut operating expenses significantly, offsetting modest declines in passenger yields and flat passenger revenue in Q4. Capacity growth was moderate, with load factors improving slightly, while operational challenges related to airport capacity and air traffic control were noted but managed. Wage and benefit costs rose on the back of stronger earnings and benefit expenses. The company maintained a strong liquidity position, paid down debt, and continued investing in fleet modernization and network expansion, including new international routes and premium product upgrades.

Management highlighted the headwind from a strong US dollar impacting international yields but expressed confidence in ongoing positive trends for 2016. Hawaiian’s business remains concentrated on North America and Neighbor Island routes, with international routes facing competitive and currency pressures. 2015.FY:
### Financial Insights

1. **Hawaiian Airlines achieved record net income of \$182.6 million in 2015, up \$113.7 million from 2014**  
   For the full year ended December 31, 2015, Hawaiian reported GAAP net income of \$182.6 million or \$2.98 per diluted share, compared to \$68.9 million or \$1.10 per diluted share in 2014. The fourth quarter net income was \$37.9 million, a \$26.8 million increase year-over-year. Adjusted pre-tax margin improved notably, reaching 20.0% in Q3 2015 from 12.6% in the prior year period, reflecting stronger profitability. This earnings growth coincided with stable operating revenue of \$2.317 billion in 2015, essentially flat compared to 2014’s \$2.315 billion. Passenger revenue declined slightly by 1.0% year-over-year to \$2.026 billion, while other operating revenue grew 8.2% to \$292 million, driven by increased frequent flyer mile sales and cargo volume. [8-K 2016-01-26; 8-K 2015-10-19; 10-K 2016-02-08]

2. **Fuel costs fell sharply, lowering total operating expenses and CASM despite wage and rent increases**  
   Aircraft fuel expense dropped 38.4% to \$418 million in 2015 from \$678 million in 2014, driven by a 28% decline in average economic fuel cost per gallon to \$1.78 (including taxes) and a modest 3.5% increase in gallons consumed to 234 million. Fuel represented 22.1% of operating expenses in 2015, down from 32.8% in 2014. This fuel cost reduction more than offset increases in wages and benefits (+11.6% to \$500 million) and aircraft rent (+8.7% to \$116 million). Overall, CASM (cost per available seat mile) declined to 10.67¢ in 2015 from 12.12¢ in 2014, a 12% improvement, while CASM excluding fuel was slightly higher at 8.31¢ versus 8.15¢, reflecting higher non-fuel costs. [10-K 2016-02-08; 8-K 2015-04-23; 8-K 2015-07-28]

3. **Operating cash flow increased substantially, supporting debt reduction and share repurchases**  
   Net cash provided by operations was \$297.5 million for the first half of 2015, up from \$204.0 million in the same period of 2014, reflecting improved profitability and working capital management. The company used cash to repurchase convertible notes and common stock, including a \$100 million authorized stock repurchase program approved in April 2015. Debt and capital lease obligations decreased from approximately \$1.05 billion at the end of 2014 to \$914 million by September 30, 2015, with leverage ratios improving from 3.6x at Q1 to 3.1x by Q3 2015. Unrestricted cash and short-term investments remained strong, fluctuating between \$488 million and \$611 million during the year, ending at \$560 million at year-end. The company had no outstanding borrowings under its \$175 million revolving credit facility during 2015. [8-K 2015-04-23; 8-K 2015-07-28; 8-K 2015-10-19; 8-K 2016-01-26; 10-Q 2015-07-30]

### Operations Insights

4. **Capacity grew moderately by 3.8% in 2015, with passenger traffic up 4.7%, improving load factor slightly to 81.6%**  
   Available seat miles (ASM) increased to 17.7 billion in 2015 from 17.1 billion in 2014. Revenue passenger miles (RPM) grew 3.9% to 14.46 billion, while passenger load factor edged up 0.1 points to 81.6%. Passenger counts rose 4.7% to 10.67 million. Capacity growth was driven by fleet additions and network expansion, including new routes and increased frequencies on key North America and Neighbor Island routes. [10-K 2016-02-08; 8-K 2015-07-28; 8-K 2015-10-19]

5. **Network concentrated primarily on Hawaiian Islands and U.S. mainland, with 75% of passenger revenue from these markets in 2015**  
   Hawaiian’s route structure consists of Neighbor Island, North America, and International routes. Approximately 75% of passenger revenue in 2015 was generated on routes between the Hawaiian Islands and the U.S. mainland or among the islands themselves. The airline served 11 U.S. gateway cities nonstop to Hawai‘i, more than any other carrier, and operated about 213 daily scheduled flights at year-end, including approximately 160 intra-island jet flights. International service included destinations in Japan, Australia, South Korea, China, New Zealand, American Samoa, and Tahiti. [10-K 2016-02-08; 8-K 2016-01-26]

6. **Fleet modernization and capacity adjustments included retirement of Boeing 767s and additions of Airbus A330s and ATR turboprops**  
   At December 31, 2015, the fleet consisted of 18 Boeing 717-200s for Neighbor Island routes, 8 Boeing 767-300s, and 22 Airbus A330-200s for North America and international routes, plus three ATR42 turboprops for Neighbor Island service. During 2015, Hawaiian added three A330-200 aircraft under lease financing, returned two Boeing 767-300s at lease end, and purchased three ATR72 turboprops configured for cargo expansion. The comprehensive interior retrofit of the Boeing 717 fleet was completed in 2015. [8-K 2016-01-26; 8-K 2015-10-19; 10-K 2016-02-08]

7. **Operational challenges in summer 2015 due to Honolulu gate shortages and air traffic control changes caused delays**  
   Hawaiian reported that construction-related gate shortages at Honolulu International Airport and abrupt changes in air traffic control procedures lengthened flights and led to operational delays in summer 2015. Management acknowledged these external challenges affected on-time performance despite the airline’s leading national ranking in punctuality for the prior 11 years. [8-K 2015-10-19]

### Commercial Strategy Insights

8. **Revenue per available seat mile (RASM) declined 3.0% in 2015 due to yield pressure and currency headwinds despite higher load factors**  
   Operating revenue per ASM fell to 13.07¢ in 2015 from 13.47¢ in 2014, a 3.0% decrease. Passenger yield (revenue per revenue passenger mile) declined 4.6% to 14.02¢, attributed to a stronger U.S. dollar impacting international fares and the reduction of fuel surcharges. Load factor improvements partially offset yield declines, but overall unit revenue softened. Other operating revenue, including frequent flyer mile sales and cargo, increased 8.2%, helping total revenue remain stable year-over-year. [10-K 2016-02-08; 8-K 2015-01-29; 8-K 2015-07-28]

9. **Expanded seasonal and new routes, including year-round service from Los Angeles to Lihu‘e and increased Japan flights**  
   Hawaiian reintroduced seasonal summer services from Los Angeles and Oakland to Lihu‘e and Kona with plans to start year-round service between Los Angeles and Lihu‘e in January 2016. The airline also announced expanded service to Japan, adding daily nonstop flights from Honolulu to Tokyo Narita starting July 2016. These network moves aimed to deepen penetration in key feeder markets and international gateways. [8-K 2016-01-26; 8-K 2015-07-28]

10. **Product upgrades included completion of Boeing 717 interior retrofit and launch of new premium A330 cabin for 2016**  
    The comprehensive interior refurbishment of the Boeing 717-200 fleet was completed in 2015, standardizing seat configurations. Hawaiian also announced a new premium cabin featuring 180-degree lie-flat seats on A330 aircraft starting in 2016, targeting enhanced customer experience on longer-haul international and North America routes. The airline debuted a new onboard safety video featuring crew and family members, reinforcing brand identity. [8-K 2016-01-26; 8-K 2015-10-19]

### Labor Insights

11. **Wages and benefits rose 11.6% in 2015, reflecting increased staffing and wage pressures amid capacity growth**  
    Wages and benefits expense increased to \$500 million in 2015 from \$447 million in 2014. Employee headcount was 5,439 as of mid-2015. The rise in labor costs aligned with expanded operations and fleet growth. No material labor disputes or contract renewals were disclosed for 2015. [10-Q 2015-07-30; 10-K 2016-02-08]

### Corporate Insights

12. **Currency and market concentration risks remain material due to revenue dependence on Hawaiian and U.S. mainland markets and foreign currency exposure**  
    Approximately 75% of passenger revenue derives from the Hawaiian Islands and U.S. mainland routes, concentrating exposure to regional demand and competitive dynamics. Strengthening of the U.S. dollar negatively impacted international yields and revenue. Hawaiian acknowledged competitive disadvantages relative to larger network carriers with more diversified geographic footprints. Fuel price volatility and currency fluctuations are ongoing market risks partially mitigated through hedging programs. [10-K 2016-02-08; 8-K 2015-01-29; 10-Q 2015-04-24]

---

### Wrap Up

In 2015, Hawaiian Airlines delivered record profitability supported by sharply lower fuel costs, moderate capacity growth, and improved operational efficiency. Despite flat total operating revenue and softer unit revenues driven by currency headwinds and yield pressure, cost control and fuel savings expanded margins substantially. The airline invested in fleet modernization, refurbished its Boeing 717 fleet, and prepared to introduce a new premium cabin product. Operational challenges at Honolulu airport and competitive pressures in core Hawaiian-U.S. mainland markets were noted risks. Labor costs increased in line with growth, while liquidity remained robust, enabling debt reduction and share repurchases.

Management’s outlook for 2016 emphasized continuing the maturation of recent route expansions, cost discipline, and enhancement of value-added products, while anticipating a moderation of the U.S. dollar’s negative impact on international markets. No material litigation, regulatory, or catastrophic operational events were disclosed for 2015. The company’s financial and operational performance reflects the concentrated nature of its network and exposure to jet fuel and currency market risks, managed through hedging and prudent capital allocation.

2016.Q1:
### Financial Insights

1. **Hawaiian Airlines reported a 2.0% increase in operating revenue to \$551.2 million in Q1 2016, driven by a 2.7% rise in passenger revenue to \$482.0 million.** Passenger revenue growth was primarily from domestic routes, which increased by \$25.4 million due to higher capacity (+6.1% ASM), improved load factor, and slightly higher yields. 7. **Available seat miles (ASM) increased 3.3% to 4.37 billion, while revenue passenger miles (RPM) rose 5.8% to 3.54 billion, lifting load factor by 2.0 points to 81.1%.** Passenger yield declined 2.9% to 13.61 cents, and PRASM (passenger revenue per ASM) was down 0.5% to 11.04 cents, reflecting the mix effect of increased domestic capacity and weaker international yields. 13. **The frequent flyer program, HawaiianMiles, contributed to other operating revenue through sales of miles, but no material changes in program economics or accounting were reported for Q1 2016.** The company noted pending accounting standard changes that will affect revenue recognition for miles earned, with potential significant impacts when adopted [10-K filed 2016-02-08; 10-Q filed 2016-04-22].

In Q1 2016, Hawaiian Airlines delivered improved financial results driven by revenue growth on domestic routes, a substantial reduction in fuel costs, and disciplined cost management despite rising labor expenses. Labor agreements contributed to higher non-fuel unit costs, partially offset by fuel savings. Market risks from fuel price volatility and foreign exchange remain, with derivative instruments introducing earnings volatility. Hawaiian’s revenue concentration in Hawai'i-related markets and competitive environment continue to pose strategic challenges.

   Fuel gallons consumed rose 4.2% to 244.1 million gallons, consistent with capacity growth. The average economic fuel cost per gallon declined 25.5% to \$1.52, reducing fuel expense despite higher consumption. Fuel costs represented 17% of operating expenses in 2016, down from 22% in 2015, reflecting both the fuel price decline and improved fuel efficiency [10-K 2017-02-16; 8-K 2017-01-24].

### Labor Insights

9. **Labor costs increased due to wage growth, profit sharing, and new collective bargaining agreements.**  
   Wages and benefits rose 11.2% to \$555.5 million in 2016, driven by labor contract ratifications and a \$5 million profit sharing bonus paid in December 2016. The company also expected to record a \$20 million payment upon ratification of a proposed collective bargaining agreement reached with contract groups during the year.     Hawaiian continued to serve more U.S. gateway cities (11) nonstop than any other airline, with daily flights to multiple California cities, Las Vegas, Phoenix, Portland, Seattle, and New York City. Internationally, new service to Tokyo’s Narita and Haneda airports was added in 2016. ### Corporate Insights

11. **Market risk exposures managed via fuel and currency hedges; concentration in Hawai‘i market remains a risk.**  
    Hawaiian faces commodity price risk from jet fuel and foreign currency risk, mitigated by financial derivatives and hedging instruments. Fuel costs comprised 17% of operating expenses in 2016. The company’s revenue is heavily concentrated in Hawai‘i and between Hawai‘i and the U.S. mainland—about 74% of passenger revenue in 2016—exposing it to region-specific demand or capacity shifts. Management acknowledged that reduced demand or increased competition on these routes would have a disproportionate adverse impact on financial results [10-K 2017-02-16].

### Wrap Up

In 2016, Hawaiian Airlines delivered significant financial improvement, with net income rising over 25% and margins expanding, supported by revenue growth, disciplined capacity increases, and substantially lower fuel costs. Operational expansion included new Asian routes and fleet additions, driving record passenger volumes and higher load factors. Labor costs increased due to collective bargaining agreements and profit sharing, partially offsetting fuel savings. The company maintained a strong liquidity position with manageable debt. Notable fourth-quarter charges for Boeing 767 fleet impairment and labor bonuses affected adjusted earnings but did not obscure the underlying operational progress.

Management’s disclosed risks center on fuel price volatility, currency fluctuations, and the airline’s concentrated market exposure to Hawai‘i and its main visitor corridors. Hawaiian’s strategy for 2017 focuses on maturing recently launched routes, enhancing sales channels, cost discipline, and value-added service offerings, aiming to sustain profitability within its unique geographic and competitive environment. No material operational disruptions, regulatory actions, or litigation affecting financials were reported for 2016.

7. **Capacity increased 3.5% in 2017Q1 measured by available seat miles (ASMs), with passenger traffic rising 7.2% in revenue passenger miles (RPMs), leading to a 2.9-point improvement in load factor to 84.0%.** Passenger count grew 2.2% to 2.7 million. ### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ 2017Q1 results reflect a revenue increase driven by higher fares, load factors, and international route expansions, offset by rising fuel prices and labor costs that compressed GAAP net income and margins. The airline grew capacity modestly while improving operational efficiency metrics such as load factor and yield. Fuel expenses surged due to both increased consumption and a sharp rise in fuel prices, despite a fuel hedge program covering about 41% of 2017 requirements. Labor costs increased significantly following a new pilot contract and benefit cost reclassifications. Hawaiian maintained strong liquidity with \$740 million in cash and investments and reduced debt levels in 2016. The fleet plan includes retiring aging Boeing 767s by end-2018 and future deliveries of fuel-efficient Airbus A321neo and A330-800neo aircraft.

Management raised 2017 capacity and fuel consumption guidance and expects continued pressure on operating costs, with CASM excluding fuel projected to rise mid-single digits for the full year. The company’s financial and operational performance remains closely tied to tourism flows to Hawai‘i and fuel market volatility, with labor negotiations ongoing for flight attendants. The rise in fuel cost per gallon was 20.0% in Q4 to \$1.86, with economic fuel costs per gallon increasing 21.9% to \$1.84 [8-K 2018-01-29]. ### Operations Insights

7. **Passenger traffic grew 6.7% in Q4 2017 to 2.91 million passengers, with revenue passenger miles (RPMs) up 4.9% and available seat miles (ASMs) up 5.0%, resulting in a stable load factor of 86.0%.**

### Commercial Strategy Insights

10. **Revenue growth was supported by yield improvements of 2.8% in Q4 and 4.5% for the full year, driven by strong demand and relatively steady industry capacity, especially on North America routes.**

11. **The Company announced a new partnership with Japan Airlines effective March 25, 2018, involving code sharing, lounge access, and frequent flyer reciprocity, with plans to pursue a joint venture subject to antitrust immunity.**  
    This alliance aims to enhance connectivity between Hawai‘i and Japan, expanding customer options [8-K 2017-10-19; 10-K 2018-02-13].

### Labor Insights

12. **Labor costs increased significantly with wages and benefits up 19.1% in Q4 and 18.3% for the full year, reflecting contract amendments and benefit plan terminations.**

The Company was negotiating with the Flight Attendants union (AFA), representing 29% of employees, with no assurance of timely resolution as of year-end [8-K 2017-10-19; 10-K 2018-02-13].

### Route Network Insights

13. **The Company continued to expand its network in 2017 and early 2018, including new daily non-stop service between Portland and Maui starting January 2018, and announced additional new routes from San Diego and Long Beach to Hawai‘i for mid-2018.**  
    Seasonal service expansions included daily non-stop flights between Narita and Honolulu and increased frequencies between Honolulu and Auckland, New Zealand [8-K 2018-01-29].

14. **Hawaiian planned to retire its Boeing 767-300 fleet by the end of 2018, supported by sale-leaseback transactions in 2017 and an agreement to purchase three 767s in 2018 for subsequent sale, aligning with fleet modernization goals.**  
    This reflects a strategic shift toward newer aircraft like the A321neo and A330-200 [8-K 2018-01-29; 10-K 2018-02-13].

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ fourth quarter 2017 results capped a year of record earnings and passenger growth, driven by expanded capacity, improved yields, and disciplined cost management despite rising fuel prices and increased labor costs. The fleet modernization advanced with new A321neos and cargo turboprops, while the route network grew with new U.S. West Coast and international services. Labor negotiations with flight attendants remained unresolved at year-end, representing a potential operational risk. Capital returned to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases, supported by solid liquidity and manageable debt levels.

Looking ahead, the Company projected modest capacity growth of 3.0% to 5.0% for Q1 2018, with expected increases in fuel consumption and operating costs primarily due to wages and pilot training for the new A321neos. The new partnership with Japan Airlines and ongoing fleet renewal indicate strategic efforts to strengthen competitive positioning, while risks from fuel price volatility, labor negotiations, and industry capacity remain relevant variables. No material operational disruptions, accidents, or regulatory actions were disclosed for the period.

For 2017, Hawaiian Airlines reported record passengers, revenue, and net income, driven by moderate capacity growth, improved load factors, and higher yields. 4. **Operating expenses increased 14.1% year-over-year in 2018 to \$2.5 billion, led by a 36.1% surge in aircraft fuel costs and an 8.2% rise in wages and benefits.** Fuel expense rose from \$440.4 million in 2017 to \$599.5 million in 2018 due to a 23.5% increase in economic fuel cost per gallon (\$2.10 vs. \$1.70) and 5.3% higher fuel consumption. Wages and benefits increased to \$684.7 million from \$633.0 million, reflecting capacity growth and presumably wage inflation [10-K 2019-02-13; 8-K 2019-01-29].

5. **Unit costs per available seat mile (CASM) increased due to fuel and maintenance costs, with Q4 2018 CASM (GAAP) estimated between 12.29¢ and 12.62¢, and CASM excluding fuel between 9.35¢ and 9.54¢.** The increase in CASM excluding fuel was partly offset by lower aircraft rent (-7% in Q4 2018 vs. prior year) and some non-recurring maintenance cost offsets. Fuel cost per gallon averaged \$2.20 in Q4, up nearly 20% year-over-year [8-K 2018-12-06; 8-K 2019-01-29].

6. **The company returned \$126.7 million to shareholders during 2018 via \$102.5 million in share repurchases and \$24.2 million in dividends, and announced a new \$100 million share repurchase program through 2020.** At year-end, unrestricted cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments totaled \$501 million, with outstanding debt and capital lease obligations of \$710 million [8-K 2019-01-29].

### Operations Insights

7. **Hawaiian carried a record 11.8 million passengers in 2018, a 2.9% increase over 2017, and operated 5.07 billion available seat miles (ASM) in Q4, up 5.6% year-over-year.** Revenue passenger miles (RPM) grew 3.9% in Q4 to 4.29 billion, but load factor declined 1.4 points to 84.6%. For the full year, RPM increased 5.5% to 17.21 billion, ASM rose 6.1% to 20.17 billion, and load factor dipped 0.5 points to 85.3% [8-K 2019-01-10; 8-K 2019-01-29].

8. **Yield (passenger revenue per RPM) declined 2.5% in Q4 2018 to 14.92¢, and full year yield decreased 0.8% to 15.13¢, pressured by competitive capacity and softer pricing in North America and Neighbor Island markets.** Passenger revenue per ASM (PRASM) fell 3.6% in Q4 to 13.04¢ and 0.5% for the year to 13.01¢ [8-K 2019-01-29].

9. **Capacity growth was focused on North America and Neighbor Island routes, including expansions to Southern California and the Pacific Northwest, and new service announced to Boston starting April 2019.** The fleet grew with the delivery of nine Airbus A321neo aircraft in 2018, bringing the total to 11, supporting expansion on U.S. West Coast routes. The company plans to retire all Boeing 767-300s in early 2019, completing the transition to a more modern, single-aisle fleet for better capacity management [8-K 2019-01-10; 10-K 2019-02-13].

10. **Fuel consumption increased 5.3% year-over-year in 2018 to 273.8 million gallons, with economic fuel cost per gallon rising 23.5% to \$2.10, driving a 36.1% increase in total fuel expense.** The company hedged approximately 34% of its 2019 fuel requirements as of December 31, 2018, with fuel derivatives not designated for hedge accounting, causing volatility in reported earnings [8-K 2019-01-29; 10-K 2019-02-13].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

11. **Other operating revenue grew 24.6% in 2018 to \$234.6 million, primarily driven by a \$31.8 million increase in loyalty program income due to an amended co-branded credit card partnership with Barclays, and \$9.0 million in higher cargo revenue from increased freight volumes and a new inter-island cargo freighter operation.** The loyalty program enhancements included reciprocal frequent flyer benefits with Japan Airlines and an expanded codeshare partnership with JetBlue, including new connections via Boston [10-K 2019-02-13; 8-K 2019-01-29].

12. **Hawaiian filed for antitrust immunity with Japan Airlines to create a joint venture aimed at service expansion and consumer benefits, with operations expected to commence in late 2019 pending regulatory approval.** This partnership builds on existing codeshare and frequent flyer reciprocal benefits launched earlier in 2018 [8-K 2019-01-29; 10-K 2019-02-13].

### Labor Insights

13. **As of December 31, 2018, approximately 84% of Hawaiian’s employees were unionized, with the Association of Flight Attendants (representing 29% of employees) in collective bargaining negotiations since January 2017.** The company disclosed uncertainty about the timing or success of these negotiations [10-K 2019-02-13].

### Route Network Insights

14. **Hawaiian expanded its domestic U.S. mainland network in 2018 with new daily nonstop flights to Long Beach and San Diego, expanded service to Maui and Kona, and announced new service from Boston starting April 2019, increasing connectivity to Hawai'i.** The fleet transition to A321neos supports these longer thin routes, with retirement of older Boeing 767-300 aircraft planned in early 2019 [8-K 2019-01-10; 10-K 2019-02-13].

15. **Internationally, passenger revenue increased 12.0% in 2018 driven by higher passenger counts and fares on routes to Japan, Australia, South Korea, and other Pacific destinations, despite suspending service to Beijing in October 2018.** The international network benefits from partnerships with Japan Airlines and other carriers, enhancing market access [10-K 2019-02-13; 10-Q 2018-10-24].

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ 2018 fourth quarter and full year results reflect a challenging environment marked by rising fuel costs, increased competitive capacity, and weather disruptions that pressured yields and margins despite record passenger traffic and modest revenue growth. The company managed a 5.6% capacity increase in Q4 and expanded its U.S. mainland and international network, supported by fleet modernization with A321neos and plans to retire older widebody aircraft. Operating expenses, especially fuel and labor-related costs, rose sharply, compressing margins and net income compared to 2017. Hawaiian’s commercial strategy included loyalty program growth and strategic partnerships, notably with Japan Airlines, positioning for future network expansion. Labor negotiations remain ongoing with a significant portion of the workforce unionized. Liquidity was solid with \$501 million in cash and investments, and the company returned capital to shareholders while maintaining \$710 million in debt.

**Guidance for 2019 Q1 and Full Year:** Hawaiian expects ASM growth of 1.5% to 3.0% in Q1 2019, with operating revenue per ASM down 3.0% to 6.0%, and cost per ASM excluding fuel up 1.0% to 4.0%. Fuel gallons consumed are expected to decline slightly, with fuel cost per gallon forecasted between \$1.91 and \$2.05. The effective tax rate is guided at 25% to 27% for the full year 2019. The company anticipates completing its fleet transition by retiring all Boeing 767s in early 2019 and continuing to mature routes and improve cost structure [8-K 2019-01-29].

In 2018, Hawaiian Airlines grew its top-line passenger and other revenues, supported by record passenger traffic and fleet expansion, especially with Airbus A321neo deliveries. ### Financial Insights

1. **Slight revenue decline despite increased capacity; net income down year-over-year**  
   For Q2 2019, Hawaiian Airlines reported operating revenue of \$712.2 million, a 0.5% decrease from \$715.4 million in Q2 2018, despite a 2.7% increase in available seat miles (ASMs) to 5.15 billion. Passenger revenue was \$653.4 million, down 0.3%, reflecting a 3.7% increase in revenue passenger miles (RPMs) but a 3.7% decline in passenger yield to 14.56 cents per RPM. Operating cost per ASM (CASM) decreased 2.5% to 12.09 cents, driven largely by an 8.1% reduction in aircraft fuel expense. However, wages and benefits rose 5.0% to \$180.1 million, and depreciation and amortization increased 20.1% to \$39.5 million due to fleet additions. GAAP net income for Q2 2019 was \$57.8 million, down \$21.6 million from \$79.5 million in Q2 2018, with diluted EPS of \$1.21 versus \$1.56. The decline in net income reflects lower yields and increased labor and depreciation costs, partially offset by fuel cost savings [8-K 2019-07-30, 10-Q 2019-07-30].

   Aircraft fuel expense declined 8.1% to \$140.6 million due to a 2.0% reduction in gallons consumed (67.3 million gallons) and a 6.3% decrease in average fuel price per gallon to \$2.09. However, realized losses on fuel derivative contracts of \$3.1 million in Q2 2019 contrasted with \$10.8 million gains in Q2 2018, resulting in a 1.0% increase in economic fuel expense to \$143.7 million. Fuel accounted for 23% of operating expenses in Q2 2019, down from 25% in the prior year period. As of June 30, 2019, Hawaiian hedged approximately 48% of its projected fuel needs for the remainder of 2019 with crude oil call options [10-Q 2019-07-30].

   CASM excluding aircraft fuel and non-recurring items rose 0.3% to 9.38 cents per ASM in Q2 2019. This increase was driven by a 5.0% rise in wages and benefits to \$180.1 million and a 20.1% increase in depreciation and amortization to \$39.5 million due to the addition of nine Airbus A321neo aircraft since June 2018. Maintenance expenses declined 4.7%, but aircraft and passenger servicing costs increased 2.6% [10-Q 2019-07-30].

4. **Capital returned to shareholders and strong liquidity position maintained**  
   In Q2 2019, Hawaiian returned \$25.3 million to shareholders via \$19.6 million in share repurchases and \$5.7 million in dividends. As of June 30, 2019, unrestricted cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments totaled \$539 million, compared to outstanding debt and finance lease obligations of \$565 million. The Board declared a quarterly cash dividend of 12 cents per share payable August 30, 2019 [8-K 2019-07-30].

### Operations Insights

5. **Capacity growth of 2.7% with improved load factor and increased block hours**  
   Hawaiian increased ASMs by 2.7% to 5.15 billion in Q2 2019. Revenue passenger miles rose 3.7% to 4.49 billion, resulting in an improved passenger load factor of 87.1%, up 0.8 points from 86.3% in Q2 2018. Revenue block hours operated increased 6.5% to 54,840 hours, reflecting higher utilization of the fleet [10-Q 2019-07-30].

   During the first half of 2019, Hawaiian took delivery of three Airbus A321neo aircraft, increasing the total A321neo fleet to 13 as of June 30, 2019, with plans to add four more in 2019 and a final 18th in early 2020. The company retired its Boeing 717-200 aircraft facility with scheduled payments of approximately \$45 million, increasing its unencumbered fleet to 37 aircraft. Depreciation increased accordingly due to the larger owned fleet [8-K 2019-07-30, 10-Q 2019-07-30].

7. **Fuel efficiency improved via operational initiatives including adoption of Pacelab Flight Profile Optimizer**  
   Hawaiian became the first U.S. airline to adopt the Pacelab Flight Profile Optimizer, a software application that uses real-time aircraft and weather data to optimize flight routes for safety, comfort, and fuel efficiency. This initiative aims to reduce annual fuel consumption and carbon emissions, contributing to the 8.1% reduction in fuel expense [8-K 2019-07-30].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

8. **Revenue mix shifted with domestic capacity reductions on short-haul routes and international capacity declines**  
   Domestic operating revenue decreased by \$8.9 million for the six months ended June 30, 2019, primarily due to a 2.3% decline in passengers flown and a 2.4% reduction in average fares, attributed to capacity reductions on shorter haul routes that outpaced growth on longer haul routes. International revenue decreased by \$3.8 million in Q2 2019 due to reduced capacity. Despite this, Hawaiian expanded service with new routes launched in 2019, including five-times-weekly nonstop service between Honolulu and Boston, daily service between Kahului and Sacramento, and announced additional daily flights between San Francisco and Honolulu starting October 2019 [10-Q 2019-07-30, 10-Q 2019-04-24].

Operating revenue per ASM declined 3.1% to 13.81 cents. Management noted ongoing competitive pressures in the domestic market with industry capacity at historically high levels [10-Q 2019-07-30, 10-Q 2019-04-24].

10. **Partnerships advanced with Japan Airlines and Virgin Australia to expand network and frequent flyer benefits**  
    Hawaiian and Japan Airlines filed for antitrust immunity in 2018 to create a joint venture for expanded service and consumer benefits. Reciprocal frequent flyer benefits between HawaiianMiles and JAL Mileage Bank members became effective in October 2018. Additionally, an expanded codeshare agreement with Virgin Australia launched in April 2019 broadened access for travelers from Australia and New Zealand [10-Q 2019-07-30, 10-Q 2019-04-24, 8-K 2019-04-23].

### Labor Insights

11. **Workforce grew slightly with 7,360 active employees as of June 30, 2019; labor costs increased 5%**  
    Hawaiian’s active employee count rose from 7,299 at March 31, 2019, to 7,360 at June 30, 2019. Wages and benefits expense increased 5.0% year-over-year to \$180.1 million in Q2 2019, reflecting wage inflation and possibly expanded staffing to support network growth and operational demands [10-Q 2019-07-30].

### Route Network Insights

12. **Network expansion included new East Coast and West Coast routes and increased Tokyo service**  
    In Q2 2019, Hawaiian launched new nonstop services between Honolulu and Boston, Kahului and Sacramento, and announced additional daily flights between San Francisco and Honolulu starting October 2019. The company also received tentative U.S. Department of Transportation approval to allocate a new slot for service to Tokyo Haneda Airport, expected to begin before the 2020 Olympic Games, expanding existing Tokyo-Honolulu and Tokyo-Kona routes [8-K 2019-07-30, 10-Q 2019-07-30].

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ 2019 Q2 results reveal a mixed financial and operational picture. Revenue edged slightly lower despite capacity growth, driven by yield declines and softer demand in certain domestic and international markets. Operating costs benefited from lower fuel prices and consumption, but increased labor and depreciation expenses compressed margins and net income. The airline continued fleet modernization with Airbus A321neo deliveries and retired older Boeing 717-200 aircraft, supporting operational efficiency initiatives including advanced flight optimization software.

Commercially, Hawaiian expanded its network with new East and West Coast routes and advanced partnerships with Japan Airlines and Virgin Australia, positioning for growth in transpacific markets pending regulatory approvals. Labor costs rose modestly alongside a slight workforce increase. Liquidity remained strong with substantial cash reserves and manageable debt, alongside ongoing shareholder returns via dividends and share repurchases.

**Guidance Summary:** For Q3 2019, Hawaiian expected ASMs to range between a 1.5% decrease and a 0.5% increase year-over-year, operating revenue per ASM to decline between 1.5% and 4.5%, and operating cost per ASM (excluding fuel and non-recurring items) to increase 3.5% to 6.5%. For full-year 2019, ASMs were projected to grow 1.5% to 2.5%, with operating cost per ASM (excluding fuel and non-recurring items) increasing 1.0% to 2.5%, and an effective tax rate between 26% and 28% [8-K 2019-07-30, 10-Q 2019-07-30]. 2. **Operating revenue decreased 0.5% year-over-year to \$755.2 million, driven by a 0.4% decline in passenger revenue and a 1.6% drop in other revenue.** Passenger revenue fell to \$694.3 million from \$697.2 million in 2018Q3, while other operating revenue declined to \$60.9 million from \$61.9 million. Total operating revenue was \$755.2 million versus \$759.1 million in 2018Q3 [10-Q 2019-10-22].

3. **Operating expenses declined 0.7% to \$638.5 million, led by a 14.9% reduction in aircraft fuel expense, partially offset by higher wages and benefits (+3.5%) and maintenance costs (+7.4%).** Fuel expense fell to \$138.6 million from \$162.9 million due to lower fuel prices and consumption. Wages and benefits rose to \$182.9 million from \$176.6 million, and maintenance expenses increased to \$61.4 million from \$57.1 million. Depreciation and amortization increased 14.4% to \$41.6 million reflecting fleet additions [10-Q 2019-10-22].

4. **Unit costs per available seat mile (CASM) were essentially flat year-over-year at 11.98 cents, with CASM ex-fuel and non-recurring items rising 4.9% to 9.38 cents.** Fuel cost per ASM declined from 3.05 to 2.60 cents, reflecting favorable fuel prices and consumption. The increase in CASM excluding fuel indicates rising non-fuel operating costs [10-Q 2019-10-22, 8-K 2019-10-07].

5. **Fuel consumption fell 3.3% to 69.7 million gallons, with average fuel price per gallon down 11.9% to \$1.99, driving an 8.3% decrease in economic fuel expense to \$142.0 million.** Fuel costs represented 22% of operating expenses in 2019Q3 versus 25% in 2018Q3. The company’s fuel hedging program resulted in realized losses of \$3.4 million in the quarter, reversing prior gains [10-Q 2019-10-22].

6. **Cash and short-term investments grew to \$745 million at quarter end, up from \$738 million at June 30, 2019, while total debt and finance lease obligations increased to \$782 million from \$565 million at June 30, 2019.** The company returned \$25.7 million to shareholders in the quarter via \$20.0 million in share repurchases and a \$5.7 million dividend. The increase in debt reflects new Japanese Yen-denominated debt collateralized by aircraft and lease extensions [8-K 2019-10-22, 8-K 2019-07-30, 10-Q 2019-10-22].

### Operations Insights

7. **Third quarter 2019 system-wide revenue passenger miles (RPM) rose 2.7% to 4.68 billion on a 0.4% decrease in available seat miles (ASM), lifting load factor 2.7 points to 87.8%.** Passenger traffic growth combined with slightly reduced capacity improved operational efficiency. Revenue passengers increased 1.1% to 3.07 million [8-K 2019-10-07, 10-Q 2019-10-22].

8. **Passenger yield declined 3.0% to 14.85 cents per RPM, while passenger revenue per ASM (PRASM) was flat at 13.05 cents, reflecting higher load factors offsetting lower yields.** Operating revenue per ASM (RASM) was also essentially unchanged at 14.16 cents. The yield decline is attributed to competitive pressures and capacity shifts between short- and long-haul routes [10-Q 2019-10-22].

9. **Revenue block hours increased 1.7% to 56,088 hours, with a 3.3% reduction in fuel gallons consumed per block hour, reflecting operational efficiencies and fleet modernization.** The fleet included six additional Airbus A321neo aircraft placed into service since September 2018, contributing to lower fuel consumption and higher utilization [10-Q 2019-10-22, 8-K 2019-07-30].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

10. **Hawaiian expanded its route network with new services planned or commenced in 2019, including additional daily flights between Honolulu and San Francisco, and new routes to Fukuoka, Japan, and Las Vegas.** The company received U.S. Department of Transportation approval for an additional daily nonstop flight between Tokyo Haneda and Honolulu starting March 2020. Seasonal and supplemental services were also announced for key routes using the A321neo fleet [8-K 2019-10-22, 10-Q 2019-07-30].

11. **The company introduced Main Cabin Basic fares in all North American markets in September-October 2019, targeting price-sensitive travelers amid heightened competition.** This fare option adds to Hawaiian’s product portfolio and is part of its strategy to address competitive pressures on yields [8-K 2019-10-22].

12. **Hawaiian and Japan Airlines continued to pursue a joint venture with antitrust immunity (ATI), receiving a tentative ruling from the U.S. DOT to approve the joint venture without ATI in September 2019.** Hawaiian is preparing a substantive response to seek reconsideration of the ATI determination, indicating ongoing regulatory risk related to the partnership [10-Q 2019-10-22].

### Route Network Insights

13. **Fleet modernization progressed with the delivery of two Airbus A321neo aircraft in 2019Q3, increasing the A321neo fleet to 15 aircraft, while the Boeing 717-200 fleet was retired.** The company extended leases on three A330 aircraft for cost savings and flexibility, and entered into Japanese Yen-denominated debt financing collateralized by four A330s and two A321neos [8-K 2019-10-22, 8-K 2019-07-30].

14. **System capacity (ASM) was reduced slightly by 0.4% in 2019Q3, reflecting capacity rationalization on shorter-haul routes offset by growth in longer-haul international and domestic markets.** This capacity management contributed to increased load factors and stabilized unit revenues [8-K 2019-10-07, 10-Q 2019-10-22].

### Labor Insights

15. **The workforce grew modestly to 7,389 active employees as of September 30, 2019, up from 7,360 at June 30, 2019.** Wages and benefits expense increased 3.5% year-over-year in 2019Q3, reflecting wage inflation and staffing levels consistent with operational expansion [10-Q 2019-10-22].

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ 2019 third quarter results show modest revenue pressure amid intensifying competition, with a slight decline in passenger yields offset by improved load factors and capacity discipline. Fuel cost reductions driven by lower prices and consumption helped contain operating expenses, though non-fuel costs increased. The company maintained solid profitability and cash generation, returning capital to shareholders while increasing debt to finance fleet acquisitions and lease extensions. Operationally, Hawaiian optimized capacity with a focus on longer-haul routes and expanded its network with new flights, including international service growth supported by fleet modernization, notably the growing Airbus A321neo presence.

Commercially, Hawaiian responded to competitive fare pressures by introducing Main Cabin Basic fares and advancing a strategic partnership with Japan Airlines, though regulatory uncertainty remains regarding antitrust immunity. Labor costs rose moderately consistent with workforce growth and operational needs. The company’s liquidity position strengthened significantly, with cash and investments of \$745 million at quarter-end, supporting ongoing capital commitments and shareholder returns. The fleet and route network initiatives position Hawaiian for continued network expansion into 2020, balanced against the challenges of competitive yield pressure and regulatory risk related to its joint venture efforts.

**Guidance Overview:** For 2019Q3, Hawaiian raised its operating revenue per ASM expectations due to better-than-anticipated yields in long-haul markets, particularly international. It narrowed its operating cost per ASM guidance range, expecting a slight increase to a slight decrease year-over-year. For the full year 2019, Hawaiian projects a corporate effective tax rate of 26% to 28%, expects a 1.5% to 2.5% increase in ASMs, and anticipates a 2.1% to 3.2% decrease in cost per ASM, driven by fuel cost improvements and operational efficiencies [8-K 2019-10-22, 10-Q 2019-07-30, 10-Q 2019-10-22].
2019.Q4:
### Financial Insights

1. **Full-year 2019 net income declined by \$9.2 million to \$224.0 million despite a slight pre-tax margin improvement.** Hawaiian reported GAAP net income of \$224.0 million for 2019, down \$9.2 million from 2018, while pre-tax margin increased marginally by 0.2 points to 10.8% [8-K 2020-01-30]. Adjusted net income fell \$55.9 million to \$218.9 million, with adjusted pre-tax margin down 2.1 points to 10.5%. Diluted EPS rose slightly by \$0.09 to \$4.71 on a reduced share count [8-K 2020-01-30].

2. **Fourth quarter 2019 GAAP net income rose \$18.1 million to \$49.7 million, but adjusted net income fell \$3.3 million to \$45.9 million.** Q4 pre-tax margin improved by 3.6 points to 9.6%, though adjusted pre-tax margin declined 0.4 points to 8.9%. Diluted EPS increased to \$1.07 from \$0.64 in the prior year quarter [8-K 2020-01-30].

3. **Operating revenue was essentially flat for full-year 2019 at \$2.83 billion, with passenger revenue down 0.2%.** Passenger revenue totaled \$2.598 billion, a slight decrease from 2018, while other operating revenue was stable at \$234.5 million [10-K 2020-02-12]. Domestic routes generated approximately 74% of passenger revenue in 2019, consistent with prior years [10-K 2020-02-12].

4. **Operating expenses declined 0.7% to \$2.5 billion in 2019, driven primarily by a 9.5% reduction in aircraft fuel costs.** Fuel expense fell from \$599.5 million to \$542.6 million due to lower average fuel prices and modestly reduced consumption (270 million gallons vs. 274 million), with economic fuel cost per gallon stable at \$2.06 [10-K 2020-02-12; 8-K 2019-10-22]. Wage and benefit expenses increased 5.7% to \$723.7 million [10-K 2020-02-12].

5. **Cost per available seat mile (CASM) declined 3.1% for the full year to 12.16 cents, but CASM excluding fuel and non-recurring items rose 2.3%.** This indicates that fuel savings offset underlying cost pressures, including wage increases [10-Q 2019-10-22]. The company expected full-year 2019 CASM to decrease 2.3% to 2.9% [8-K 2019-10-22].

6. **Capital returned to shareholders totaled \$91.6 million in 2019 through \$68.8 million in share repurchases and \$22.8 million in dividends.** This reflects continued shareholder returns despite competitive and cost pressures [8-K 2020-01-30].

### Operations Insights

7. **System capacity (available seat miles, ASM) grew 2.0% in 2019 while revenue passenger miles (RPM) rose 3.5%, improving load factor by 1.3 points to 86.6%.** Fourth quarter ASM increased 3.6% and RPM 5.6%, with a 1.6 point load factor gain to 86.2% [8-K 2020-01-30; 10-K 2020-02-12]. This suggests better utilization and demand relative to capacity.
