8. **Passenger yield (revenue per RPM) declined 3.6% for the full year and 3.8% in Q4, reflecting competitive pricing pressure.** Passenger revenue per ASM (PRASM) dropped about 2.2% for the year [8-K 2020-01-30; 10-K 2020-02-12].

9. **Fleet changes included delivery of six Airbus A321neo aircraft, increasing the A321neo fleet to 17, and retirement of the last Boeing 767 aircraft.** The company also extended leases on several Airbus A330 and Boeing 717 aircraft to manage costs while maintaining flexibility [8-K 2020-01-30; 10-K 2020-02-12].

10. **Route network expanded with new daily East Coast service between Boston and Honolulu, additional flights between Honolulu and San Francisco, and new international service to Fukuoka, Japan.** The company also received approval for an additional daily flight between Tokyo Haneda and Honolulu starting in 2020 [8-K 2020-01-30; 10-K 2020-02-12].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

11. **Hawaiian launched Main Cabin Basic fares in all North American markets to attract price-sensitive travelers, reflecting a strategic response to competitive pricing pressures.** The company also introduced a new mobile app to improve the day-of-travel experience [8-K 2020-01-30].

12. **Loyalty program revenue increased by \$15.7 million in 2019, driven by co-brand credit card partnerships and increased card acquisitions and spend.** Cargo and ground handling revenues declined by about \$15.9 million due to reduced volumes [10-K 2020-02-12].

### Labor Insights

13. **Wages and benefits expenses increased 5.7% in 2019 to \$723.7 million, reflecting wage growth and possibly staffing changes.** The company had approximately 7,389 active employees as of September 30, 2019 [10-K 2020-02-12; 10-Q 2019-10-22].

### Financial Risks and Outlook

14. **Fuel price and consumption volatility remain significant risks; fuel costs accounted for about 22% of operating expenses in 2019.** Hawaiian hedged approximately 35% of its projected 2020 fuel requirements as of December 31, 2019 [10-K 2020-02-12].

15. **The company faces a highly competitive environment on its North America routes, with multiple major network carriers and new entrants like Southwest Airlines expanding capacity in 2019 and 2020.** Approximately 74% of passenger revenue is concentrated on Domestic routes, increasing exposure to competitive pressure [10-K 2020-02-12].

16. **For Q4 2019, the company expected ASM growth of 3.0% to 4.5%, operating revenue per ASM to decline 0.5% to 3.5%, and cost per ASM excluding fuel to increase 0.5% to 3.5%.** Full year 2019 guidance projected ASM growth of 1.9% to 2.4% and CASM excluding fuel increase of 1.8% to 2.6% [8-K 2019-10-22].

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ 2019 fourth quarter and full year results reflected a challenging environment marked by modest capacity growth, improved load factors, and pressure on yields amid heightened North America route competition. The company reduced operating costs, primarily through lower fuel prices and consumption, which helped offset wage increases and other cost pressures. Earnings and margins showed mixed results, with GAAP net income slightly down for the year but improved in Q4. Fleet modernization continued with new A321neo deliveries and retirement of older aircraft, supporting operational efficiency and network expansion including new East Coast and Asian routes. Loyalty program revenue contributed growth, while cargo and ancillary revenues declined.

The airline's concentration in Hawai‘i-centric Domestic routes exposes it to competitive and demand risks, amplified by the entry of new competitors and capacity expansions by legacy carriers. Fuel price volatility remains a key cost risk, partially mitigated by hedging. Hawaiian’s financial flexibility supported continued shareholder returns through dividends and share repurchases in 2019. Guidance for the end of 2019 anticipated moderate capacity growth and stable to slightly declining unit revenues, with costs excluding fuel expected to rise modestly.

No material litigation, accidents, or labor disputes were disclosed for the period ending December 31, 2019. The company’s strategic focus on competitive fare products, network growth, and customer experience enhancements aimed to address competitive pressures in its core Hawai‘i markets.
2019.FY:
### Financial Insights

1. **Full-year 2019 net income declined modestly despite a slight pre-tax margin improvement**  
   Hawaiian Airlines reported GAAP net income of \$224.0 million for 2019, down \$9.2 million from \$233.2 million in 2018, while adjusted net income decreased more significantly by \$55.9 million to \$218.9 million [8-K 2020-01-30]. The GAAP pre-tax margin rose slightly by 0.2 points to 10.8%, but the adjusted pre-tax margin fell 2.1 points to 10.5% [8-K 2020-01-30]. Diluted EPS increased slightly on a GAAP basis to \$4.71 (+\$0.09) but declined on an adjusted basis to \$4.60 (-\$0.84) [8-K 2020-01-30]. The decline in adjusted net income and margin reflects underlying pressures despite stable headline profitability.

2. **Operating revenue was essentially flat year-over-year with a slight decline in passenger revenue per ASM (PRASM)**  
   Total operating revenue for 2019 was \$2.83 billion, essentially unchanged from \$2.84 billion in 2018 (-0.2%) [10-K 2020-02-12]. Passenger revenue decreased slightly (-0.2%), with PRASM down 2.2% to 12.37 cents [10-Q 2019-10-22]. Passenger yield declined 3.6% to 14.59 cents per revenue passenger mile (RPM), offset partially by a 1.3 point increase in load factor to 86.6% [10-Q 2019-10-22]. The combination of slightly lower yields and higher load factors implies a competitive environment with pressure on fares.

3. **Operating expenses grew moderately, driven by higher wages and benefits, partially offset by lower fuel costs**  
   Operating expenses rose 4.1% year-over-year to \$2.83 billion [10-K 2020-02-12]. Wages and benefits increased 5.7% to \$723.7 million, reflecting higher employee costs [8-K 2020-01-30; 10-K 2020-02-12]. Aircraft fuel expense declined 9.5% to \$542.6 million, driven by lower fuel prices and consumption [8-K 2020-01-30; 10-K 2020-02-12]. Other costs such as maintenance (+4.2%) and aircraft and passenger servicing (+4.1%) also rose. Depreciation and amortization increased 13.6%, reflecting ongoing capital investments [10-K 2020-02-12]. The net effect was a slight increase in cost per available seat mile (CASM) excluding fuel and non-recurring items by about 2.3% [8-K 2019-10-22].

4. **Fuel consumption declined slightly with lower average fuel costs, contributing to CASM reductions**  
   Jet fuel gallons consumed decreased 2.2% to approximately 271 million gallons, while the average economic fuel cost per gallon remained flat year-over-year at about \$2.06 [8-K 2019-10-22; 10-K 2020-02-12]. This reduction in fuel consumption and stable fuel prices contributed to a 11.4% decline in fuel expense per ASM and a 3.1% reduction in total CASM [8-K 2019-10-22].

5. **Shareholder returns slowed with \$91.6 million returned in 2019 compared to \$126.7 million in 2018**  
   The company repurchased \$68.8 million of shares and paid dividends of \$22.8 million in 2019, totaling \$91.6 million returned to shareholders, down from \$126.7 million in 2018 [8-K 2020-01-30; 8-K 2019-01-29]. This reduction in capital returned coincides with the modest decline in adjusted earnings.

### Operations Insights

6. **Capacity grew modestly by 2.0% while traffic (RPMs) increased 3.5%, improving load factor**  
   Available seat miles (ASM) increased 2.0% to 20.57 billion, while revenue passenger miles (RPM) grew 3.5% to 17.81 billion [10-K 2020-02-12]. This drove a 1.3 point improvement in passenger load factor to 86.6% [10-Q 2019-10-22]. The increase in load factor despite capacity growth indicates better utilization of available seats.

7. **Fleet transition completed with retirement of Boeing 767, increasing reliance on Airbus A321 and A330**  
   During 2019, Hawaiian retired its entire Boeing 767-300 fleet and completed transition to Airbus A321 aircraft, enabling better capacity management and product optimization [8-K 2019-01-29; 10-K 2020-02-12]. The fleet as of December 31, 2019 included 20 Boeing 717-200s for Neighbor Island routes, 24 Airbus A330-200s, and 17 Airbus A321-200s for North America and international routes [10-K 2020-02-12]. This transition aligns capacity with route requirements.

8. **Route network expanded with new service to Boston, Sacramento, Las Vegas, and Fukuoka**  
   Hawaiian introduced five-times-weekly nonstop service between Honolulu and Boston, daily service between Kahului (Maui) and Sacramento, and four-times-weekly flights between Las Vegas and Maui during 2019 [8-K 2019-10-22; 10-K 2020-02-12]. It also commenced service between Honolulu and Fukuoka in late 2019 and received approval for an additional daily flight to Tokyo Haneda starting in 2020 [8-K 2019-10-22; 10-K 2020-02-12]. These expansions reflect efforts to diversify and mature the route network.

### Labor Insights

9. **Workforce grew modestly with approximately 7,389 active employees at September 2019**  
   Employee headcount increased from 7,299 at March 31, 2019, to 7,360 at June 30, 2019, and 7,389 at September 30, 2019 [10-Q 2019-07-30; 10-Q 2019-10-22]. Wages and benefits expenses increased 5.7% year-over-year, reflecting wage inflation and possibly higher staffing levels [10-K 2020-02-12]. The company was in contract negotiations with its Association of Flight Attendants as of late 2018 [10-K 2019-02-13].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

10. **Competitive pressure led to declining yields and PRASM despite robust demand for travel to Hawai‘i**  
    Management acknowledged a heightened competitive capacity environment throughout 2019, which pressured yields and operating revenue per ASM [8-K 2020-01-30; 10-Q 2019-07-30]. Yield declined 3.6% for the year [10-Q 2019-10-22]. The company introduced a Main Cabin Basic fare product in 2019 to capture price-sensitive demand [8-K 2019-10-22]. Partnerships included a pending antitrust immunity application with Japan Airlines to create a joint venture expected to begin in late 2020 or early 2021 [10-K 2020-02-12].

### Route Network Insights

11. **Network concentrated on Hawai‘i gateway cities in North America and Asia-Pacific with growing frequencies**  
    Hawaiian operated daily flights connecting Hawai‘i to 13 U.S. gateway cities, including new service to Boston and expanded frequencies in Northern California and Pacific Northwest markets [10-K 2020-02-12; 8-K 2019-10-22]. International routes included Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand, American Samoa, and Tahiti [10-K 2020-02-12]. The Neighbor Island network comprised daily flights among the six Hawaiian Islands [10-K 2020-02-12].

### Financial Liquidity and Capital Commitments

12. **Liquidity remained strong with over \$500 million in unrestricted cash and manageable debt levels**  
    As of June 30, 2019, Hawaiian held \$539 million in unrestricted cash, equivalents, and short-term investments against outstanding debt and finance leases of \$565 million [8-K 2019-07-30]. Debt maturities included \$230 million in noncurrent finance lease obligations and \$378 million in long-term debt as of December 31, 2019 [10-K 2020-02-12]. The company announced a \$100 million new share repurchase program in December 2018, but repurchases slowed in 2019 [8-K 2019-01-29; 8-K 2020-01-30].

### Risks and Uncertainties

13. **Heightened competition and capacity growth in domestic markets pose ongoing revenue pressure**  
    Management repeatedly cited elevated competitive capacity in the domestic network as a key challenge in 2019, leading to expected declines in operating revenue per ASM and pressure on yields [10-Q 2019-04-24; 10-Q 2019-07-30; 10-Q 2019-10-22]. The company’s ability to sustain margins depends on managing costs and optimizing its route network amid this environment.

14. **Labor contract negotiations with flight attendants remain unresolved as of December 2018**  
    Approximately 84% of employees were unionized as of December 31, 2018, with the Association of Flight Attendants contract amendable January 1, 2017, and ongoing negotiations with no assurance of timely resolution [10-K 2019-02-13]. This labor uncertainty constitutes a potential operational and financial risk.

---

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ 2019 financial results reflected the tension between modest growth in traffic and capacity and ongoing competitive pressures that compressed yields and adjusted profitability. The company completed its fleet transition away from Boeing 767s to Airbus A321s and A330s, enabling more tailored capacity deployment aligned with its expanding route network that added new destinations on both U.S. coasts and in Asia. Operating expenses rose moderately, driven by higher labor costs, while fuel costs declined due to lower prices and consumption. Despite these headwinds, Hawaiian maintained a solid GAAP pre-tax margin and returned capital to shareholders, though at a reduced level compared to 2018. The company’s liquidity position remained strong with ample cash and manageable debt.

The airline’s commercial strategy focused on product segmentation and network expansion, including a pending joint venture with Japan Airlines, while managing a challenging competitive environment in domestic markets. Labor negotiations with flight attendants remained an unresolved risk as of year-end 2019. Overall, Hawaiian’s 2019 performance showed operational resilience amid external pressures but highlighted ongoing challenges in yield management and cost control within a highly competitive and capacity-intense market.

2020.Q1:
### Financial Insights

1. **Sharp revenue decline in March 2020 and Q1 due to COVID-19 travel restrictions**  
   Hawaiian Airlines reported a 45.4% year-over-year (YoY) drop in passengers transported in March 2020 (542,456 vs. 993,548 in March 2019) and a 40.9% decline in revenue passenger miles (RPMs) for the same month. Available seat miles (ASMs) fell 11.9%, leading to a 28.4 percentage point (pts) decline in load factor to 58.0% from 86.4% in March 2019. For the first quarter (Q1) 2020, passengers transported decreased 16.3% YoY and RPMs dropped 10.0%, despite a 2.6% increase in ASMs, resulting in a 10.5 pts load factor decline to 74.6% [8-K filed 2020-04-09].  
   Management attributed these declines primarily to government-mandated travel restrictions and quarantine orders related to the COVID-19 pandemic, which intensified in March and led to the suspension of international routes and a nearly 40% reduction in flight schedules systemwide in April [8-K filed 2020-03-20].

2. **Operating revenue and earnings impacted by COVID-19; prior 2019 full-year results showed modest declines**  
   For full-year 2019, Hawaiian’s operating revenue was essentially flat compared to 2018 (\$2.832 billion vs. \$2.837 billion), with passenger revenue stable at about \$2.598 billion. Net income for 2019 was \$224.0 million, down \$9.2 million YoY, and adjusted net income was \$218.9 million, down \$55.9 million. The pre-tax margin was 10.8%, up 0.2 pts from 2018 on a GAAP basis but adjusted pre-tax margin declined 2.1 pts to 10.5% [8-K filed 2020-01-30].  
   For Q4 2019, net income was \$49.7 million, up \$18.1 million YoY; however, adjusted net income fell slightly by \$3.3 million. Diluted EPS for 2019 was \$4.71, up \$0.09, but adjusted EPS declined \$0.84 to \$4.60 [8-K filed 2020-01-30].

3. **Cost management initiatives in response to demand collapse; suspension of share repurchases and executive pay cuts**  
   In March 2020, Hawaiian announced capacity reductions of 8-10% in April and 15-20% in May relative to original 2020 plans, later increasing schedule reductions to 95% in April due to worsening demand. The Company instituted cost-cutting measures including reducing contractor spend, hiring freezes, voluntary unpaid leave offers, deferring capital expenditures, and consolidating check-in operations at Honolulu airport [8-K filed 2020-03-18, 2020-03-20].  
   Hawaiian suspended its stock repurchase program in March 2020 and senior executives and board members agreed to 10-20% voluntary pay reductions through at least June 2020 [8-K filed 2020-03-18]. The Company acknowledged it did not have sufficient cash to sustain operations indefinitely under the pandemic conditions [8-K filed 2020-03-20].

4. **Fuel costs declined in 2019 but expected to remain a significant expense; fuel hedging coverage at 35% for 2020**  
   Aircraft fuel expense decreased 9.5% in 2019 to \$542.6 million from \$599.5 million in 2018, driven by an 8.2% decline in average fuel price per gallon (\$2.01 vs. \$2.19), with gallons consumed down 1.4% [10-K filed 2020-02-12]. Economic fuel costs (which include realized hedge settlements) were \$555.0 million in 2019, down 3.3% YoY. Hawaiian hedged approximately 35% of projected 2020 fuel requirements as of December 31, 2019 [10-K filed 2020-02-12].  
   For Q1 2020, the Company lowered its economic fuel cost per gallon guidance to \$1.97 from \$2.06 in 2019, while affirming estimates for gallons consumed [8-K filed 2020-03-09].

5. **Liquidity bolstered by credit facility draw and CARES Act loan application; financial covenants and restrictions apply**  
   Hawaiian drew down its revolving credit facility in March 2020 to strengthen cash reserves amid the pandemic [8-K filed 2020-03-18]. The Company applied for a secured \$364 million loan under the CARES Act Economic Relief Program in April 2020, with a 5-year term and collateral to be determined [8-K filed 2020-04-20].  
   Conditions of the CARES Act loan include restrictions on involuntary furloughs, executive compensation limits through March 2022, suspension of dividends and share buybacks through September 2021, and requirements to maintain pre-pandemic service levels until March 2022 unless exempted by the U.S. Department of Transportation [8-K filed 2020-04-20]. Hawaiian received an exemption related to the Hawai‘i quarantine order to maintain minimal connectivity [8-K filed 2020-03-23].

### Operations Insights

6. **Capacity and network changes driven by pandemic; suspension of select international routes and Neighbor Island services**  
   Hawaiian reduced flight capacity systemwide by nearly 40% in April 2020, including suspending three-times-weekly flights between Kona and Tokyo Haneda, four-times-weekly Honolulu-Haneda, and five-times-weekly Honolulu-Incheon through April 20, 2020 [8-K filed 2020-03-18, 2020-03-23].  
   The airline also suspended ‘Ohana by Hawaiian service between Honolulu and Kapalua starting March 25, 2020 but maintained essential interisland cargo service [8-K filed 2020-03-23].  
   Prior to the pandemic, Hawaiian operated approximately 260 scheduled flights daily across North America, Neighbor Island, and International routes, including newly launched routes in 2019 to Boston, Sacramento, Las Vegas, and Japan’s Fukuoka, with a fleet comprising 17 Airbus A321neos, 24 Airbus A330-200s, and 20 Boeing 717-200s [10-K filed 2020-02-12, 8-K filed 2020-01-30].

7. **Load factor and yield pressure from demand collapse; Q1 2020 load factor down 10.5 pts YoY**  
   Despite a 2.6% increase in ASMs in Q1 2020, RPMs declined 10.0% leading to a 10.5 pts fall in load factor to 74.6%, reflecting weaker demand and flight cancellations [8-K filed 2020-04-09].  
   The Company noted that if no new bookings occurred after March 5, 2020, revenue per ASM (RASM) would be down about 12% YoY for Q1 [8-K filed 2020-03-09].

### Labor Insights

8. **New five-year contract reached with flight attendants amid pandemic; voluntary pay cuts for executives**  
   Hawaiian reached an agreement in principle on a new five-year contract with the Association of Flight Attendants in March 2020, with ratification expected after finalization [8-K filed 2020-03-18].  
   Concurrently, senior executives and board members took voluntary 10-20% pay reductions effective immediately through at least June 2020 [8-K filed 2020-03-18].  
   The Company offered voluntary unpaid leave to various employee groups and implemented a hiring freeze as part of cost-cutting measures [8-K filed 2020-03-20].

### Route Network Insights

9. **Fleet modernization continued in 2019 with retirement of Boeing 767 and expansion of A321neo fleet**  
   Hawaiian retired its last Boeing 767-300 aircraft during 2019, completing the transition to Airbus A321 aircraft, which now number 17 after delivery of six new A321neos in 2019 [8-K filed 2020-01-30, 10-K filed 2020-02-12].  
   The Company expanded its network with new nonstop routes launched in 2019 to Boston, Sacramento, Las Vegas, and Fukuoka, Japan, and increased frequencies on existing routes including San Francisco [8-K filed 2020-01-30].  
   International ASMs declined 4.2% in 2019 due to capacity reductions on lower-performing routes and suspension of Beijing service in late 2018, partially offset by new routes and increased frequencies [10-K filed 2020-02-12].

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines entered 2020 with a stable financial and operational footing, having completed fleet modernization and modest network expansion in 2019. However, the rapid onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in Q1 2020 severely disrupted demand, with March passenger volumes and RPMs plunging 40-45% YoY and load factors collapsing by over 28 pts in March and 10.5 pts for the quarter. The Company responded with aggressive capacity cuts, suspensions of international routes, and broad cost containment measures including suspending stock repurchases and executive pay reductions. Hawaiian also secured liquidity through credit facility draws and applied for a CARES Act loan, which imposed operational and compensation restrictions through 2021-2022. Despite these actions, the Company acknowledged insufficient cash to sustain operations indefinitely under pandemic conditions.

**Guidance Update:** Hawaiian withdrew its prior Q1 and full-year 2020 financial guidance in March 2020 due to the uncertainty surrounding COVID-19 impacts. Before withdrawal, the Company had expected ASMs to grow 7.5-10.5% in Q1 and 5.5-8.5% for the full year, with operating revenue per ASM declining 4.5-7.5% for Q1 and costs per ASM excluding fuel down slightly to flat for the full year. The pandemic has rendered these estimates obsolete, with the Company emphasizing that Q1 2020 results and subsequent periods will not be indicative of future performance [8-K filed 2020-03-09, 2020-03-23].
2020.Q2:
### Financial Insights

1. **Revenue collapsed 91.6% year-over-year in 2020Q2 to \$60.0 million due to COVID-19 travel restrictions and quarantines.** Passenger revenue fell 95.4% to \$29.8 million, with domestic revenue down 94.6% and international down 98.0%. Total operating revenue for the six months ended June 30, 2020 declined 54.8% to \$619.1 million versus 2019 [10-Q 2020-07-28; 8-K 2020-07-28]. This reflected a 92.1% reduction in available seat miles (ASMs) for the quarter and a 46.2% reduction for six months, driven by mandated travel quarantines, especially the State of Hawai‘i’s 14-day quarantine for all travelers [10-Q 2020-07-28].

2. **GAAP net loss was \$106.9 million in 2020Q2, improving from a \$144.4 million loss in 2020Q1, but adjusted net loss widened to \$174.7 million from \$34.0 million in Q1.** Diluted EPS was negative \$2.33 GAAP and negative \$3.81 adjusted, compared to negative \$3.14 and negative \$0.74, respectively, in Q1 [10-Q 2020-07-28; 8-K 2020-07-28; 8-K 2020-05-05]. The adjusted loss includes \$34.0 million of special items in Q2 related to a new five-year flight attendant contract ratified in March 2020 [10-Q 2020-07-28].

3. **Operating cost per available seat mile (CASM) surged to 51.03 cents in 2020Q2 from 12.09 cents in 2019Q2, reflecting the sharp capacity cuts.** Excluding fuel and non-recurring items, unit costs rose to 68.26 cents from 9.38 cents, a 628% increase, demonstrating the impact of fixed costs spread over drastically reduced capacity [8-K 2020-07-28]. Fuel expense per ASM fell 37.7% to 1.70 cents due to lower fuel prices and consumption [8-K 2020-07-28].

4. **Fuel expense plummeted 95% to \$7.0 million in 2020Q2, driven by an 88.5% drop in gallons consumed and a 56.9% drop in average fuel price per gallon to \$0.90, including taxes and delivery [8-K 2020-07-28].** Economic fuel expense, which adjusts for hedge settlements, declined 93.2% to \$9.8 million [8-K 2020-07-28].

5. **Cash and liquidity remained strong with \$761 million in unrestricted cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments at June 30, 2020, down slightly from \$815 million at March 31, 2020.** Total debt and finance lease obligations increased to \$1.006 billion from \$976 million at March 31 [8-K 2020-07-28; 8-K 2020-05-05]. Air traffic liability declined to \$554 million from \$624 million at March 31, reflecting reduced advance ticket sales [8-K 2020-07-28; 8-K 2020-05-05].

6. **Net cash provided by operating activities for the six months ended June 30, 2020 was only \$3.5 million, a sharp decline from \$311.2 million in the prior year, reflecting the collapse in demand and revenue [10-Q 2020-07-28].** Capital expenditures were \$94.0 million for the six months, down from \$151.6 million in 2019, reflecting reduced investment [10-Q 2020-07-28].

### Operations Insights

7. **Capacity was slashed by more than 92% in 2020Q2 as Hawaiian operated an extremely limited schedule due to the State of Hawai‘i’s mandatory 14-day self-quarantine for all travelers, which was only lifted for neighbor island travel on June 16, 2020.** Revenue passenger miles (RPMs) fell 97.9% to 95 million in 2020Q2 from 4.49 billion in 2019Q2, and available seat miles (ASMs) fell 92.1% to 409 million from 5.16 billion [8-K 2020-07-28]. Load factor collapsed from 87.1% to 23.2% [8-K 2020-07-28].

8. **Passenger traffic recovered modestly on neighbor island routes after quarantine lift on June 16, 2020, but longer haul and international flights remained severely curtailed or suspended.** International passenger revenue dropped 98% in 2020Q2 with 100% capacity reduction as all international flights were suspended in late March 2020 [10-Q 2020-07-28].

9. **Revenue passenger miles for the six months ended June 30, 2020 declined 55.8% to 3.81 billion from 8.62 billion in 2019, with ASMs down 46.2% [8-K 2020-07-28].** Domestic routes accounted for approximately 74% of passenger revenue for the six months ended June 30, 2020, down from 73% in Q1, highlighting the revenue concentration and exposure to domestic travel restrictions [10-Q 2020-07-28].

10. **Aircraft utilization and flight hours dropped sharply, with revenue block hours operated falling 88.2% in 2020Q2 to 6,496 hours from 54,840 hours in 2019Q2 [8-K 2020-07-28].** Jet fuel consumption fell 88.5% to 7,759 gallons in 2020Q2 from 67,277 gallons in 2019Q2, consistent with the capacity cuts [8-K 2020-07-28].

### Labor Insights

11. **The workforce shrank slightly from 7,492 active employees at March 31, 2020 to 7,418 at June 30, 2020, reflecting modest reductions despite severe operational cuts [10-Q 2020-07-28; 10-Q 2020-05-07].** In April 2020, Hawaiian ratified a new five-year collective bargaining agreement with its flight attendants represented by the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, effective through April 2025, which included ratification payments and increased medical cost sharing [8-K 2020-05-05; 10-Q 2020-07-28].

12. **Management announced plans in July 2020 for further employee headcount reductions in 2021, reflecting expectations of a 10-15% capacity reduction for summer 2021 versus historical averages, with voluntary reduction options offered to mitigate involuntary cuts [8-K 2020-07-10].** Executive and board compensation reductions of 10% to 50% were implemented through at least September 30, 2020 [10-Q 2020-05-07].

### Route Network Insights

13. **Hawaiian maintains a network concentrated on the Hawaiian Islands, North America, and the Pacific region, with approximately 54% of passenger revenue generated from North America routes in the first half of 2020.** The airline faces competition from larger network carriers such as Alaska, American, Delta, Southwest, and United, which have broader U.S. mainland networks and feed traffic, whereas Hawaiian's Honolulu and Maui hubs primarily serve as destinations rather than origins [10-Q 2020-07-28].

14. **Capacity reductions and route suspensions began with suspensions to South Korea and Japan in late February 2020, followed by suspensions to Australia and New Zealand in mid-March, and complete international service suspension in late March due to COVID-19 travel restrictions and quarantines [10-Q 2020-07-28; 8-K 2020-05-05].** Neighbor island service resumed partially after June 16, 2020, but international and longer haul flights remained suspended [8-K 2020-07-28].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

15. **Passenger revenue per available seat mile (PRASM) dropped 42.7% in 2020Q2 to 7.27 cents from 12.68 cents in 2019Q2, reflecting lower yields and load factors amid the pandemic [10-Q 2020-07-28].** Yield per RPM increased 115% in Q2 to 31.3 cents from 14.6 cents in 2019Q2, likely due to the very low load factor and capacity, but fell 3.8% for the six months [10-Q 2020-07-28]. The yield increase in Q2 is a mathematical effect of very low traffic and does not reflect volume.

16. **Frequent flyer revenue transportation component collapsed 90% in Q2 to \$3.6 million from \$39.8 million in 2019Q2, consistent with the severe traffic drop [10-Q 2020-07-28].** Other operating revenue (cargo, ground handling, commissions) declined 48.5% in Q2 to \$30.2 million [8-K 2020-07-28].

### Corporate Insights

17. **Hawaiian raised liquidity through financing transactions in July 2020, including \$114 million raised by sale and leaseback of two Airbus A321neo aircraft and an enhanced equipment trust certificate (EETC) offering of approximately \$262 million in July 2020 [8-K 2020-07-28; 8-K 2020-07-29].** The company also received \$111.6 million in CARES Act Payroll Support Program grants during the first half of 2020, which helped offset operating expenses [10-Q 2020-07-28].

18. **The CARES Act support restricts the company from paying dividends through at least September 30, 2021, and imposes executive compensation limits through March 24, 2022 [10-Q 2020-05-07].** The company also has obligations to continue serving pre-pandemic markets until March 1, 2022, subject to DOT approval [10-Q 2020-05-07].

19. **Management highlights ongoing risk from uncertain timing and pace of recovery, potential resurgence of COVID-19 cases, continued travel restrictions, and industry-wide capacity from competitors, which could affect future financial results [10-Q 2020-07-28].** The company’s revenue concentration in Hawai‘i and dependency on leisure travel increases exposure to these risks [10-Q 2020-07-28].

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ 2020Q2 results reflect an unprecedented collapse in demand and capacity due to COVID-19-related travel restrictions, particularly the State of Hawai‘i’s 14-day quarantine. Passenger revenue and operating revenue fell by over 90%, with capacity cut by more than 92%, leading to a GAAP net loss of \$106.9 million and adjusted net loss of \$174.7 million. Despite severe cuts, fixed costs drove a large increase in unit costs per ASM. Fuel costs declined sharply due to reduced flying and lower prices. Cash reserves remained substantial at \$761 million, supported by government aid and financing transactions, but operating cash flow was minimal. The fleet operated at a fraction of normal hours, with international routes fully suspended and domestic routes limited until quarantine easing mid-June.

The airline ratified a new labor contract with flight attendants in Q2 but anticipates further headcount reductions aligned with expected capacity cuts in 2021. Hawaiian’s network remains concentrated on Hawai‘i and North America, where competition from larger network carriers and ongoing travel restrictions pose ongoing challenges. Yield and load factor metrics were distorted by the collapse in traffic, and frequent flyer revenue plunged. Management flagged continued uncertainty around recovery timing and the impact of extended quarantines and competitor capacity. CARES Act restrictions limit dividends and executive pay while requiring continued service on pre-pandemic routes.

**Guidance:** Hawaiian expects July and August 2020 capacity to remain about 85-86% below 2019 levels, with operating expenses not declining proportionally due to fixed costs. The company is taking steps to preserve liquidity, including sale-leaseback transactions and new financing, and continues to monitor developments related to COVID-19 and related government policies [8-K 2020-07-28].

No material litigation, accidents, or regulatory actions were disclosed in the filings for 2020Q2.
2020.Q3:
### Financial Insights

1. **Revenue collapsed by nearly 90% year-over-year in 2020Q3 due to COVID-19 and Hawaii quarantines, with total revenue falling to \$76.0 million from \$755.2 million in 2019Q3.** Passenger revenue declined 94.3% to \$39.8 million, driven by a capacity reduction of 80.1% domestically and a near-total shutdown of international operations, which saw a 99.4% revenue decline on zero capacity. Other operating revenue, including cargo and loyalty programs, also dropped 40.5% to \$36.2 million [10-Q 2020-10-28; 8-K 2020-10-27].

2. **Net loss narrowed slightly but remained substantial at a GAAP loss of \$97.1 million (\$2.11 per diluted share) in 2020Q3, compared to a GAAP profit of \$80.1 million a year earlier; adjusted net loss was \$172.7 million (\$3.76 per diluted share).** The adjusted net loss improved marginally from \$174.7 million in 2020Q2, reflecting continued revenue collapse and cost containment efforts [10-Q 2020-10-28; 8-K 2020-10-27].

3. **Operating expenses fell but not in proportion to capacity reductions, keeping unit costs elevated; total operating expenses were \$197.1 million in 2020Q3, down from \$638.5 million in 2019Q3.** Wages and benefits declined by 89.3% to \$19.5 million, aircraft fuel expense dropped 89.5% to \$14.5 million due to lower consumption and fuel prices, and maintenance costs were down 69.6% to \$18.7 million. However, depreciation and amortization remained relatively steady at \$36.7 million, reflecting fixed asset base [10-Q 2020-10-28].

4. **Unit economics deteriorated sharply: operating cost per available seat mile (CASM) soared to 51.03 cents versus 12.09 cents in 2019Q3, driven by fixed costs and low capacity; CASM excluding fuel and special items was 68.26 cents compared to 9.38 cents previously.** Operating revenue per ASM (RASM) was 14.65 cents, a 6.1% increase year-over-year, but insufficient to offset the surge in unit costs. Fuel cost per ASM declined due to lower fuel prices and consumption [8-K 2020-10-27].

5. **Liquidity was bolstered to \$979.1 million in unrestricted cash, equivalents, and short-term investments by September 30, 2020, up from \$760.9 million at June 30, 2020.** The company raised approximately \$421 million in new financing during 2020Q3, including \$114 million from sale-leaseback of two Airbus A321neo aircraft and \$262 million from issuance of Enhanced Equipment Trust Certificates (EETCs) backed by two Airbus aircraft [10-Q 2020-10-28; 8-K 2020-10-27].

6. **Outstanding debt and finance lease obligations increased to \$1.299 billion at September 30, 2020 from \$1.006 billion at June 30, 2020, reflecting new borrowings.** Air traffic liability (deferred ticket revenue) was \$515 million, down from \$554 million at June 30, 2020, consistent with lower bookings and travel activity [8-K 2020-10-27; 8-K 2020-07-28].

### Operations Insights

7. **Capacity remained severely curtailed in 2020Q3, with available seat miles (ASM) down 86.5% to 718,405 thousand from 5,331,914 thousand in 2019Q3, reflecting Hawaii’s mandatory 14-day quarantine for all incoming travelers.** Revenue passenger miles (RPM) declined 96.0% to 185,788 thousand, and passenger load factor plunged to 23.2% from 87.1% in 2019Q3. The airline operated an extremely limited schedule, especially on international routes which were effectively suspended [10-Q 2020-10-28; 8-K 2020-10-27].

8. **Domestic routes accounted for approximately 92% of total revenue in 2020Q3, but domestic passenger revenue fell 92.3% on an 80.1% capacity reduction compared to 2019, illustrating the heavy reliance on North America traffic.** Neighbor Island routes made up about 21.5% of passenger revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2020, with some rebuilding of schedules following easing of neighbor island quarantines mid-year. International routes generated just 1,250 thousand dollars in 2020Q3, down 99.4% on zero capacity [10-Q 2020-10-28].

9. **Fuel consumption fell 80.8% to 13.4 million gallons in 2020Q3 compared to 69.7 million gallons in 2019Q3, driven by the capacity reduction and lower fuel prices; average fuel price per gallon including taxes fell 45.2% to \$1.09.** Economic fuel expense (including realized losses on fuel derivatives) declined 88.3% to \$16.6 million [10-Q 2020-10-28; 8-K 2020-10-27].

### Labor Insights

10. **The workforce was reduced by over 32% in 2020Q3, with approximately 2,400 employees leaving through voluntary and involuntary separation programs, including nearly 2,100 voluntary separations.** The company implemented permanent and extended voluntary leave programs across workgroups and prepared for involuntary reductions effective October 1, 2020. Active employees numbered 7,087 as of September 30, 2020, down from 7,418 at June 30, 2020 [10-Q 2020-10-28; 8-K 2020-10-27].

11. **In March 2020, Hawaiian reached a new five-year collective bargaining agreement with the Association of Flight Attendants, ratified in April 2020, which included ratification bonuses and changes to pay and medical benefits.** The company recorded \$23.5 million in ratification bonuses during the nine months ended September 30, 2020, with \$20.2 million related to service prior to 2020 [10-Q 2020-10-28].

### Route Network Insights

12. **The delivery schedule for 10 Boeing 787-9 aircraft was deferred, with new expected deliveries now spread from 2022 to 2026 instead of earlier, with the first aircraft delivery now scheduled for September 2022.** This deferral aligns with reduced demand and capacity needs [8-K 2020-10-27].

13. **The airline’s network remains concentrated on Hawaii routes, with approximately 75.3% of passenger revenue generated from Domestic routes (Neighbor Island plus North America), 24.7% from International routes during the nine months ended September 30, 2020.** The airline faces competition from major U.S. network carriers on North America routes, which have geographic diversification and hub networks that Hawaiian lacks. Increased competitor capacity on routes to and within Hawaii poses ongoing risks to market share and yields [10-Q 2020-10-28; 10-Q 2020-07-28].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

14. **Following the announcement in September 2020 of Hawaii’s pre-travel testing program effective October 15, 2020, allowing travelers to bypass the 14-day quarantine with a negative COVID-19 test, Hawaiian began rebuilding its Neighbor Island and North America flight schedules in anticipation of demand increases.** However, management noted that the timing and pace of recovery remain uncertain due to ongoing travel restrictions and COVID-19 case fluctuations [10-Q 2020-10-28; 8-K 2020-10-27].

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ 2020Q3 results reflect the profound disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and Hawaii’s stringent travel quarantines. Revenue collapsed nearly 90% year-over-year, driven by an 86.5% cut in capacity and near-elimination of international flights. Despite cost reductions, fixed expenses kept unit costs elevated, resulting in a GAAP net loss of \$97.1 million and adjusted net loss of \$172.7 million. The company strengthened liquidity through new financings and sale-leasebacks, raising cash to nearly \$1 billion by quarter-end.

Operationally, Hawaiian maintained a minimal schedule, with load factors plunging to 23.2%. Workforce reductions exceeded 30%, with voluntary and involuntary separations implemented to align staffing with demand. The airline deferred new aircraft deliveries to 2022–2026 and faced ongoing competitive pressures from larger network carriers. Hawaii’s October 15, 2020 pre-travel testing program prompted some schedule rebuilding, but recovery timing remains uncertain amid continuing restrictions.

Management’s forward-looking comments highlighted ongoing cost control, liquidity preservation, and cautious capacity planning, including an anticipated 15–25% capacity reduction for summer 2021 relative to historical averages, with corresponding headcount reductions planned. No new material risks beyond those stemming from the pandemic and competitive environment were disclosed for the period.
2020.Q4:
### Financial Insights

1. **Severe revenue decline drove a \$163 million GAAP net loss in 2020Q4 on capacity down 72% vs. 2019Q4**  
   Hawaiian Airlines reported total operating revenue of \$149.7 million in Q4 2020, an 78.9% decline from \$708.1 million in Q4 2019. Passenger revenue fell 85.9% to \$91.8 million, reflecting an 83.4% drop in revenue passengers flown and an 87.4% decrease in revenue passenger miles (RPMs). Capacity, measured in available seat miles (ASMs), decreased 72.7% year-over-year. The resulting GAAP net loss was \$162.6 million, a \$212.3 million deterioration from a net income of \$49.7 million in Q4 2019. The pre-tax margin was negative 152.8%, down 162.4 percentage points. These figures illustrate the steep revenue contraction primarily due to the COVID-19 pandemic and related travel restrictions [8-K 2021-01-26; 10-K 2021-02-12; Table 1].

2. **Costs declined less than capacity and revenue, limiting margin recovery despite fuel savings**  
   Operating expenses in Q4 2020 were \$197.1 million, down from \$638.5 million in Q4 2019 (a 69.1% reduction), but not proportional to the 72.7% capacity cut or 78.9% revenue decline. Wages and benefits fell 89.3% compared to the same quarter prior year, partly due to workforce reductions (see Labor Insights). Aircraft fuel expense dropped 80.8% to \$26.3 million, aided by a 69% reduction in fuel gallons consumed and a 37.1% decrease in economic fuel cost per gallon to \$1.29. Despite these reductions, the fixed-cost nature of many expenses constrained operating leverage, contributing to a large operating loss of \$119.6 million [10-Q 2020-10-28; 8-K 2021-01-26; 10-K 2021-02-12].

3. **Cash and liquidity contracted modestly in Q4 but remained substantial at \$864 million; debt stable at \$1.3 billion**  
   As of December 31, 2020, Hawaiian held \$864 million in unrestricted cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments, down from \$979 million at September 30, 2020. Outstanding debt and finance lease obligations remained around \$1.3 billion. The company raised approximately \$41 million net in Q4 through its at-the-market equity offering program and anticipated \$168 million from the Payroll Support Program Extension in early 2021. Air traffic liability (customer prepayments) was \$534 million at year-end, slightly up from \$515 million at Q3-end [8-K 2021-01-26; 8-K 2020-10-27; 10-K 2021-02-12].

4. **Capital expenditures planned at \$50-70 million for 2021, down sharply from prior years**  
   Hawaiian expects capital spending in 2021 to be approximately \$50 to \$70 million, reflecting scaled-back investment amid the pandemic. The timing of Boeing 787-9 aircraft deliveries was deferred, with the first now expected in September 2022 instead of earlier dates, spreading deliveries through 2026 [8-K 2020-10-27; 8-K 2021-01-26].

### Operations Insights

5. **Capacity doubled sequentially in Q4 2020 vs. Q3 but remained 72% below 2019 levels**  
   Capacity measured by ASM was 1.43 billion in Q4 2020, up from 0.98 billion in Q3 2020 but down 72.7% from 5.24 billion in Q4 2019. Revenue passengers flown increased from 2,893 thousand in Q4 2019 to only 480 thousand in Q4 2020 (-83.4%). Load factor was reported at 40% in Q4 2020, reflecting both the depressed demand and capacity management efforts [8-K 2021-01-26; 10-K 2021-02-12].

6. **Network service restored to all pre-pandemic U.S. mainland and key international points by Q4-end**  
   The airline reinstated nonstop service from Honolulu to Las Vegas, Phoenix, San Jose, Oakland, New York, and Boston, as well as to Tokyo-Haneda, Osaka, and Seoul. Despite this, capacity remained significantly reduced compared to 2019. Hawaiian also announced new routes launching in March and April 2021 to Austin, Orlando, Ontario (California), and a new daily flight between Kahului and Long Beach [8-K 2021-01-26; 10-K 2021-02-12].

7. **Approximately 16% of fleet was temporarily parked as of December 31, 2020 due to reduced demand**  
   Capacity reductions led to parking of about 16% of the fleet. The fleet composition remained 19 Boeing 717-200s for Neighbor Island routes, 24 Airbus A330-200s, and 18 Airbus A321-200s for North America and international routes, plus ATR42 and ATR72 aircraft for Neighbor Island passenger and cargo services [10-K 2021-02-12].

### Labor Insights

8. **Workforce reduced by over 2,400 employees (32%) by October 2020, mostly voluntary separations**  
   In Q3 2020, Hawaiian reduced its workforce by approximately 2,400 employees, more than 32% of the total, primarily through voluntary leave programs. Involuntary reductions began October 1, 2020. The company recorded \$17.5 million in special severance and benefit costs in Q3 2020 related to these actions [8-K 2020-10-27; 10-Q 2020-10-28].

9. **New five-year contract with flight attendants ratified in April 2020 includes ratification bonus and benefit changes**  
   Hawaiian reached a new collective bargaining agreement with the Association of Flight Attendants in March 2020, ratified in April. The agreement runs through April 2025 and includes a ratification payment over one year, increased medical cost sharing, improved pay scales, and medical savings contributions for retirees. The company recognized \$23.5 million in ratification bonuses during the first nine months of 2020 [10-Q 2020-10-28].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

10. **Pre-travel testing program launched October 15, 2020, enabling quarantine bypass and supporting recovery**  
    The State of Hawai‘i’s pre-travel testing program allowed travelers with a negative COVID-19 test to avoid the 14-day quarantine. Hawaiian partnered to provide mail-in test kits and drive-through testing labs in mainland gateways. The program was credited with beginning a recovery phase, as bookings increased post-launch, although demand remained volatile and below 2019 levels. The company planned to implement the Hawai‘i Pre-Clear Program in Q1 2021 to validate testing prior to departure [8-K 2021-01-26; 10-K 2021-02-12].

11. **Passenger revenue composition shifted heavily toward Domestic routes, which accounted for 78% of 2020 revenue**  
    In 2020, approximately 78% of passenger revenue was generated from Domestic routes (Neighbor Island and North America), down from 74% in 2019. International routes accounted for about 22%. Passenger revenue declined 74.4% year-over-year to \$664.8 million, with domestic revenue down 69.0% and international revenue down 72.1% [10-K 2021-02-12].

12. **Other operating revenue declined 23.2% due to lower cargo volumes and loyalty program revenue**  
    Other operating revenue was \$180.0 million in 2020, down from \$234.5 million in 2019. Cargo revenue fell by \$20.9 million due to reduced volumes, and loyalty program revenue decreased by \$20.1 million due to lower credit card spend and fewer new cardholders. Ground handling and freight services also declined by \$13.3 million [10-K 2021-02-12].

### Route Network Insights

13. **International service suspended to several destinations through mid-2021 due to COVID-19**  
    Flights to Pago Pago (American Samoa), Papeete (Tahiti), Sydney and Brisbane (Australia), Auckland (New Zealand), and Sapporo and Fukuoka (Japan) were suspended through at least Q2 2021. The company continued scheduled service to Tokyo, Osaka, and Seoul [10-K 2021-02-12].

### Corporate Insights

14. **Significant risks remain from COVID-19 volatility, government travel restrictions, and competitive pressures**  
    Hawaiian highlighted ongoing uncertainty from the COVID-19 pandemic, including potential changes or suspension of the pre-travel testing program, resurgence of infections, new virus strains, and travel restrictions affecting bookings and capacity. The company noted competitive disadvantages relative to major U.S. network carriers, particularly on North America routes where Hawaiian lacks extensive feeder networks, relying instead on code-share partnerships like JetBlue. The concentration of business in Hawai‘i and dependence on tourism were cited as risk factors [10-K 2021-02-12; 10-Q 2020-10-28].

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ Q4 2020 results reflect the ongoing severe impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, with passenger volumes and revenue plummeting by over 70% year-over-year, despite a doubling of capacity from the prior quarter. Costs declined but less than proportionally, due to fixed expenses and workforce retention costs, resulting in a large operating loss and a net loss of \$163 million. The launch of Hawai‘i’s pre-travel testing program in October 2020 enabled a partial recovery in traffic and restoration of service to all pre-pandemic U.S. mainland and key international destinations, though capacity remained heavily curtailed and fleet parking persisted. The company reduced its workforce by nearly one-third and deferred capital expenditures, while maintaining liquidity of \$864 million and stable debt levels. Risks remain elevated due to the uncertain trajectory of the pandemic, government policies, and competitive dynamics in the Hawai‘i market.

For Q1 2021, Hawaiian guided capacity to be down approximately 50% versus Q1 2019, with revenues expected to be 72-74% below Q1 2019 but 14-23% higher than Q4 2020, reflecting modest recovery. Cash burn was forecasted at \$1.3 to \$1.5 million per day, improved from prior estimates. The company planned to implement additional safety protocols and expand its route network with new U.S. mainland destinations in spring 2021, contingent on the continuation of the pre-travel testing program and evolving travel demand conditions [8-K 2021-03-24; 8-K 2021-01-26].
2020.FY:
### Financial Insights

1. **Hawaiian Airlines' 2020 revenue collapsed 70% as COVID-19 slashed passenger demand, driving a \$511 million net loss**  
   For the full year ended December 31, 2020, Hawaiian's total operating revenue fell 70.2% to \$844.8 million from \$2.83 billion in 2019. Passenger revenue dropped 74.4% to \$664.8 million, with domestic and Pacific segment revenues down sharply. The steep revenue decline was due to COVID-19-related travel restrictions and quarantines that began in early 2020, drastically reducing demand. Hawaiian reported a GAAP net loss of \$510.9 million in 2020, compared to net income of \$224.0 million in 2019, with pre-tax margin declining by 93.7 percentage points to -82.9%. Adjusted net loss was \$551.0 million, reflecting similar trends [8-K 2021-01-26; 10-K 2021-02-12].  

2. **Operating expenses fell but not proportionally; CASM rose 17% in Q1 2020 as fixed costs persisted amid capacity cuts**  
   In Q1 2020, operating expenses increased to \$727.2 million from \$604.1 million in Q1 2019, despite early pandemic impacts. Operating cost per available seat mile (CASM) rose 17.3% to 14.60¢ from 12.45¢, driven by a 10.5-point load factor drop and a 2.6% ASM increase. Excluding fuel and non-recurring items, CASM was stable at around 9.78¢. Fuel costs per ASM declined 12.7%, reflecting lower fuel prices and consumption. The company’s fixed cost base limited expense reductions despite capacity cuts [10-Q 2020-05-07; 8-K 2020-05-05].  

3. **Fuel expense plunged 70% in 2020 due to lower consumption and prices, partially offsetting revenue losses**  
   Aircraft fuel expense including taxes and delivery fell 70.3% to \$161.4 million in 2020 from \$542.6 million in 2019. Fuel gallons consumed declined 60.7% to 106.2 million gallons, and economic fuel cost per gallon dropped 22.3% to \$1.60. The company’s economic fuel expense, which includes realized gains/losses on hedges, fell 69.3% [10-K 2021-02-12; 8-K 2021-01-26].  

4. **Liquidity remained robust with \$864 million cash at year-end, but debt increased to \$1.3 billion**  
   At December 31, 2020, Hawaiian held \$864 million in unrestricted cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments, down modestly from \$979 million at September 30, 2020. Outstanding debt and finance lease obligations rose from \$1.0 billion at mid-2020 to \$1.3 billion by year-end. Air traffic liability declined from \$624 million in March 2020 to \$534 million at year-end, reflecting lower ticket sales and deferred revenue. The company also secured approximately \$168 million from the Payroll Support Program Extension in January 2021 [8-K 2021-01-26; 10-K 2021-02-12; 8-K 2020-07-28].  

5. **Capital expenditures and fleet delivery timing deferred; Boeing 787-9 deliveries pushed from 2020 to 2022-2026**  
   Hawaiian delayed delivery of Boeing 787-9 aircraft under its purchase agreement, now expecting first delivery in September 2022 with remaining deliveries through 2026. The company planned full year 2021 capital expenditures of \$50–70 million, reflecting cautious investment amid ongoing demand uncertainty [8-K 2020-10-27; 8-K 2021-01-26].  

### Operations Insights

6. **System capacity collapsed 63% in 2020 with passenger traffic down 74%, load factor falling from 86.6% to 60.6%**  
   Available seat miles (ASM) dropped 63.3% to 7.53 billion from 20.57 billion in 2019. Revenue passenger miles (RPM) fell 74.4% to 4.56 billion. Passenger load factor declined 26 percentage points to 60.6%. Passenger count plunged 71.4% to 3.35 million from 11.7 million. The declines were driven by mandated quarantines, travel restrictions, and route suspensions starting in March 2020, with system-wide capacity reduced by 95% in April 2020 [10-K 2021-02-12; 8-K 2020-04-09].  

7. **Domestic routes accounted for 75% of passenger revenue but faced sustained weakness due to quarantines and competition**  
   Domestic routes, including North America and inter-island flights, generated approximately 75.3% of passenger revenue in the first nine months of 2020, down from 74% in 2019. Hawaiian operated a reduced schedule with daily flights to major U.S. gateway cities and inter-island routes, but mandatory 14-day quarantines within Hawai‘i and from the mainland suppressed demand. Competition from major network carriers on North America routes remained a challenge [10-Q 2020-07-28; 10-K 2021-02-12].  

8. **International service was suspended early in the pandemic and only partially resumed; international revenue dropped sharply**  
   Hawaiian suspended all international service in March 2020 due to government-imposed travel restrictions and quarantines. At year-end, limited scheduled service operated between Hawai‘i and select cities in Japan and South Korea. International revenue fell 73.6% in 2020, with international routes accounting for the Pacific segment revenue of \$204.7 million, down from \$774.6 million in 2019 [10-K 2021-02-12; 8-K 2020-05-07].  

9. **Flight operations reduced from 260 daily flights at 2019 year-end to 118 scheduled flights at December 31, 2020**  
   The schedule reduction reflected pandemic-related demand collapse and state quarantine policies. Hawaiian maintained essential service levels on North America, Neighbor Island, and limited international routes, adjusting capacity to align with demand and regulatory requirements [10-K 2021-02-12].  

### Labor Insights

10. **Workforce reduced by over 32% through voluntary and involuntary separations, including furloughs and layoffs**  
    Active employees declined from approximately 7,492 at March 31, 2020, to 7,418 at June 30, 2020, and further to 7,087 by September 30, 2020. The company implemented voluntary leave programs and involuntary reductions effective October 1, 2020, reducing workforce by about 2,400 employees (over 32%), with nearly 2,100 reductions through voluntary means [10-Q 2020-07-28; 10-Q 2020-10-28; 8-K 2020-10-27].  

11. **New five-year contract reached with Association of Flight Attendants in March 2020 amid pandemic challenges**  
    Hawaiian reached an agreement in principle on March 16, 2020, for a five-year contract with the Association of Flight Attendants covering flight attendants, with final ratification pending. This occurred as the company was beginning to face pandemic-related operational disruptions [8-K 2020-03-18].  

### Commercial Strategy Insights

12. **Hawaiian implemented enhanced health and safety protocols and waived change fees to support customer confidence**  
    The airline adopted enhanced cleaning procedures, modified boarding and inflight service to minimize COVID-19 transmission risk, and eliminated change fees on all flights to increase travel flexibility. These measures aimed to adapt to evolving customer needs during the pandemic [10-K 2021-02-12; 8-K 2021-01-26].  

### Route Network Insights

13. **Network rationalized with suspension of many international routes and focus on core U.S. mainland and Neighbor Island markets**  
    Hawaiian suspended service to South Korea and Japan in late February 2020 and all international routes in March 2020, resuming limited service to Japan and South Korea by year-end. The domestic network remained focused on major U.S. gateway cities and inter-island flights, with daily nonstop flights to multiple California cities, Seattle, Portland, Las Vegas, Phoenix, Boston, and New York [10-K 2021-02-12; 8-K 2020-05-07].  

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines experienced a profound collapse in demand and revenue in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and related travel restrictions. Passenger volumes fell over 70%, and capacity was cut by nearly two-thirds, driving a large net loss of \$511 million. Operating expenses declined less sharply due to fixed cost structure, pushing unit costs higher in early 2020. The airline preserved liquidity, ending the year with \$864 million in cash but increased debt to \$1.3 billion. Workforce reductions exceeded 30%, and international service was largely suspended. Hawaiian adjusted its network and deferred fleet deliveries in response to ongoing uncertainty. The company implemented health and safety protocols and flexible ticketing policies to support recovery efforts.  

Looking ahead, Hawaiian’s first quarter 2021 capacity was expected to remain about 50% below 2019 levels, with ongoing impact from the State of Hawai‘i’s pre-travel testing program and uncertain demand recovery. Capital expenditures were planned conservatively at \$50–70 million for 2021. The company also engaged in financing activities, including a \$800 million senior secured notes offering tied to its loyalty program, and anticipated receiving \$168 million under the federal Payroll Support Program Extension. No material labor contract disruptions or regulatory events were disclosed for 2020.

2021.Q1:
### Financial Insights

1. **Net loss narrowed substantially in 2021Q1 amid steep revenue decline and capacity cuts**  
   Hawaiian Holdings reported a GAAP net loss of \$60.7 million (\$1.23 per diluted share) for the quarter ended March 31, 2021, improving from a net loss of \$144.4 million (\$3.14 per diluted share) in 2020Q1. Total operating revenue fell 67.4% year-over-year to \$182.2 million, driven by a 50.4% reduction in available seat miles (ASM) and a 71.6% drop in revenue passenger miles (RPM). Domestic passenger revenue declined 65.0% on a 34.4% capacity reduction compared to 2020Q1, while international passenger revenue plummeted 93.4% due to capacity being down 87.7% [10-Q 2021-04-28; 8-K 2021-04-27].

2. **Operating expenses fell 64.9%, but cost per ASM excluding fuel increased sharply**  
   Operating expenses decreased to \$255.4 million from \$727.2 million in 2020Q1, a 64.9% reduction, reflecting capacity cuts and cost containment. However, cost per ASM (CASM) declined only 29.5% to 10.29 cents, while CASM excluding fuel and non-recurring items rose 46.2% to 14.30 cents, indicating fixed costs and inefficiencies remained significant on reduced flying. Aircraft fuel expense dropped 57.9% to \$47.7 million, reflecting 53.1% fewer gallons consumed and a 10.7% lower average fuel price per gallon (\$1.59 vs. \$1.78) [10-Q 2021-04-28].

3. **Passenger yield and load factor weakened, depressing unit revenue**  
   Passenger yield (revenue per RPM) declined 3.9% to 13.04 cents, while load factor plunged 31.9 points to 42.7% due to lower demand and capacity management during the pandemic. Passenger revenue per ASM (PRASM) fell 45.0% to 5.57 cents, and operating revenue per ASM (RASM) dropped 34.6% to 7.34 cents, underscoring severe revenue pressure on available capacity [10-Q 2021-04-28].

4. **Liquidity improved with \$1.9 billion cash and \$2.1 billion debt at quarter-end after sizable financings**  
   As of March 31, 2021, Hawaiian held \$1.9 billion in unrestricted cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments, up \$1.0 billion from December 31, 2020, supported by a \$1.2 billion senior secured notes issuance in February 2021 and a \$109 million net equity raise via an at-the-market offering in March 2021. Outstanding debt and finance lease obligations increased by \$852 million to \$2.1 billion. Air traffic liability rose to \$687 million, up \$154 million from year-end 2020 [8-K 2021-04-27; 10-Q 2021-04-28].

5. **Capital expenditures planned at \$50-\$60 million for full year 2021**  
   The Company expects capital spending of approximately \$50 to \$60 million for 2021, down from higher levels in prior years, reflecting a focus on liquidity preservation amid the pandemic [8-K 2021-04-27].

### Operations Insights

6. **Capacity was 50% of 2019 levels, with North America routes recovering faster than international**  
   Hawaiian operated at 51% of its 2019 system capacity in 2021Q1, with 73% of North America, 38% of Neighbor Island, and 12% of International 2019 capacity levels. The rebound in North America demand occurred mainly in March 2021, supporting a 70.8% capacity increase over 2020Q4. International routes remained severely depressed due to ongoing travel restrictions [8-K 2021-04-27; 10-Q 2021-04-28].

7. **Network expansion included four new North America routes launched in March-April 2021**  
   Hawaiian introduced nonstop flights from Honolulu to Austin, Texas; Orlando, Florida; Ontario, California; and Long Beach, California to Maui in early 2021. Summer 2021 plans include increasing frequencies on less-than-daily routes, such as daily service between Kahului (Maui) and Long Beach, and twice-weekly service between Honolulu and Orlando [8-K 2021-04-27; 8-K 2021-01-26].

8. **Fuel consumption fell 53.1%, with economic fuel cost per gallon down 12.6% to \$1.60**  
   Jet fuel gallons consumed dropped to 29.9 million from 63.8 million in 2020Q1, reflecting reduced flying. Economic fuel expense (GAAP fuel plus realized hedge settlements) declined 58.9% to \$47.9 million. The average economic fuel cost per gallon decreased from \$1.83 to \$1.60, partially offsetting volume declines [10-Q 2021-04-28].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

9. **Passenger revenue heavily concentrated in Domestic routes (93.4% in 2021Q1) and North America (75.5% in Q1)**  
   The majority of Hawaiian’s revenue continues to derive from Domestic routes (including Neighbor Island and North America), accounting for 93.4% of passenger revenue in 2021Q1, with North America alone representing 75.5%. International passenger revenue was only 6.6% in 2021Q1, reflecting ongoing pandemic restrictions [10-Q 2021-04-28].

10. **Pre-travel testing programs and vaccine rollout supported demand rebound in March 2021**  
    The State of Hawai‘i’s Safe Travels program, which allows travelers to bypass quarantine with negative COVID-19 tests, remained in place in 2021Q1. Hawaiian implemented the Hawai‘i Pre-Clear Program to validate testing prior to departure. Management attributed increased bookings and close-in demand in North America in March 2021 to these programs and vaccine availability [8-K 2021-04-27; 8-K 2021-03-24].

### Labor Insights

11. **Workforce stood at 5,913 active employees as of March 31, 2021, prior to separations**  
    Hawaiian reported 5,913 active employees at quarter-end before applying voluntary and involuntary separation programs. The company had issued recall notices to furloughed employees under the Payroll Support Program Extension (PSP Extension) to support ongoing operations [10-Q 2021-04-28; 8-K 2021-01-26].

### Route Network Insights

12. **International routes remained heavily curtailed with service suspensions through mid-2021**  
    Flights to Australia, New Zealand, American Samoa, Tahiti, and certain Japanese cities were suspended through at least mid-2021. The international network remained constrained by government restrictions, contributing to a 93.4% drop in international passenger revenue [10-K 2021-02-12; 10-Q 2021-04-28].

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ 2021Q1 financial and operational results reflect a continuing but uneven recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic. Revenue and capacity remained severely depressed relative to pre-pandemic levels, especially on international routes, but the company achieved a significant reduction in net loss compared to 2020Q1. Operationally, Hawaiian rebuilt capacity by 70.8% versus 2020Q4, driven primarily by North America demand recovering in March 2021, supported by the State of Hawai‘i’s pre-travel testing program and vaccine rollout. Cost reductions were substantial but fixed costs and lower load factors kept unit costs elevated. Liquidity strengthened materially through debt and equity raises, with cash balances nearly doubling to \$1.9 billion at quarter-end, while debt increased to \$2.1 billion. The company expanded its North America network with four new routes launched and plans to increase frequencies in summer 2021. Labor headcount stood at 5,913 before separations, with recall efforts underway under government support programs. International routes remained largely suspended due to travel restrictions.

**Guidance:** Hawaiian expects 2021 full-year capital expenditures between \$50 and \$60 million. For 2021Q1, the company projected total revenue down approximately 72-74% versus 2019Q1, and capacity down about 50% versus 2019Q1. Cash burn was forecasted at \$1.3 to \$1.5 million per day, improved from earlier estimates. The company anticipates second quarter 2021 capacity to be down 30-33% versus 2020Q2 [8-K 2021-04-27; 8-K 2021-03-24]. No material litigation, accidents, or labor disruptions were disclosed for the quarter.
2021.Q2:
### Financial Insights

1. **Hawaiian Airlines narrowed its GAAP net loss substantially in 2021Q2, reporting a \$6.2 million loss on \$410.8 million revenue versus a \$106.9 million loss on \$60.0 million revenue in 2020Q2.**  
   The improved net loss of \$6.2 million in 2021Q2 compared to a \$106.9 million loss in 2020Q2 reflects a 584.6% increase in total operating revenue, primarily from passenger revenue growth as travel restrictions eased. Adjusted net loss remained significant at \$73.8 million, indicating ongoing pandemic-related challenges. Operating income was \$18.5 million in 2021Q2 versus a loss of \$149.0 million in 2020Q2. Pre-tax margin improved by 252.2 percentage points to -2.0% [10-Q 2021-07-29; 8-K 2021-07-28].

2. **Revenue recovery was concentrated in Domestic routes, driven by North America, with 95.9% of passenger revenue from Domestic routes in 2021Q2 and a 1,183.6% increase in Domestic passenger revenue versus 2020Q2.**  
   Passenger revenue for Domestic routes increased to \$341.6 million, up 1,183.6% on a 721.9% capacity increase compared to 2020Q2. International passenger revenue also rose 366.3% but remained a small portion (\$14.7 million) due to ongoing international travel restrictions. Total operating revenue remained 42% below 2019Q2 levels on 30% lower capacity. The North America network notably exceeded June 2019 traffic levels in June 2021, reflecting the easing of travel restrictions and vaccination progress [10-Q 2021-07-29; 8-K 2021-07-28].

3. **Operating expenses excluding non-recurring items declined 23% year-over-year to \$478.4 million in 2021Q2, reflecting cost control despite capacity increases and higher fuel prices.**  
   Total operating expenses were \$392.3 million in 2021Q2, down from higher levels in 2020Q2, but excluding non-recurring items, expenses were higher due to increased operations. Wages and benefits rose 20.4% year-over-year to \$170.9 million, attributed to increased operations and capacity. Aircraft fuel expense surged 1,097.2% to \$83.8 million due to a 472.8% increase in gallons consumed and a doubling of average fuel price per gallon to \$1.89. Maintenance, materials and repairs rose 165.0% to \$37.1 million, and aircraft and passenger servicing increased by 747.5% to \$25.7 million, both reflecting higher utilization [10-Q 2021-07-29].

4. **Fuel costs per gallon increased sharply by 110% year-over-year in 2021Q2, with economic fuel expense per gallon rising from \$0.90 to \$1.89, contributing to a 759.5% increase in economic fuel expense despite ongoing recovery.**  
   Hawaiian did not hold fuel derivative positions in 2021Q2, unlike prior periods, resulting in no realized losses on fuel derivatives. The spike in fuel prices contributed materially to operating costs, partially offset by increased revenues but constraining margin recovery [10-Q 2021-07-29].

5. **The termination of the ‘Ohana by Hawaiian operations in 2021Q2 resulted in a one-time special charge of \$8.98 million, including a \$6.4 million asset write-down and \$2.6 million early termination of a Capacity Purchase Agreement (CPA).**  
   This termination followed temporary suspension of ‘Ohana operations in late 2020. The related ATR turboprop fleet assets were reclassified as held-for-sale, valued at \$29.5 million as of June 30, 2021. The decision reflects a strategic shift and impacts fleet composition and operating cost structure [10-Q 2021-07-29].

6. **Liquidity improved to \$2.4 billion as of June 30, 2021, including \$2.2 billion in unrestricted cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments, supported by \$173.4 million in U.S. government grants and \$31.4 million in loans under Payroll Support Program extensions.**  
   Debt and finance lease obligations rose slightly to \$2.2 billion. The company had \$31.8 million restricted cash designated for debt servicing. Hawaiian maintained compliance with debt covenants as of June 30, 2021. The company’s liquidity position was strengthened compared to March 31, 2021, when liquidity was \$2.1 billion, reflecting ongoing capital management during recovery [10-Q 2021-07-29; 8-K 2021-07-28].

### Operations Insights

7. **Capacity increased materially in 2021Q2, operating at 70% of 2019Q2 system capacity, with 97% capacity on North America routes, 57% on Neighbor Island routes, and 11% on International routes.**  
   Available seat miles (ASM) rose 766% year-over-year to 3.55 billion in 2021Q2, with revenue passenger miles (RPM) up 2,807.7% to 2.76 billion. Passenger load factor improved to 78.0% from 23.2% in 2020Q2, reflecting increased demand and network rebuilding. The company expanded service to new U.S. mainland destinations (Austin, Orlando, Ontario) and increased frequencies on existing routes, including daily Maui-Long Beach service and seasonal Phoenix-Maui flights [10-Q 2021-07-29; 8-K 2021-07-28].

8. **International operations remained severely constrained by travel restrictions, accounting for only 4.1% of passenger revenue in 2021Q2, with capacity at 11% of 2019 levels and international passenger revenue up 366% year-over-year but still depressed.**  
   Hawaiian resumed limited international service, including reinstating Tahiti flights in August 2021 following a quarantine-free travel agreement. However, international demand is still affected by government restrictions and vaccine uncertainties, limiting near-term recovery and revenue diversification [10-Q 2021-07-29; 8-K 2021-07-28].

### Labor Insights

9. **Active employee headcount modestly increased to 5,968 as of June 30, 2021, from 5,913 at March 31, 2021, reflecting gradual rehiring amid network expansion.**  
   The company previously reduced headcount by approximately 21% compared to March 31, 2020, due to COVID-19 impacts and voluntary and involuntary separation programs. Wages and benefits expense rose 20.4% in 2021Q2 compared to 2020Q2, driven by increased operations [10-Q 2021-07-29; 10-Q 2021-04-28].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

10. **Hawaiian expanded its loyalty program partnerships and relaxed policies to support recovery, including eliminating expiration of HawaiianMiles and introducing a partnership with Boyd Gaming Corporation for enhanced rewards.**  
    These moves aim to bolster guest engagement and revenue amid a recovering travel environment. The company also maintained complimentary meals on transpacific routes and no change fees on Main and Premium Cabin seats, adapting to evolving customer needs [8-K 2021-07-28; 8-K 2021-04-27].

### Route Network Insights

11. **The company expanded its U.S. mainland network with new nonstop routes to Austin, Orlando, and Ontario, and increased frequency on Maui-Long Beach, Phoenix-Maui, and Las Vegas-Maui routes, primarily targeting leisure travelers from North America.**  
    Network rebuilding focused on North America and Neighbor Island markets, with international services remaining limited. Hawaiian operated 64 daily nonstop flights to 16 U.S. gateway cities, more than any other airline serving Hawai‘i, supporting its domestic revenue concentration [10-Q 2021-07-29; 8-K 2021-07-28; 8-K 2021-04-27].

12. **Fleet composition remained stable with 69 aircraft as of June 30, 2021, including 24 A330-200s, 18 A321neos, 19 Boeing 717-200s, and 8 ATR turboprops (the latter held for sale following termination of ‘Ohana operations).**  
    The company reduced its fleet by two aircraft compared to June 30, 2020, reflecting the exit of ‘Ohana operations and fleet rationalization. The ATR turboprop fleet was classified as held-for-sale, signaling a strategic shift away from regional turboprop service [10-Q 2021-07-29].

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines made substantial progress toward financial and operational recovery in 2021Q2 as the easing of COVID-19 travel restrictions and vaccine rollouts drove a sharp rebound in domestic passenger revenue and capacity. The airline narrowed its GAAP net loss to \$6.2 million on a 585% revenue increase year-over-year, though adjusted losses remained significant. Cost pressures intensified due to a doubling of fuel prices and increased utilization-related expenses, partially offsetting margin gains. The termination of ‘Ohana by Hawaiian and reclassification of related assets marked a notable fleet and network adjustment.

Liquidity strengthened to \$2.4 billion, supported by government grants and capital markets activity, positioning Hawaiian to sustain operations during ongoing recovery phases. Network expansion focused heavily on North America and Neighbor Island routes, with international operations still constrained by travel restrictions. Labor costs rose modestly alongside gradual workforce rehiring. The airline’s commercial and loyalty initiatives aimed to enhance customer retention amid a recovering leisure travel market.

**Guidance and Outlook:** Hawaiian expects third quarter 2021 capacity to recover to 77-80% of 2019 levels, driven by North America and Neighbor Island flying, with international demand timing uncertain. Operating expenses excluding non-recurring items are expected to rise due to capacity growth, higher fuel prices, increased airport fees, and preparation for international service resumption. The company anticipates continued revenue improvement with sustained strength in North America demand and steady Neighbor Island recovery [8-K 2021-07-28].

Total revenue rose sharply but remained down 33% compared to the third quarter of 2019, on 21% lower capacity.    Domestic passenger revenue rose 1,017.9% on a 457.5% capacity increase, while international passenger revenue grew 1,769%, though international capacity remained heavily constrained. Overall passenger load factor improved to 75.9% from 25.6% in 2020Q3 [10-Q 2021-10-27].

   Wages and benefits rose to \$180.4 million, up from \$148.6 million in 2020Q3, attributed to increased operations. Aircraft fuel expense surged to \$108.8 million from \$14.5 million due to a 66.9% increase in fuel cost per gallon and a 292.7% increase in gallons consumed. Maintenance, materials, and repairs also increased substantially. Government grants recognized in the period amounted to a \$78.3 million reduction in operating expenses [10-Q 2021-10-27].

   Fuel gallons consumed increased nearly threefold to 52.6 million gallons. Hawaiian held no fuel derivative positions during the quarter, resulting in no realized fuel hedge gains or losses [10-Q 2021-10-27; 8-K 2021-10-26].

6. **Liquidity remained strong with \$2.2 billion available at September 30, 2021, including \$235 million undrawn revolving credit facility; debt outstanding was \$2.1 billion, down \$63 million from June 30, 2021.**

   Passenger load factor improved to 75.9% from a depressed 25.6% in 2020Q3, indicating better utilization as travel restrictions eased. Domestic routes accounted for 94.9% of passenger revenue, with international routes still significantly constrained by travel restrictions [10-Q 2021-10-27].

9. **Fleet composition remained stable with 68 aircraft at September 30, 2021, including 24 A330-200s, 18 A321neos, 19 717-200s, and turboprops used for 'Ohana by Hawaiian operations classified as held for sale following termination of those routes.**  
   The 'Ohana turboprop fleet (ATR 42 and ATR 72) was permanently suspended and classified as assets held for sale as of September 30, 2021 [10-Q 2021-10-27; 10-Q 2021-07-29].
