    International passenger revenue remained suppressed, down 66.7% on a 60.7% capacity reduction year-to-date compared to 2020, reflecting ongoing international travel restrictions [8-K 2021-10-26; 8-K 2021-10-07].

### Labor Insights

11. **Active employee count increased slightly to 6,403 at September 30, 2021 from 5,968 at June 30, 2021, reflecting gradual rehiring or return to work as operations expanded.**  
    The company had previously ratified a five-year collective bargaining agreement with flight attendants in April 2020 with provisions including ratification payments and improved pay scales [10-Q 2021-10-27; 10-Q 2021-07-29].

### Route Network Insights

12. **Domestic routes, primarily between Hawai'i and U.S. mainland, dominate Hawaiian's revenue base, producing approximately 94.9% of passenger revenue in 2021Q3, with international routes only 5.1%.**  
    The airline faces competition on North America routes from major network carriers with broader geographic diversification and alliance networks, which may affect Hawaiian’s competitive positioning. Hawaiian relies on code-share agreements to supplement international connectivity [10-Q 2021-10-27].

### Wrap Up

In 2021Q3, Hawaiian Airlines showed a marked financial improvement with a return to GAAP net income of \$14.7 million on sharply increased revenues driven by a rebound in passenger demand, particularly on domestic routes. Capacity and traffic recovered substantially from 2020 pandemic lows, but remained below 2019 pre-pandemic levels, with international travel still heavily constrained by government restrictions. Operating expenses rose with the recovery, notably fuel costs which more than doubled per gallon year-over-year, while government grants provided significant expense offsets. The company’s liquidity position remained strong with over \$2 billion in cash and equivalents, supporting cautious capital spending and debt reduction efforts.

The airline’s labor force stabilized with a modest increase in active employees, and fleet adjustments included the permanent suspension and sale of the 'Ohana turboprop operations. Hawaiian continued to face competitive pressures on its core North America routes from larger network carriers and alliance members, with limited international exposure. Management noted ongoing uncertainty from COVID-19 variants impacting bookings and cancellations, and adjusted 2021Q3 revenue and expense expectations downward compared to prior guidance. The company anticipates further network rebuilding, especially on domestic and Neighbor Island routes, while international recovery timing remains uncertain. Capital expenditures are planned conservatively between \$40 million and \$45 million for full year 2021.

No material operational disruptions, labor disputes, or regulatory issues were disclosed for the quarter. The company remains subject to risks from pandemic-related travel restrictions, fuel price volatility, and competitive dynamics concentrated in Hawai'i and the U.S. mainland markets.

The ATR aircraft were classified as assets held for sale as of year-end and expected to be sold in 2022 [10-K 2022-02-10, 10-Q 2021-10-27].

### Operations Insights

8. **Capacity recovery was uneven, with 4Q21 capacity down 19% versus 2019 and full year 2021 capacity down 29%, reflecting slow international network restoration.** Hawaiian’s available seat miles (ASM) were 14.4 billion in 2021, up 91.5% from 2020 but still 29% below 2019. Passenger load factor improved to 69.2% in 2021 from 60.6% in 2020 but remained below the 86.6% pre-pandemic level. The international network remained constrained with some routes (e.g., Japan, Australia, New Zealand) suspended or only partially restored through year-end [10-K 2022-02-10, 8-K 2022-01-25].

9. **Revenue passenger miles (RPM) nearly doubled in 2021 to 10.0 billion but were still 44% below 2019, with domestic RPM growth offset by international declines.** Domestic RPM increased 128% year-over-year but remained 32% below 2019 levels. International RPM was down 81% from 2019 due to ongoing travel restrictions [10-K 2022-02-10].

10. **Hawaiian launched four new routes in 2021, expanding its U.S. mainland network despite pandemic challenges.** New nonstop flights commenced from Honolulu to Austin, Orlando, and Ontario, and from Maui to Long Beach between March and April 2021. Some international services resumed, including flights to French Polynesia, American Samoa, and Sydney, Australia, but others remained suspended [8-K 2022-01-25, 10-K 2022-02-10].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

11. **Passenger revenue per available seat mile (PRASM) and yield remain below pre-pandemic levels but showed improvement in 2021.** PRASM increased to 9.51 cents in 2021 from 8.83 cents in 2020 but remained below 12.63 cents in 2019. Yield declined 5.8% year-over-year to 13.74 cents, reflecting competitive pricing and demand mix [10-K 2022-02-10].

12. **Frequent flyer revenue grew significantly in 2021, with no expiration of miles effective April 2021 to enhance loyalty program value.** Frequent flyer revenue from the transportation component increased to \$106.8 million in 2021 from \$48.6 million in 2020. The company also maintains a subscription program (Premier Club) to generate ancillary revenue and encourage repeat business [10-K 2022-02-10].

### Labor Insights

13. **The workforce increased modestly to 6,674 employees at year-end 2021, reversing pandemic-related workforce reductions, with a new five-year flight attendant contract ratified in April 2020.** Actions taken in 2020 to reduce headcount were partially reversed as domestic demand improved. The new collective bargaining agreement with flight attendants runs through April 2025 [10-Q 2021-10-27, 10-K 2022-02-10].

### Route Network Insights

14. **International operations remained constrained by pandemic-related restrictions, with some routes indefinitely suspended and others operating on adjusted schedules.** Flights to Auckland and Brisbane remained suspended at year-end 2021, with indefinite suspension of Brisbane service announced in January 2022. The company expects full restoration of its historical Japan network by summer 2022, delayed from earlier expectations [8-K 2022-03-22, 10-K 2022-02-10].

15. **The termination of the ‘Ohana by Hawaiian regional operations reduced fleet complexity but eliminated service on certain interisland routes.** The ATR-42 and ATR-72 aircraft were removed from service and classified as held for sale. The termination included a \$6.4 million asset write-down and \$2.6 million early termination charge related to the capacity purchase agreement [10-K 2022-02-10].

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ 2021 fourth quarter and full year results reflect a partial recovery from the severe impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, with revenues and capacity still significantly below 2019 levels but improving compared to 2020. Domestic leisure travel demand drove the revenue rebound, while international operations remained depressed due to ongoing restrictions. Elevated fuel prices and increased consumption substantially raised operating costs, partially offsetting revenue gains. The company maintained strong liquidity, reduced debt interest costs through tender offers, and managed labor costs prudently amid operational ramp-ups. Strategic route expansions on the U.S. mainland and the termination of the regional ‘Ohana operation marked key network adjustments. Management anticipates further recovery in international demand and expects to restore its Japan network by summer 2022, although uncertainties remain due to the evolving pandemic environment.

**Guidance Overview:**  
As of March 2022, Hawaiian updated its 2022 outlook, now expecting full-year capacity to be down 2% to 6% versus 2019, a downward revision from prior guidance of down 3% to up 1%. The company anticipates first quarter 2022 revenues down 26.5% to 29.5% versus 2019, improved from prior guidance of down 31% to 35%, driven by better-than-expected demand and higher fares. Fuel consumption is expected to be down 6.5% to 10.5% versus 2019, reflecting capacity adjustments. The full restoration of the Japan network is now expected by summer 2022, delayed by several months [8-K 2022-03-22].

### Financial Insights

   Hawaiian Airlines reported a GAAP net loss of \$122.8 million, or \$2.39 per diluted share, on total operating revenue of \$477.2 million for the quarter ended March 31, 2022. This compares to a net loss of \$60.7 million, or \$1.23 per diluted share, on \$182.2 million revenue in the same period of 2021. The revenue increase of 161.9% was primarily driven by a rebound in passenger demand, especially domestic, but operating expenses more than doubled to \$625.0 million, leading to a wider operating loss of \$147.8 million versus \$73.2 million in 2021Q1 [10-Q 2022-04-27; 8-K 2022-04-26].

   Passenger revenue grew 193.9% year-over-year to \$404.0 million, with domestic passenger revenue up 193.8% to \$377.2 million on capacity growth of 68.4%. This was supported by a 175.7% increase in passenger counts and a 6.6% increase in average fares compared to 2021Q1. International passenger revenue was \$26.8 million, up 195.2% from 2021 but still down 82.8% versus 2019 levels, reflecting ongoing travel restrictions [10-Q 2022-04-27; 8-K 2022-04-26].

Other expenses such as maintenance (+62.5%), wages (+27%), and rentals also increased as operations expanded [10-Q 2022-04-27].

   Despite revenue growth, Hawaiian reported EBITDA losses driven by still depressed international demand and elevated costs. Adjusted EBITDA loss of \$105.5 million reflects ongoing pandemic impacts and the cost of rebuilding capacity [8-K 2022-04-26].

   Hawaiian held \$1.6 billion in unrestricted cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments as of March 31, 2022, down slightly from \$1.7 billion at year-end 2021. ### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ 2022 first quarter results reflect a strong domestic recovery with passenger revenue nearly tripling and load factors improving significantly as pandemic restrictions eased, notably after Hawai‘i ended its Safe Travels program in March. However, international operations remain heavily constrained by foreign government restrictions, with international passenger revenue still down sharply versus pre-pandemic levels. Elevated fuel prices and consumption, along with increased maintenance and labor costs, drove a 42.5% rise in unit costs, resulting in a widened net loss of \$122.8 million despite nearly tripled revenues. The fleet remains stable with the regional ATR turboprops held for sale following the 2021 termination of ‘Ohana by Hawaiian. Hawaiian’s liquidity position remains strong with \$1.6 billion in cash and investments, though restrictions on share repurchases and dividends persist through September 2022.

The company suspended full-year guidance due to uncertainty around international travel recovery but projects second quarter capacity down 11.5% to 14.5% versus 2019, mainly due to delayed restoration of Japan routes. Adjusted EBITDA is expected to improve sequentially but remain negative. Risks include ongoing travel restrictions, competitive pressures especially on North America routes, and volatile fuel prices that could continue to pressure margins and cash flow. Hawaiian continues to monitor market conditions and adjust capacity accordingly while emphasizing its loyalty program and premium product performance in the domestic market.

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines' 2022Q2 results show a continuing recovery from the pandemic trough, with revenue substantially higher year-over-year and nearing pre-pandemic levels on domestic routes. The company reduced its quarterly net loss significantly compared to 2022Q1, driven by strong demand and improved yields, particularly in premium cabins. However, international operations remain heavily constrained by travel restrictions, especially in Japan, limiting full network recovery and capacity growth. Rising fuel prices and increased maintenance costs pressured operating expenses, causing CASM to rise sharply despite some cost control outside fuel. The termination and asset disposition of the 'Ohana regional operation continued, with related gains and write-downs reflected in the quarter. Workforce levels increased modestly as the airline scaled operations.

The airline’s network expansion plans for international routes in mid-2022 signal a gradual reopening, but capacity remains below 2019 levels overall. 17. **Risks include ongoing COVID-19 impacts, competitive pressures from major network carriers on key routes, inflationary cost pressures, and international travel restrictions.**  
    Hawaiian cited uncertainties from pandemic-related travel demand fluctuations, competitor capacity increases on North America-Hawai‘i routes, fuel price volatility, and labor market constraints as risks that could materially affect results [10-Q 2022-04-27; 10-K 2023-02-15; 8-K 2023-01-31]. The company’s revenue concentration in domestic routes (89% of 2022 passenger revenue) heightens vulnerability to domestic demand shocks [10-K 2023-02-15].

---

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ 2022 financial and operational performance reflected a significant recovery from the depths of the COVID-19 pandemic, with total revenue rising strongly but still trailing 2019 levels amid capacity constraints, particularly in international markets. The airline’s domestic network led the rebound, operating above pre-pandemic capacity and driving improved yields and load factors. Rising fuel prices and inflationary cost pressures increased unit costs, partially offsetting revenue gains and contributing to a continued GAAP net loss of \$240 million for the year. Liquidity and balance sheet metrics remained solid, supporting ongoing network restoration and strategic investments, including a new long-term cargo partnership with Amazon.

International route restoration progressed but remained incomplete by year-end, with capacity at less than half of 2019 levels. Labor costs increased with workforce expansion and new contracts, while premium product enhancements and loyalty program growth supported commercial recovery. The company highlighted ongoing risks from COVID-19 uncertainties, competitive pressures on key domestic routes, and inflation. Management’s guidance for 2022 reflected capacity down 2% to 6% from 2019 and capital expenditures capped near \$135 million, underscoring cautious optimism amid persistent headwinds. No material litigation, accidents, or strikes were reported in the filings for 2022.

2023.Q1:
### Financial Insights

1. **Hawaiian Airlines’ 2023Q1 operating revenue rose 28.4% year-over-year, driven mainly by a 35.8% increase in passenger revenue amid strong leisure demand, while other revenue declined 12.4% due to lower cargo revenue.** Total operating revenue reached \$612.6 million, up from \$477.2 million in 2022Q1. Passenger revenue increased to \$548.5 million from \$404.0 million, with domestic routes accounting for \$486.1 million and Pacific international routes \$126.5 million [8-K 2023-04-25; 10-Q 2023-04-26].

2. **Despite revenue growth, Hawaiian reported a GAAP net loss of \$98.3 million in 2023Q1, an improvement of \$35.0 million from a \$133.3 million loss in 2022Q1, with adjusted net loss narrowing to \$111.8 million from \$130.3 million.** Operating loss improved 20.6% to \$117.4 million. EBITDA loss reduced by \$37.2 million to negative \$70.3 million. Diluted EPS loss narrowed to \$(1.91) from \$(2.60) [8-K 2023-04-25].

3. **Operating cost per available seat mile (CASM) increased modestly to 14.85 cents from 14.66 cents, despite a slight reduction in CASM excluding fuel and non-recurring items to 11.04 cents from 11.07 cents.** Fuel expense per ASM rose 13.6% to 4.02 cents from 3.54 cents, reflecting higher fuel prices and consumption [8-K 2023-04-25; 10-Q 2023-04-26].

4. **Aircraft fuel expense increased 30.9% to \$197.6 million due to a 21.4% rise in fuel gallons consumed (64.9 million gallons vs. 53.4 million) and a 7.8% increase in average fuel price per gallon to \$3.05.** The increase in fuel consumption was attributed partly to operational inefficiencies caused by runway construction at Honolulu's airport and substitution of less fuel-efficient A330 aircraft for A321s due to engine delays [8-K 2023-04-25; 10-Q 2023-04-26].

5. **Wages and benefits expense rose 19.1% to \$241.9 million, driven by increased operations, contractual wage increases, inflationary pressures, and a \$17.7 million signing bonus related to a new four-year pilot contract ratified in February 2023.** The contract includes pay scale increases, improved benefits, and enhanced postretirement and disability plans [8-K 2023-04-25; 10-Q 2023-04-26].

6. **Capital expenditures surged to \$106.2 million in 2023Q1 from \$9.1 million in 2022Q1, reflecting investments including pre-delivery payments for new aircraft and infrastructure.** Net cash provided by operating activities improved to \$118.3 million from \$22.2 million. The company ended 2023Q1 with \$1.4 billion in unrestricted cash and short-term investments and \$1.7 billion in outstanding debt and finance lease obligations, maintaining \$1.6 billion in total liquidity including a \$235 million undrawn revolving credit facility [8-K 2023-04-25].

### Operations Insights

7. **Capacity (available seat miles, ASM) grew 15.4% to 4.92 billion, with revenue passenger miles (RPM) increasing 28.7% to 3.85 billion and passenger load factor rising 8.1 points to 78.2%.** These reflect recovery from the COVID-19 impact in 2022Q1 and strong leisure demand. Revenue per ASM rose 11.3% to 12.46 cents, and passenger yield increased 5.1% to 14.27 cents [8-K 2023-04-25; 10-Q 2023-04-26].

8. **Operational disruptions included Pratt & Whitney engine delays limiting A321neo aircraft availability, forcing substitution with less fuel-efficient A330 aircraft on some routes, runway construction at Honolulu International Airport, and air traffic control delays.** These factors degraded on-time performance and increased fuel consumption by 21.4%, adversely affecting financial results [8-K 2023-04-25].

9. **Hawaiian operated 52,228 revenue block hours in 2023Q1, up 16.4% from 44,883 hours in 2022Q1, reflecting higher flight activity as operations rebuild.** The fleet comprised 63 aircraft as of March 31, 2023, down from 68 in 2022Q1, with plans to add new Boeing 787-9 aircraft deliveries starting late 2023 and continuing through 2027 [10-Q 2023-04-26; 8-K 2023-01-31].

### Labor Insights

10. **Labor costs increased notably, reflecting contractual wage increases and inflation, with a \$17.7 million one-time signing bonus expense related to the pilot collective bargaining agreement ratified in February 2023.** The agreement covers four years through 2027 and includes pay scale increases and benefit improvements [8-K 2023-04-25; 10-Q 2023-04-26].

11. **As of March 31, 2023, Hawaiian had 7,218 active employees, supporting expanded operations and initiatives including new technology deployments and fleet modernization.** No labor disruptions or strikes were reported in the filings [10-Q 2023-04-26].

### Route Network Insights

12. **Hawaiian’s domestic network, including 15 U.S. mainland gateway cities, accounted for approximately 80.7% of passenger revenue in 2023Q1, with international routes comprising about 19.3%.** The international network is recovering, excluding Japan, with resumed flights to Auckland, New Zealand, and Tokyo Haneda, and new service to Rarotonga, Cook Islands starting May 2023 [8-K 2023-04-25; 10-Q 2023-04-26].

13. **Fleet availability challenges due to Pratt & Whitney engine delays for the A321neo limited capacity growth and forced operational adjustments, including the use of less fuel-efficient A330 aircraft on some routes.** Hawaiian also plans to begin freighter operations under an Air Transportation Services Agreement with Amazon in late 2023, involving 10 Airbus A330-300F aircraft [8-K 2023-04-25; 10-Q 2023-04-26].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

14. **Strong leisure demand supported premium product sales both domestically and internationally, with positive momentum in ancillary offerings such as Extra Comfort and preferred seating.** Passenger revenue per ASM (PRASM) improved 17.2% to 11.16 cents [8-K 2023-04-25].

### Risks and Other Disclosures

16. **Hawaiian faces risks from concentrated reliance on the domestic Hawaiian market, where about 80% of passenger revenue is generated, exposing it to competitive pressure from major U.S. network carriers and limited geographic diversification.** The company noted that increased competitor capacity on North America to Hawai'i routes could materially impact its results [10-Q 2023-04-26; 10-K 2023-02-15].

17. **Fuel price volatility and supply chain constraints remain key risk factors, with fuel costs representing about 29% of operating expenses in 2022.** Hawaiian hedges approximately 21% of its fuel requirements for 2023 but experienced a 30.9% increase in fuel expense in 2023Q1 [10-K 2023-02-15; 8-K 2023-04-25].

18. **Operational disruptions from runway construction and air traffic control delays at Honolulu International Airport continue to impair on-time performance and operational efficiency, increasing costs and reducing scheduling flexibility.** These factors constrained Hawaiian’s ability to fully capitalize on demand and capacity expansion [8-K 2023-04-25].

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ first quarter 2023 results show significant revenue recovery driven by strong leisure demand and a rebound in passenger volumes, especially on domestic routes. However, the company remained unprofitable, with losses narrowing due to improved operating leverage but offset by rising fuel costs, labor expenses, and operational inefficiencies linked to fleet availability and airport construction disruptions. Capacity grew moderately but was constrained by A321 engine delays, requiring less efficient aircraft substitutions that increased fuel consumption. Hawaiian’s liquidity position remained solid, supported by \$1.4 billion in cash and investments and a \$235 million undrawn credit facility.

The airline’s network is recovering internationally with new routes planned, and commercial efforts focus on premium product sales and technology enhancements. Risks highlighted include concentrated exposure to the Hawaiian domestic market, competitive pressures from major U.S. carriers, fuel price volatility, and ongoing operational disruptions at its primary hub. The company’s pilot labor agreement ratified in early 2023 added one-time costs and will raise wages in subsequent periods. Hawaiian’s capital spending increased sharply as it invests in fleet renewal and infrastructure to support long-term growth and the launch of freighter operations with Amazon.

**Guidance:** For 2023Q2, Hawaiian expects ASMs to increase 10.5% to 13.5% year-over-year, with operating revenue per ASM projected to decline 8.5% to 11.5%, and CASM excluding fuel and non-recurring items to be flat to up 3%. Fuel consumption is forecast to rise 16.5% to 19.5%, with an economic fuel price per gallon of \$2.62. The full-year 2023 fuel consumption guidance was raised to 12.5% to 15.5% growth, with a fuel price assumption of \$2.70 per gallon [8-K 2023-04-25].
2023.Q2:
### Financial Insights

1. **Operating revenue grew modestly despite a significant capacity increase, with international revenue surging on Japan-originating traffic**

Passenger revenue rose 4.5% to \$645.0 million year-over-year (YoY). However, CASM excluding fuel and non-recurring items rose 1.9% to 11.08¢, reflecting increased labor and other costs. Non-recurring items included a \$5.97 million contract termination amortization and the absence of a \$17.7 million pilot signing bonus expense recorded in Q1 [8-K 2023-07-25; 10-Q 2023-07-26].

   Hawaiian’s GAAP operating loss improved by \$16.5 million to a \$9.6 million loss in Q2 2023, supported by higher revenue and lower fuel costs. Adjusted EBITDA increased by \$25.2 million to \$26.3 million. Net loss narrowed to \$12.3 million from \$47.4 million in Q2 2022, with adjusted net loss improving by \$22.0 million to \$24.1 million. Diluted EPS loss improved to -\$0.24 from -\$0.92 [8-K 2023-07-25; 10-Q 2023-07-26].

   Hawaiian reported \$1.3 billion in unrestricted cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments and total liquidity of \$1.6 billion including a \$235 million undrawn revolving credit facility. Outstanding debt and finance lease obligations remained at \$1.7 billion as of June 30, 2023 [8-K 2023-07-25].

   The Company revised full-year 2023 capital expenditure guidance downward from \$330–380 million to \$265–295 million, reflecting a delay in Boeing 787-9 aircraft deliveries, with the first 787-9 now expected in January 2024, two months later than previously planned. Hawaiian holds a purchase agreement for 10 Boeing 787-9s with options for 10 more [8-K 2023-07-25; 10-Q 2023-07-26].

### Operations Insights

6. **Capacity increased 11.0% YoY with a 12.5% rise in revenue passenger miles (RPM), driven by recovering international demand and strong leisure travel**  
   Hawaiian’s ASM rose 11.0% to 5.01 billion and RPM increased 12.5% to 4.35 billion in Q2 2023 versus Q2 2022, yielding a 1.0 point increase in load factor to 86.7%. Neighbor Island load factor was 75.3%, the highest since 2015. The North America route load factor was 90.4%, the highest Q2 level since 2017. International capacity grew 141.4%, with international load factor up 16.2 points YoY. The increase in Japan-originating traffic notably contributed to this improvement [8-K 2023-07-25; 10-Q 2023-07-26].

   Fuel gallons consumed rose to 66.4 million in Q2 2023 from 57.5 million in Q2 2022, a 15.4% increase driven by higher capacity and operational challenges including runway construction at Honolulu and aircraft up-gauging due to supply-chain-related A321neo availability issues. The average fuel price per gallon dropped 36.5% to \$2.51, reducing overall fuel expense despite higher consumption [10-Q 2023-07-26; 8-K 2023-04-25].

8. **Transitioned A330 aircraft maintenance in-house to improve control and efficiencies**  
   Hawaiian completed the transition of A330 maintenance from vendor-managed services to internal management in Q2 2023. This shift enables greater operational control and potential cost efficiencies, though the filing does not quantify financial impact [8-K 2023-07-25].

9. **Operational pressures from competitor capacity increases on Neighbor Island routes led to yield declines**  
   Neighbor Island traffic, accounting for about 18% of domestic revenue in Q2 2023, faced increased competitive capacity and low fares, resulting in a 19.7% decline in revenue yield compared to Q2 2022. This competitive pressure is expected to continue as a headwind [10-Q 2023-07-26].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

10. **International route recovery contributed significantly to revenue growth, but remains below pre-pandemic levels**  
    International passenger revenue surged 160.2% YoY in Q2 2023 driven by capacity increases, especially from Japan. Despite this, international revenue remains down approximately 21.5% compared to Q2 2019, reflecting a lagging recovery relative to domestic routes.     Other operating revenue, which includes cargo, decreased 16.8% YoY to \$61.9 million in Q2 2023. Cargo revenue fell \$5.2 million, primarily due to lower volumes, partially offsetting gains in passenger revenue [10-Q 2023-07-26].

    In February 2023, Hawaiian’s pilots ratified a four-year CBA including signing bonuses, pay scale increases, improved health benefits, and enhanced postretirement plans. ### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines' Q2 2023 results reflect a recovery phase characterized by robust leisure demand, especially on international routes fueled by Japan-originating traffic, and a substantial capacity increase of 11%. Despite the revenue growth of 2.2%, revenue per ASM fell due to this capacity expansion outpacing revenue gains. Operating costs per ASM showed improvement on a GAAP basis, largely driven by a significant drop in fuel prices, although excluding fuel and non-recurring items, unit costs rose slightly, reflecting inflationary pressures and labor cost increases from recently ratified pilot agreements.

Operationally, Hawaiian managed higher passenger volumes and improved load factors, yet faced yield pressure on Neighbor Island routes amid increased competition. The transition of A330 maintenance in-house signals a strategic move toward operational control. Cargo revenue declined, indicating some softness outside passenger operations. Liquidity remains strong, supporting capital investments, although Boeing 787 deliveries are delayed, reducing near-term capital expenditures.

**Guidance Overview:** For Q3 2023, Hawaiian expects ASM growth of approximately 4.5% to 7.5% with RASM declining 2.0% to 5.0% versus Q3 2022. Full-year 2023 guidance includes ASM growth of 8.5% to 10.5%, CASM excluding fuel and non-recurring items rising 3.0% to 5.0%, and capital expenditures lowered to \$265–295 million due to Boeing delivery delays [8-K 2023-07-25; 10-Q 2023-07-26]. ### Financial Insights

### Operations Insights

5. **Capacity grew 4.1% in Q3 2023, but was below prior guidance due to Pratt & Whitney engine inspections causing A321neo aircraft shortages and reduced growth.**

   International capacity increased 43.6% in Q3 2023, with passenger revenue rising 90.9% year-over-year [10-Q 2023-10-25]. However, international travel demand remains depressed relative to 2019, partly due to currency headwinds such as a weak Japanese Yen [10-Q 2023-07-26; 10-Q 2023-10-25].

   Wages and benefits rose to \$248.9 million in Q3 2023 from \$206.3 million in Q3 2022, reflecting higher pay scales, signing bonuses, improved health benefits, and postretirement plan enhancements [10-Q 2023-10-25; 8-K 2023-10-24].     This follows increased bookings from Japan, an important but slower-recovering market [8-K 2023-10-24; 8-K 2023-07-25]. The Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner is expected to enter service on select West Coast routes starting April 15, 2024 [8-K 2023-10-24].

12. **Loyalty program revenue grew modestly despite declines in cargo and other operating revenue, reflecting increased credit card spend and new cardholder acquisitions.**  
    For the nine months ended September 30, 2023, loyalty-related revenue increased \$6.4 million year-over-year, while cargo revenue declined \$18.7 million due to lower volumes [10-Q 2023-10-25].

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ 2023 third quarter results reflect the combined impact of external shocks and operational constraints. The devastating Maui wildfires sharply curtailed demand on Neighbor Island routes, contributing to a revenue decline despite network-wide capacity growth. Concurrently, accelerated Pratt & Whitney engine inspections reduced A321neo availability, limiting capacity expansion and disrupting operations. These factors pressured yields and margins, leading to a substantial increase in operating loss compared to 2022.

Fuel costs declined due to lower prices despite higher consumption, partially offsetting cost pressures from rising wages following a new pilot contract and inflationary impacts on servicing and purchased services. Liquidity declined amid sustained capital expenditures, including deferred Boeing 787 deliveries now expected starting in early 2024. International routes showed notable recovery, supported by increased capacity and resumed Japan service, though demand remains below pre-pandemic levels.

**Guidance for Q4 2023 and full year 2023** includes expected ASM growth of 1.5% to 4.5% in Q4, with RASM down 10% to 13%, and CASM up 2% to 4.1%, excluding fuel and non-recurring items rising 6.5% to 9.5%. Fuel consumption is forecast to increase 5% to 8% with an economic fuel price near \$3.12/gallon. Full-year capacity growth is now expected at 8% to 10%, slightly below prior estimates, reflecting ongoing engine availability issues and Maui recovery impacts [8-K 2023-10-24; 8-K 2023-09-05]. The company anticipates continued operational challenges into 2024 from these factors.

6. **Capacity grew 3.4% in 2023Q4 (ASMs 5.1 billion vs. 4.93 billion in 2022Q4), while revenue passenger miles (RPMs) increased 5.9%, lifting load factor 1.9 points to 82.7%.**  
   Despite capacity growth, passenger yield declined 12.7% to 14.26¢ per RPM and passenger revenue per ASM (PRASM) fell 10.7%, reflecting fare pressure. The higher load factor partially offset yield declines.  
   [8-K filed 2024-01-30; 10-K filed 2024-02-15]

7. **Traffic and capacity were affected by Pratt & Whitney’s accelerated removals and inspections of the PW1100G-JM engines on Hawaiian’s Airbus A321neo fleet, causing lower-than-expected capacity growth and operational disruptions extending into 2024.**  
   This engine shortage constrained capacity expansion plans, particularly on North America and International routes, and contributed to operational challenges including upgauging aircraft and runway construction impacts at Honolulu.  
   [8-K filed 2023-10-24; 10-K filed 2024-02-15]

8. **Maui wildfires in August 2023 caused a sharp decline in travel to Maui and increased ticket refunds, with recovery underway but demand still below historical levels by year-end.**  
   Hawaiian responded by evacuating over 17,000 displaced people and transporting emergency supplies. Travel to Maui improved steadily in Q4 but remained a drag on revenue. Non-Maui routes and international markets (especially Japan) showed solid demand recovery.  
   [8-K filed 2023-10-24; 8-K filed 2024-01-30]

9. **The company launched its freighter operation with the entry into service of an A330-300F aircraft on October 2, 2023, under an eight-year contract with Amazon, with plans to increase to six freighters by end of 2024.**  
   This new cargo operation represents a strategic diversification, though its financial impact was not yet material in 2023.  
   [10-K filed 2024-02-15; 8-K filed 2023-10-24]

### Commercial Strategy Insights

10. **Passenger revenue increased 10.3% year-to-date through September 2023, driven by international market recovery and premium product performance, but fourth quarter passenger revenue per ASM declined 10.7% due to pandemic-related revenue base effects and wildfire impacts.**  
    Premium cabin products continued to perform well, and international load factor improved by 20.7 points year-over-year, notably supported by recovery in Japan-originating traffic.  
    [8-K filed 2024-01-30; 10-Q filed 2023-10-25]

11. **Other operating revenue, primarily cargo and contract services, declined 16.2% in 2023 compared to 2022, reflecting a normalization after elevated pandemic-related cargo demand in 2022.**  
    This reduction contributed to the overall revenue decline in Q4 and full year 2023 despite passenger revenue growth.  
    [8-K filed 2024-01-30]

12. **Hawaiian announced new routes and service expansions for 2024, including new daily nonstop service between Salt Lake City and Honolulu starting May 15, 2024, and expanded service to Sacramento with flights to Kauaʻi and Kona.**  
    These network expansions aim to grow North America connectivity and Neighbor Island service.  
    [8-K filed 2024-01-30]

### Labor Insights

13. **Labor costs increased notably in 2023 following ratification of a new four-year pilot contract in February 2023, which included signing bonuses, pay scale increases, and benefit enhancements, resulting in a \$17.7 million expense in Q1 2023.**  
    Wages and benefits rose 14.3% year-over-year to \$951.5 million in 2023, reflecting contractual wage growth and staffing to support capacity increases.  
    [8-K filed 2023-10-24; 10-K filed 2024-02-15]

### Route Network Insights

14. **Fleet composition at year-end 2023 included 19 Boeing 717-200s for Neighbor Island routes, 24 Airbus A330-200s, and 18 Airbus A321neos primarily for North America and International routes; the Boeing 787-9 was delivered in February 2024 and expected to enter service in April 2024.**  
    The ATR turboprop fleet was fully exited by October 2023, following the termination of the 'Ohana by Hawaiian regional operation.  
    [10-K filed 2024-02-15; 10-Q filed 2023-10-25]

15. **Hawaiian’s network includes approximately 150 daily flights within the Hawaiian Islands and nonstop service to 15 U.S. gateway cities, more than any other airline; international service connects Hawai'i with Japan, Australia, New Zealand, South Korea, and South Pacific destinations.**  
    The airline remains the largest and longest-serving carrier in Hawaiʻi, with a significant share of passenger revenue from Domestic routes (79% in 2023) and North America routes (64%).  
    [10-K filed 2024-02-15; 10-Q filed 2023-10-25]

### Corporate Insights

16. **On December 3, 2023, Hawaiian Holdings entered into a definitive merger agreement to be acquired by Alaska Air Group for approximately \$1.9 billion, including \$0.9 billion net debt, subject to regulatory and shareholder approvals, with expected closing in 12-18 months.**  
    The transaction aims to combine networks, expand destinations, and maintain Hawaiian’s presence and commitment in Hawaiʻi, including robust Neighbor Island service and union workforce preservation. Regulatory review was ongoing as of February 2024, with a second request for information received from the DOJ Antitrust Division.  
    [8-K filed 2023-12-04; 8-K filed 2024-02-07; 8-K filed 2024-03-27]

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ 2023Q4 results reflected a challenging environment marked by operational disruptions from Pratt & Whitney engine shortages and the impact of the Maui wildfires, which depressed demand to a key destination. Despite capacity growth and improving international markets, the company reported a significantly wider net loss and margin compression due to lower yields, higher labor costs from a new pilot contract, and reduced cargo revenues. Operationally, Hawaiian expanded its freighter service under a long-term Amazon contract and prepared for new fleet additions, including the Boeing 787-9. The company’s liquidity remained robust with over \$1 billion available, supporting ongoing capital investments and debt obligations.

Strategically, Hawaiian advanced its network with new U.S. mainland routes and strengthened its premium product offerings. The announcement of the pending acquisition by Alaska Air Group introduces substantial corporate change, with integration and regulatory approval processes underway. This transaction is expected to reshape Hawaiian’s competitive positioning and network reach upon closing, contingent on customary conditions. The company’s outlook for 2024 includes modest capacity growth, cost increases, and fuel price assumptions aligned with recent trends, while operational challenges from engine shortages are expected to persist into the year.
2023.FY:
### Financial Insights

1. **Full-year 2023 revenue rose 2.8% on 8.1% higher capacity, but the airline remained unprofitable with a \$260.5 million GAAP net loss.** Hawaiian’s operating revenue for 2023 was \$2.72 billion, up from \$2.64 billion in 2022, driven by an 8.1% increase in available seat miles (ASMs). Despite revenue growth, the GAAP net loss widened slightly by \$20.4 million year-over-year. Adjusted net loss was \$313.5 million, worsening by \$103.1 million versus 2022. The pre-tax margin declined by 1.0 percentage point to -12.1%, reflecting ongoing operating challenges [8-K 2024-01-30; 10-K 2024-02-15].

2. **Passenger revenue increased 5.3% to \$2.46 billion, but yield declined 6.7% and PRASM fell 2.8%, indicating softer unit pricing despite volume growth.** Passenger revenue per revenue passenger mile (yield) dropped from 15.64¢ in 2022 to 14.59¢ in 2023, while passenger revenue per ASM (PRASM) fell from 12.53¢ to 12.18¢. Passenger load factor improved 3.4 points to 83.5%, driven by an 8.4% ASM increase and 12.9% RPM growth. This suggests Hawaiian grew traffic but at lower fare levels or with increased discounting [10-K 2024-02-15; 8-K 2024-01-30].

3. **Operating costs rose 5.5% to \$3.01 billion, with wages and fuel as major drivers; CASM excluding fuel and non-recurring items increased modestly, but total CASM rose due to fuel and other factors.** Wages and benefits grew 14.2% to \$951.5 million, partly due to a new pilot contract ratified in February 2023 with signing bonuses and pay raises totaling \$17.7 million expensed in Q1. Fuel expense declined 6.3% to \$766.1 million, reflecting a 15.5% reduction in economic fuel price per gallon to \$2.89, despite a 12.2% increase in fuel gallons consumed driven by higher capacity and some inefficiencies. Maintenance, servicing, and other costs increased, contributing to a total operating cost per ASM (CASM) of 14.90¢ in 2023, up 0.36¢ from 14.54¢ in 2022. CASM excluding fuel and non-recurring items was 11.29¢, up 0.51¢, indicating cost pressure beyond fuel [10-K 2024-02-15; 8-K 2023-04-25; 8-K 2023-07-25].

4. **Fuel efficiency was impaired in Q1 2023 due to Pratt & Whitney engine shortages forcing substitution of less fuel-efficient A330s for A321s, increasing fuel burn and costs.** Hawaiian reported a 21.4% year-over-year increase in jet fuel consumption in Q1 2023 with a 7.8% rise in average fuel cost per gallon to \$3.05, attributed to fleet disruptions caused by engine delays and maintenance issues. These operational constraints negatively affected scheduling, on-time performance, and financial results [8-K 2023-04-25].

5. **Liquidity declined through 2023, with unrestricted cash and short-term investments falling from \$1.4 billion at Q1 to \$908.5 million at year-end, while total debt and finance leases remained steady at \$1.7 billion.** Despite cash burn, Hawaiian maintained \$1.1 billion in liquidity at year-end, including a \$235 million undrawn revolving credit facility. The company was in compliance with debt covenants as of December 31, 2023 [8-K 2023-04-25; 8-K 2023-07-25; 8-K 2024-01-30; 10-K 2024-02-15].

6. **Capital expenditures were guided to remain stable at approximately \$265-\$295 million for 2023, primarily reflecting aircraft deliveries and related investments.** The delivery schedule of Boeing 787 aircraft influenced capex timing, with the first 787-9 delivery occurring in February 2024 and planned entry into service in April 2024 [8-K 2023-07-25; 10-K 2024-02-15].

### Operations Insights

7. **Capacity grew 8.4% in 2023 with 20.2 billion ASMs, driven by domestic and international expansion, but operational disruptions constrained growth and efficiency.** Revenue passenger miles increased 12.9% to 16.9 billion, with load factors rising 3.4 points to 83.5%. Hawaiian operated a fleet of 19 Boeing 717-200s for Neighbor Island routes, 24 Airbus A330-200s, and 18 Airbus A321neos primarily for North America and international routes as of year-end 2023. However, Pratt & Whitney engine shortages on A321neos caused capacity shortfalls and forced use of less efficient A330s on some routes [10-K 2024-02-15; 8-K 2023-04-25].

8. **International traffic recovered strongly, with a 20.7-point year-over-year increase in international load factor in Q4 2023, supported by increased Japan-originating traffic and resumption of routes such as Tokyo Haneda to Kona.** International capacity rose sharply, with a 141.4% increase in capacity and 160.2% revenue growth in Q2 2023 compared to 2022. The company resumed service to destinations including Auckland and Tokyo Haneda and planned Boeing 787-9 deployment on West Coast routes in 2024 [8-K 2023-07-25; 8-K 2023-10-24].

9. **The Maui wildfires in August 2023 caused a sharp decline in traffic to Maui in Q3, with gradual recovery by Q4 but demand remaining below historical levels.** Hawaiian supported relief efforts by transporting first responders and essential cargo, carrying over 193,000 pounds of goods. Non-Maui and international markets maintained solid demand despite the disruption [8-K 2023-10-24; 8-K 2024-01-30].

10. **Hawaiian launched freighter operations in October 2023 under an agreement with Amazon, operating 10 Airbus A330-300 freighters with options to expand, marking a strategic diversification into cargo.** The Air Transportation Services Agreement (ATSA) with Amazon commenced on October 2, 2023, with plans for a long-term partnership potentially extending beyond the initial eight-year term [8-K 2023-07-25; 10-K 2024-02-15].

### Labor Insights

11. **Labor costs increased notably in 2023, driven by a ratified four-year pilot contract with ALPA including signing bonuses, pay scale increases, and enhanced benefits, resulting in a \$17.7 million one-time expense in Q1 2023.** Wages and benefits rose 14.2% year-over-year, reflecting ongoing investment in workforce compensation amid operational recovery [8-K 2023-04-25; 8-K 2023-07-25].

### Route Network Insights

12. **Fleet modernization advanced with delivery of Boeing 787-9 aircraft in early 2024 and planned expansion of A321neo service, supporting network growth and enhanced long-haul capabilities.** The 787-9 is expected to enter service on select West Coast routes in April 2024. Hawaiian also announced the purchase of five Boeing 717-200 aircraft previously leased, consolidating its Neighbor Island fleet [8-K 2023-10-24; 10-K 2024-02-15].

13. **The announced merger agreement with Alaska Air Group in December 2023, valued at approximately \$1.9 billion including \$0.9 billion of net debt, aims to create an integrated Pacific and U.S. West Coast network with expanded connectivity and loyalty benefits.** The merger is subject to regulatory and shareholder approvals and expected to close within 12-18 months of announcement. Hawaiian will operate as a subsidiary post-merger with commitments to maintain robust Neighbor Island service and union workforce [8-K 2023-12-04; 8-K 2024-01-30; 10-K 2024-02-15].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

14. **Premium product demand remained strong across domestic and international markets in 2023, contributing to revenue growth despite overall yield pressure.** Sales of Extra Comfort and preferred seating options showed positive momentum. The loyalty program, HawaiianMiles, continued to generate significant revenue, with frequent flyer transportation revenue rising modestly to \$184 million in 2023 [8-K 2023-04-25; 10-K 2024-02-15].

15. **The company introduced sustainability-focused guest amenities and published its 2023 Corporate Kuleana Report outlining environmental commitments including a decarbonization roadmap targeting 10% sustainable aviation fuel use by 2030 and a 45% reduction in life-cycle jet fuel emissions per revenue ton mile by 2035.** New in-flight amenity kits designed in collaboration with a Hawai‘i lifestyle brand debuted in late 2023 with a focus on sustainability [8-K 2023-10-24; 8-K 2024-01-30].

### Wrap Up

In 2023, Hawaiian Airlines expanded capacity and grew revenue modestly while continuing to operate at a significant net loss. The company faced operational headwinds from Pratt & Whitney engine shortages and the Maui wildfires, which constrained efficiency and capacity growth. Despite a challenging cost environment marked by higher labor expenses and fuel consumption inefficiencies, Hawaiian maintained solid demand, particularly in leisure and premium segments, and made strategic investments in fleet modernization and cargo operations. The announced merger with Alaska Air Group represents a major strategic development with potential to reshape Hawaiian’s network and market positioning, pending regulatory approval. Liquidity declined but remained adequate, with stable debt levels and ongoing capital commitments focused on fleet renewal.

Guidance for 2023 included increases in jet fuel consumption of 12.5% to 15.5% and a lower economic fuel price per gallon than prior estimates, reflecting a dynamic fuel cost environment. The company also highlighted continued operational risks from engine maintenance issues and the uncertain recovery pace of international travel, emphasizing the ongoing unpredictability in demand patterns post-pandemic. No material litigation or labor disputes were disclosed beyond the ratified pilot contract.

This summary synthesizes Hawaiian’s 2023 financial and operational disclosures without extrapolating beyond reported facts and management commentary.

2024.Q1:
### Financial Insights

1. **Passenger revenue rose 6.4% year-over-year to \$583.4 million in 2024Q1, but the operating loss widened to \$148.6 million from \$117.4 million in 2023Q1.** Passenger revenue growth outpaced capacity growth (ASMs up 2.7%), driven by a 5.9% increase in revenue passenger miles (RPMs) and a 2.4-point increase in load factor to 80.6%. Despite this, operating costs increased faster, with total CASM (cost per ASM) rising 5.9% to 15.72¢, including a 7.1% increase in CASM excluding fuel and non-recurring items to 11.82¢. Fuel costs per gallon declined 8.5% to \$2.79, reducing fuel expense per ASM by 7.0% to 3.74¢, partly offsetting the cost pressure. 2. **Cash generation was positive but modest, with net operating cash flow of \$254,000 in 2024Q1, down sharply from \$118.3 million in 2023Q1, reflecting higher losses and working capital changes.** Investing activities used \$33.3 million, primarily for property and equipment additions, while financing activities provided \$110.6 million, including \$131.4 million of new long-term borrowings partially offset by debt repayments. Cash, cash equivalents, and restricted cash increased to \$248.1 million from \$170.5 million at year-end 2023, supported by liquidity of \$1.15 billion including an undrawn \$235 million revolving credit facility. Outstanding debt and finance lease obligations rose to \$1.75 billion [10-Q 2024-04-24].

3. **Significant special items and merger-related costs impacted earnings comparability.** The 2023Q1 period included a \$17.7 million signing bonus and vacation liability true-up related to a pilot collective bargaining agreement (CBA), while 2024Q1 included \$8.5 million in special items. ### Operations Insights

4. **Capacity grew 2.7% year-over-year in 2024Q1 while RPMs increased 5.9%, lifting load factor by 2.4 points to 80.6%, reflecting improved demand across Hawaiian’s network.** Revenue passengers increased 1.1% to 2.62 million. Revenue passenger yield was stable, rising slightly by 0.4% to 14.33¢ per RPM, resulting in a 3.5% increase in PRASM (passenger revenue per ASM) to 11.55¢. Total operating revenue per ASM (RASM) increased 2.6% to 12.78¢. Flight block hours and fuel consumption were essentially flat, with a 0.2% decrease in block hours and 4.3% increase in jet fuel gallons consumed, reflecting operational efficiency and network changes [10-Q 2024-04-24; 8-K 2024-04-23].

5. **Fuel efficiency benefits partly offset by higher maintenance and other operating expenses.** Fuel expense per ASM declined 7.0% due to an 8.5% drop in fuel price per gallon to \$2.79, despite a 4.3% increase in fuel volume consumed. Maintenance, materials, and repairs rose sharply by 41% to \$71.0 million from \$50.3 million, indicating elevated maintenance activity. Other operating expenses including wages and benefits increased 8.3% to \$262 million, driven by wage inflation and CBA-related costs [10-Q 2024-04-24].

6. **Operational disruptions due to Pratt & Whitney engine shortages continue to constrain capacity growth, particularly domestically.** Management disclosed that accelerated removals and inspections of the PW110G-JM engines began in July 2023, resulting in lower-than-expected capacity growth in 2023 and anticipated ongoing disruptions through 2024 and potentially beyond. Neighbor Island traffic, representing 22.2% of domestic passenger revenue, increased 17.8%, indicating resilience in interisland markets despite capacity constraints [10-K 2024-02-15; 10-Q 2024-04-24].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

7. **Revenue growth was supported by network expansion and product enhancements, including new routes and onboard connectivity upgrades.** Hawaiian launched new daily service between Salt Lake City and Honolulu starting May 2024 and added flights from Sacramento to Līhuʻe and Kona. Summer flight increases were announced for Honolulu to Austin, Boston, Las Vegas, and Pago Pago, along with a fourth daily flight between Honolulu and Los Angeles. Starlink inflight WiFi was installed and offered free on all 18 A321neo aircraft, enhancing the guest experience [8-K 2024-04-23].

8. **Passenger revenue composition remained stable with domestic routes generating the bulk of revenue.** Domestic passenger revenue was \$492.4 million in 2024Q1, up modestly from \$486.1 million in 2023Q1. Pacific (primarily international) revenue rose 21% to \$153.2 million. Frequent flyer transportation revenue increased slightly to \$43.8 million, while marketing and brand-related frequent flyer revenue remained steady at \$28.6 million. Other revenue, including cargo, declined 3.1% to \$62.1 million due to lower cargo volumes [10-Q 2024-04-24].

### Route Network Insights

9. **Fleet modernization and expansion continue with the introduction of Boeing 787-9 aircraft and growth of the freighter operation.** Hawaiian took delivery of its first Boeing 787-9 in February 2024 under a purchase assignment and leaseback, entering revenue service in mid-April 2024. The airline expects to operate six aircraft under the Amazon Air Transportation Services Agreement (ATSA) by year-end 2024. Additionally, Hawaiian received a second Airbus A330-300 freighter from Amazon, operating between New York JFK and San Bernardino, marking expansion in freighter services [10-Q 2024-04-24; 8-K 2024-04-23].

10. **The airline is disposing of its 'Ohana by Hawaiian turboprop fleet, completing sales of remaining ATR 72-200 aircraft in October 2023, with parts sales planned for 2024.** The termination of 'Ohana operations was announced in 2021, and assets were classified as held-for-sale. ### Labor Insights

11. **Labor costs increased, reflecting wage inflation and pilot contract expenses.** Wages and benefits rose 8.3% year-over-year to \$261.9 million in 2024Q1. The 2023 pilot collective bargaining agreement ratified in February 2023 included signing bonuses, pay scale increases, and enhanced benefits, contributing to recorded expenses in the prior year. The company employed 7,386 active employees as of March 31, 2024 [10-Q 2024-04-24; 10-K 2024-02-15].

### Corporate Insights

12. **The merger agreement with Alaska Air Group remains pending regulatory approval with no reported changes during 2024Q1.** The transaction, announced December 2023, is subject to Hart-Scott-Rodino and other approvals. Hawaiian and Alaska received a second request for information from the DOJ in February 2024. Management continues to expect completion within 12 to 18 months from announcement [8-K 2024-02-07; 8-K 2024-03-27].

13. **Risks related to fuel price volatility, foreign currency fluctuations, and competitive pressures remain material.** The company notes ongoing exposure to jet fuel price changes despite hedging programs. The weakening Japanese Yen is expected to continue depressing international demand. Competition from large network carriers with broader geographic diversification and alliance partnerships could negatively impact Hawaiian’s market share, especially on North America and Neighbor Island routes [10-K 2024-02-15; 10-Q 2024-04-24].

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines reported a 6.4% increase in passenger revenue in 2024Q1 driven by higher traffic and load factors, but operating losses widened due to rising non-fuel costs and elevated maintenance expenses. Fuel costs declined on a per-gallon basis, partially offsetting cost pressures. Capacity growth was constrained by Pratt & Whitney engine shortages, limiting domestic expansion. The airline progressed with fleet modernization, introducing its first Boeing 787-9 and expanding its Amazon-related freighter operation. Labor costs rose following a new pilot contract. Hawaiian’s network expanded with new routes and enhanced inflight connectivity. The pending merger with Alaska Air Group remains under regulatory review. Risks from fuel price volatility, currency fluctuations, and competition persist.

Management’s guidance for 2024Q2 anticipates capacity growth of 3.5% to 6.5%, a modest range for operating revenue per ASM (-1.5% to +1.5%), and an increase in operating costs per ASM of 8.4% to 10.7%, reflecting ongoing cost pressures. The full-year 2024 outlook includes expected impacts from the emerging freighter operation and continued operational challenges related to engine shortages [8-K 2024-04-23; 10-Q 2024-04-24].

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ second quarter of 2024 showed modest revenue growth driven by increased capacity and improving demand, particularly on domestic and Neighbor Island routes, alongside new route launches and fleet upgrades including Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners and freighters. However, rising operating costs—especially labor, fuel, and maintenance—and operational constraints from engine shortages widened operating losses despite higher revenues. The airline’s liquidity position strengthened through significant debt refinancing and new borrowings, supporting ongoing fleet investments amid delivery delays. Competitive pressures persist in Neighbor Island and international markets, with international demand affected by currency headwinds. Meanwhile, the pending merger with Alaska Airlines continues to generate corporate costs and awaits regulatory approval.

2024.Q3:
### Financial Insights

1. **Operating loss widened sharply in 2024Q2 despite revenue growth**  
   Hawaiian Airlines reported an operating loss of \$55.4 million for Q2 2024, compared to a loss of \$9.6 million in Q2 2023. This deterioration occurred despite a 3.5% increase in operating revenue to \$731.9 million, driven by a \$70.8 million rise in operating expenses, mainly wages and benefits, aircraft fuel, and maintenance costs. GAAP net loss for the quarter was \$67.6 million, or \$1.30 per diluted share, compared to a \$12.3 million loss (\$0.24 per share) in the prior year quarter [8-K 2024-07-30; 10-Q 2024-07-31].

2. **Passenger revenue increased modestly on growing capacity but yield pressure persisted**  
   Passenger revenue rose 3.3% year-over-year to \$666.0 million in Q2 2024, supported by a 4.1% increase in available seat miles (ASM) and a 3.8% increase in revenue passenger miles (RPM). However, passenger yield (revenue per RPM) declined slightly by 0.5%, and passenger revenue per ASM (PRASM) fell 0.8%. Domestic passenger revenue grew 3.8% on a 3.5% ASM increase, while international revenue edged up 0.8% despite a 6.8% capacity increase; international yields remained pressured, partly due to foreign currency headwinds such as a weakening Japanese Yen [10-Q 2024-07-31; 8-K 2024-07-30].

3. **Operating costs rose faster than capacity, driven by labor, fuel, and maintenance**  
   Operating cost per ASM (CASM) increased 5.3% to 15.05 cents in Q2 2024. CASM excluding fuel and non-recurring items rose 3.8% to 11.50 cents, indicating broad cost pressures beyond fuel. Fuel expense rose 7.7% to \$179.2 million due to 3.1% higher consumption and a 4.4% increase in average price per gallon (\$2.62). Maintenance, materials, and repairs expense surged 30.3% (\$16.2 million) year-over-year, driven by increased Power-By-The-Hour (PBH) costs and timing of heavy maintenance events. Wages and benefits increased by \$27.3 million, reflecting ongoing labor cost inflation [10-Q 2024-07-31; 8-K 2024-07-30].

4. **Cash and liquidity strengthened through debt refinancing and financing activities**  
   As of June 30, 2024, Hawaiian held \$1.3 billion in unrestricted cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments, up from \$908.5 million at year-end 2023. Liquidity totaled \$1.5 billion including a \$235 million undrawn revolving credit facility. The company completed a private exchange offer for its outstanding 5.75% senior secured notes due 2026, replacing \$1.19 billion of those notes with \$984.8 million of new 11.0% senior secured notes due 2029 and \$204.7 million in cash. This refinancing extended debt maturities but increased interest costs [8-K 2024-07-30; 8-K 2024-07-26; 10-Q 2024-07-31].

5. **Merger-related expenses impacted Q2 financials**  
   Hawaiian recorded \$6.5 million in special items during Q2 2024 related to merger costs with Alaska Air Group, including legal and advisory fees. No such costs were incurred in Q2 2023. The merger closed on September 18, 2024, with Hawaiian becoming a wholly owned subsidiary of Alaska Air Group [8-K 2024-07-30; 8-K 2024-09-18].

### Operations Insights

6. **Capacity expansion with new aircraft and route additions amid operational challenges**  
   Hawaiian increased capacity by 4.1% in Q2 2024, with RPM growing 3.8%. The airline took delivery of its second Boeing 787-9 in April 2024 and placed it into service in May, but experienced delivery delays of 3 to 7 months on aircraft three through seven. Hawaiian also purchased all remaining leased Boeing 717-200 aircraft during Q1 and Q2 2024. The ATR 72-200 turboprop fleet was fully divested by October 2023 [10-Q 2024-07-31; 8-K 2024-07-30].

7. **Traffic growth uneven across markets, with Neighbor Island and International routes lagging**  
   Neighbor Island routes generated 19.4% of domestic passenger revenue in Q2 2024 and grew 11.3% year-over-year, but remain down 20.8% compared to 2019 levels due to competitive pressures and capacity increases by competitors. International routes contributed 18.5% of passenger revenue in Q2 2024, with capacity up 6.2% but revenue still down roughly 20% versus pre-pandemic 2019, affected by currency headwinds and lagging recovery in international travel [10-Q 2024-07-31].

8. **Fuel consumption rose modestly due to increased operations and aircraft up-gauging**  
   Jet fuel gallons consumed increased 3.1% in Q2 2024 compared to Q2 2023, driven by higher operations and up-gauging (using larger aircraft) to offset engine availability issues on A321neo aircraft. Average fuel price per gallon rose 4.4%, contributing to a 7.7% increase in fuel expense [10-Q 2024-07-31].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

9. **Expanded network with new North America routes and freighter operations**  
   Hawaiian launched three new North America routes in Q2 2024, including daily nonstop service between Salt Lake City and Honolulu and Sacramento to Kona and Lihu’e. The airline also added its third A330-300 freighter to the fleet, commencing operations in June 2024 under its cargo agreement with Amazon. The freighter business contributed to a 6.4% increase in other operating revenue, driven mainly by cargo volume growth [8-K 2024-07-30].

10. **In-flight connectivity and guest experience investments ongoing**  
    Hawaiian deployed Starlink high-speed WiFi on its entire A321neo narrow body fleet and initiated installation on its A330 fleet, aiming for full rollout in the coming months. The airline received recognition for premium class amenities and cabin concepts, reflecting ongoing investment in product enhancements [8-K 2024-07-30].

### Labor Insights

11. **Wages and benefits expenses increased significantly due to inflation and labor agreements**  
    Wages and benefits rose \$27.3 million in Q2 2024 versus Q2 2023, reflecting cost inflation and prior ratification of a four-year collective bargaining agreement (CBA) with pilots in February 2023 that included signing bonuses and pay scale increases. The company did not incur CBA-related expenses in Q2 2024 but did in 2023, impacting comparability [10-Q 2024-07-31].

### Route Network Insights

12. **Merger with Alaska Air Group completed, expanding network and hubs**  
    On September 18, 2024, Hawaiian Airlines merged with Alaska Air Group, becoming a wholly owned subsidiary. The combined entity maintains distinct brands but expands network reach to 141 destinations, including 29 international markets, and positions Honolulu as Alaska’s second largest hub. Integration steps include loyalty program coordination, reciprocal elite status, and cross-selling tickets on each airline’s website [8-K 2024-09-18].

---

### Wrap Up

Hawaiian Airlines’ 2024Q2 financials reflect growing revenues buoyed by capacity expansion and modest passenger traffic gains, but operating losses widened sharply due to rising labor, fuel, and maintenance costs. Passenger yield pressure, particularly on international routes, and competitive dynamics on domestic and Neighbor Island routes constrained unit revenue growth. The company strengthened liquidity and extended debt maturities through a significant note exchange offer. Operationally, Hawaiian expanded its fleet with new Boeing 787-9 deliveries and grew its freighter operations, while facing aircraft delivery delays and engine availability issues that limited capacity growth. The completed merger with Alaska Air Group on September 18, 2024, marks a major network and corporate milestone, with integration efforts underway to unify loyalty programs and expand route offerings.

**Guidance for Q3 and Full Year 2024** includes expected ASM growth of 5.5% to 8.5% in Q3, with operating revenue per ASM (RASM) projected to decline 1.5% to 4.5%, and CASM expected to decrease 0.8% to 3.0%. Fuel consumption is forecasted to increase 3.0% to 6.0% in Q3 with an average fuel price around \$2.71 per gallon. Full year capital expenditures were revised downward to \$350 million to \$400 million from prior guidance of \$500 million to \$550 million, reflecting updated fleet delivery schedules and investment pacing [8-K 2024-07-30].

   Operating cost per ASM rose 5.9% to 15.72¢ in Q1 2024 and 5.3% to 15.05¢ in Q2 2024 compared to 2023, with CASM excluding fuel and non-recurring items increasing 7.1% and 7.0%, respectively [8-K 2024-07-30, 10-Q 2024-07-31]. ### Wrap Up

In 2024, Hawaiian Airlines experienced modest revenue growth driven by increased capacity and improving demand, particularly in domestic markets, but continued to report operating losses and net losses, reflecting rising operating costs and ongoing challenges such as Pratt & Whitney engine shortages. Fuel costs benefited from lower prices, but non-fuel expenses, especially wages and maintenance, rose significantly. The company advanced fleet modernization with the introduction of Boeing 787-9 aircraft and expanded its freighter operations under a long-term Amazon contract. Liquidity strengthened through a major debt exchange and new financing, while total debt increased.

Strategically, Hawaiian enhanced its guest experience with Starlink WiFi and premium airport services, and its loyalty program maintained strong engagement and revenue contribution. Labor costs rose due to contract commitments and workforce growth. The pending merger with Alaska Air Group progressed with key regulatory approvals in 2024 and is expected to close by late 2024, setting the stage for eventual integration while maintaining distinct brands in the near term. The company continues to face risks from market concentration in Hawai‘i, operational constraints, and integration uncertainties as it navigates this transitional year.

### Financial Insights

   Passenger revenues rose 13.8% to \$1.37 billion and non-ticket revenues increased 14.3% to \$1.28 billion. Total operating revenues increased \$325.7 million year-over-year. Despite this, operating income declined from \$443.7 million in 2016 to \$388.8 million in 2017, with operating margin falling from 19.1% to 14.7%. The margin compression was partly due to a 20.3% increase in operating expenses, notably a 37.5% rise in aircraft fuel expense to \$615.6 million driven by a 20.9% increase in fuel cost per gallon and 13.5% more fuel gallons consumed. A \$199.3 million tax benefit from the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act boosted net income to \$420.6 million from \$264.9 million in 2016. [10-K filed 2018-02-13]

2. **Operating costs per available seat mile (CASM) rose 3.5% to 7.63 cents, with adjusted CASM ex-fuel increasing 1.1% to 5.51 cents, reflecting higher depreciation and other operating expenses despite lower aircraft rent per ASM.**  
   The increase in CASM was driven by higher depreciation and amortization expense (up 17.5% per ASM), increased other operating expenses (+12.4% per ASM), and a small rise in landing fees. Aircraft rent per ASM declined 11.4%, reflecting ongoing fleet purchases replacing leases. Salaries, wages and benefits per ASM decreased 3.8%. Special charges, mainly \$12.6 million in lease termination costs related to aircraft and engine purchases, also impacted costs. [10-K filed 2018-02-13]

3. **Non-ticket revenues per passenger flight segment increased 2.2% to \$53.00, continuing the airline's focus on ancillary revenue through baggage fees, seat selection, and loyalty programs.**  
   Spirit’s ultra-low-cost carrier (ULCC) model relies heavily on unbundled fares with optional paid services branded as Frill Control™. Non-ticket revenues include baggage fees, advance seat assignments, itinerary changes, and revenues from the FREE SPIRIT affinity credit card program and the \$9 Fare Club subscription. This ancillary revenue stream supports low base fares and accounted for nearly half of total revenues in 2017. [10-K filed 2018-02-13]

4. **Spirit’s cash and short-term investments increased by approximately \$100 million to \$901.8 million at year-end 2017, supported by cash from operations despite higher capital expenditures and working capital needs.**  
   Net cash provided by operating activities was supported by net income of \$420.6 million, adjusted for non-cash charges including \$140.2 million depreciation/amortization. Capital expenditures were substantial, with \$354 million committed to aircraft purchases and \$128 million on other capital items. Pre-delivery deposits and payments for heavy maintenance events added to working capital requirements. The airline maintained a strong liquidity position with \$800.8 million in cash and cash equivalents and \$100.9 million in short-term investments. [10-K filed 2018-02-13, 8-K filed 2018-03-01]

5. **Interest expense increased \$15.6 million to \$57.3 million due to higher debt financing for purchased aircraft, partially offset by increased capitalized interest and interest income.**  
   At year-end 2017, Spirit had 46 purchased aircraft financed through secured long-term debt, up from 29 in 2016. Capitalized interest rose to \$13.8 million, and interest income increased to \$8.7 million, tempering the net impact on earnings. [10-K filed 2018-02-13]

### Operations Insights

6. **Spirit expanded capacity by 16.1% in 2017, growing its fleet from 95 to 112 Airbus aircraft and launching 36 new markets including two new destinations, while maintaining a high utilization rate.**  
   Available seat miles (ASMs) increased to 29.6 billion from 25.5 billion in 2016. Passenger flight segments grew 11.9% to 6.1 million. 7. **Operational disruptions from pilot work action and hurricanes in mid-2017 negatively impacted results by approximately \$80 million, including \$65 million in lost revenue and \$15 million in additional costs.**

8. **Spirit’s fleet remains exclusively Airbus A320-family with 83 A320ceo, 14 A321ceo, and 15 A319 aircraft at year-end 2017, representing the youngest fleet among major U.S. airlines.**  
   The airline maintains a high-density seating configuration under its Plane Simple™ strategy, emphasizing cost efficiency through high seat density and simplified onboard products. ### Commercial Strategy Insights

9. **Spirit focuses on price-sensitive leisure travelers through its ULCC model offering low base fares with unbundled optional services, enabling growth in passenger volume and ancillary revenues.**  
   The Bare Fares™ approach removes traditional ticket inclusions, with Frill Control™ allowing customers to pay only for selected options. This strategy supports a diversified network serving small/mid-size U.S. markets, large leisure destinations, and international routes in the Caribbean and Latin America. Non-ticket revenue growth and stable yields reflect the model’s resilience despite competitive pressures. [10-K filed 2018-02-13]

10. **Distribution is predominantly direct, with 66.2% of tickets sold via Spirit’s website in 2017, reducing sales and marketing costs and supporting the low-cost structure.**  
    Third-party travel agents accounted for 28.4%, down from 31.7% in 2016, and call center sales were 5.4%. The company also generates ancillary revenues from third-party travel insurance and onboard advertising. [10-K filed 2018-02-13]

### Route Network Insights

11. **Spirit’s network grew in 2017 with 60 destinations and 450 daily flights, adding 36 new markets and expanding into underserved leisure and international destinations, including Hartford and Pittsburgh.**  
    The airline targets a mix of large urban centers, small/mid-size cities, and international leisure markets with a demographic affinity between Fort Lauderdale and Caribbean/Latin America. [10-K filed 2018-02-13, 8-K filed 2018-03-06]

12. **Spirit plans to grow capacity approximately 23% in 2018 and target low to mid-teens percentage growth annually through 2021, with a fleet expected to reach 161 aircraft by year-end 2021.**

### Labor Insights

13. **In 2017, Spirit amended its pilot contract, providing increased flexibility and productivity tools projected to help keep adjusted CASM ex-fuel flat or down 1% in 2018 despite cost pressures.**

### Wrap Up

Spirit Airlines in 2017 expanded its network and fleet, growing revenues and passenger traffic significantly while maintaining a stable average yield. Operating margins contracted due to rising fuel costs and increased expenses related to fleet growth, depreciation, and operational disruptions including labor actions and hurricanes. The airline continued to emphasize its ULCC business model, generating nearly half of revenues from ancillary services and leveraging direct distribution channels to control costs. Liquidity remained strong with cash and investments growing despite substantial capital expenditures to support fleet expansion.

Looking ahead, Spirit targets robust capacity growth of about 23% in 2018 and low to mid-teens growth annually through 2021, supported by a young, growing Airbus fleet and a new pilot contract designed to contain unit costs. Management’s guidance for 2018 anticipates flat to slightly declining adjusted CASM ex-fuel, a modest decrease in total revenue per ASM, and capital expenditures of approximately \$649 million, reflecting continued investment in aircraft and related assets. No material litigation, accidents, or regulatory actions were disclosed that would affect the airline’s operational or financial outlook.

   These disruptions affected performance primarily from May to September 2017, reducing adjusted operating margin by approximately 1.4 points. Excluding these impacts, adjusted operating margin for 2017 would have been 17.8%, still below 2016’s 19.1% [10-K 2018-02-13 p. 52; 8-K 2018-03-06].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

8. **Spirit’s ULCC model continued to generate robust non-ticket revenue, which grew 14.3% to \$1.282 billion in 2017, representing 48% of total operating revenue.**  
   Non-ticket revenue per passenger flight segment rose 2.2% to \$53.00, driven by higher fees for baggage, seat selection, and passenger usage. The company’s unbundled “Bare Fares” and “Frill Control” options allow customers to pay only for selected services, stabilizing revenue despite competitive fare pressures. Total revenue per passenger segment increased 1.9% to \$109.49 despite a 1.8% decline in total revenue per ASM (TRASM) to 8.95 cents, reflecting a 1.6-point load factor decline [10-K 2018-02-13 pp. 45-46, 48].

### Labor Insights

10. **Labor disruptions in 2017, including a pilot work action in May, contributed to operational challenges and increased costs.**  
    The company disclosed that labor-related disruptions and hurricanes combined negatively affected results by approximately \$80 million, including higher passenger re-accommodation expenses. However, salary, wages, and benefits expense per ASM decreased 3.8% year over year, reflecting cost control despite workforce growth [10-K 2018-02-13 pp. 52, 47].

### Route Network Insights

11. **Spirit expanded its route network in 2017, launching service to 36 new markets and adding two new destinations, Hartford and Pittsburgh.**  
    The network covered 237 markets served by 60 airports across the U.S., Caribbean, and Latin America. The company focused on underserved or overpriced markets, balancing growth between large domestic markets, niche markets, and international opportunities. The average stage length increased to 999 miles, consistent with growth in mid-to-long haul domestic markets [10-K 2018-02-13 pp. 5-6, 48; 8-K 2018-03-06].

The company planned to grow the fleet to 122 aircraft by year-end 2018 and 137 by 2019, with deliveries focused on A320 family aircraft. The 2019 planned deliveries were expected to yield less than 10% capacity growth, with potential to increase to 13-15% [10-K 2018-02-13 pp. 5, 48; 8-K 2018-03-06].

### Wrap Up

Spirit Airlines’ 2017 fourth quarter and full-year results reflected continued growth in traffic and revenues, supported by capacity expansion and the company’s ULCC unbundled fare model. Despite a 14.0% increase in operating revenues and a sharp rise in net income boosted by a \$199.3 million tax benefit, operating margins compressed due to significantly higher fuel costs and increased operational expenses, including those from labor disruptions and hurricane impacts. Unit costs outside fuel rose modestly, reflecting some cost discipline, but aircraft fuel expense, representing over a quarter of operating costs, increased sharply with higher prices and consumption. The fleet grew substantially, maintaining Spirit’s youngest all-Airbus fleet, supporting network expansion into new and underserved markets.

Looking forward, Spirit guided for 2018 capacity growth of approximately 23%, with flat to slightly declining adjusted CASM ex-fuel, reflecting new pilot contracts and productivity gains. Capital expenditures were planned at \$649 million, emphasizing continued fleet investment. The company anticipated an effective tax rate near 24%, with no fuel hedging activity planned, exposing results to fuel price volatility. Operational improvements and network diversification remain priorities amid competitive and cost pressures.

No material litigation, fatalities, or regulatory actions were disclosed for 2017 Q4. The company’s liquidity position strengthened, with cash and investments exceeding \$900 million at year-end, supporting ongoing growth and capital commitments.
