### Wrap Up

Allegiant Air’s 2023Q3 filings reveal continued financial recovery and profitability driven by increased passenger revenue and ancillary sales, despite constrained capacity growth and operational challenges. 4. **Liquidity declined in Q4 with cash and investments down 14.5% year-over-year, debt increased**  
As of December 31, 2023, unrestricted cash and investments totaled \$870.7 million, down 14.5% from \$1.02 billion at year-end 2022. Meanwhile, total debt rose 7.8% to \$2.26 billion, with current maturities increasing sharply to \$439.9 million from \$152.9 million. Net debt (debt less unrestricted cash and investments) increased 28.8% to \$1.39 billion. The decline in liquidity and rise in net debt reflect capital spending and financing activity, including new debt facilities drawn to fund aircraft deliveries and pre-delivery payments. [8-K 2024-02-05; 8-K 2023-11-02; 10-K 2024-02-29]

5. **Capital expenditures increased with Sunseeker Resort opening and fleet investments**  
Q4 2023 capital expenditures, excluding capitalized interest, were \$52.7 million, including investments in the Sunseeker Resort (opened December 15, 2023), Aileron Golf Club, and aircraft-related costs. Full-year 2023 airline capital expenditures were \$430 to \$440 million, down from prior guidance, while total projected capital expenditures including Sunseeker were \$720 million. The company also incurred project debt of \$350 million for Sunseeker through September 30, 2023. The resort is expected to be EBITDA positive in 2024 but currently represents a drag on consolidated earnings. [8-K 2024-02-05; 8-K 2023-11-02; 10-K 2024-02-29]

6. **Co-brand credit card and loyalty programs contributed materially to revenue**  
Allegiant’s co-brand credit card membership grew to nearly 500,000 members by year-end 2023, generating \$119.6 million in remuneration, up 18% from 2022. The Allways Rewards loyalty program added 2.1 million members in 2023, reaching over 17 million total members, a 13% increase. These programs drive ancillary revenue streams that contribute to passenger revenue and third-party product revenue growth, diversifying Allegiant’s revenue base beyond base airfares. [8-K 2024-02-05; 10-K 2024-02-29]

### Operations Insights

7. **Stable capacity with slight decreases in scheduled service ASMs and flat passenger revenue in Q4**  
System available seat miles (ASMs) grew modestly by about 1.5% for scheduled service in 2023, with Q4 showing flat total operating revenue and slight capacity reductions during off-peak periods. The company emphasized its low-utilization, out-and-back flight model focusing on leisure travelers from underserved cities. Load factors and total revenue per available seat mile (TRASM) improved earlier in the year but Q4 revenues were flat compared to prior year. [8-K 2024-02-05; 8-K 2023-11-02]

8. **Fleet transition underway with Boeing 737 MAX deliveries starting early 2024 and Airbus retirements planned**  
Allegiant finalized amendments to its Boeing 737 MAX purchase agreement, shifting the mix toward more 737 MAX 8200 aircraft and fewer 737 MAX 7s, with deliveries beginning late 2023 and continuing through 2025. The company plans to retire 21 Airbus A320ceo aircraft by 2025, accelerating depreciation accordingly. The first 737 MAX delivery is expected to provide fleet flexibility and efficiency improvements. As of December 31, 2023, Allegiant operated 126 Airbus A320 series aircraft. [8-K 2024-02-05; 8-K 2023-10-03; 10-K 2024-02-29]

### Commercial Strategy Insights

9. **Revenue mix increasingly includes ancillary and fixed fee contract revenues**  
Passenger revenue grew 12.4% year-to-date September 30, 2023, driven by a 2.7% increase in scheduled service passengers and an 8.7% rise in average scheduled service base fare. Ancillary air-related fares increased 10.3%, supported by the rollout of the Allegiant Extra product. Third-party product revenues (including co-brand credit card marketing fees) increased 11.0%, while fixed fee contract revenue increased 12.5% due to a 19.8% increase in fixed fee departures. These diversified revenue streams complement the airline’s base fares and contribute to overall revenue stability. [10-Q 2023-11-08; 10-K 2024-02-29]

10. **Direct distribution model and brand investments support low-cost leisure focus**  
Allegiant continues to emphasize direct-to-customer distribution via allegiant.com, avoiding Global Distribution System fees and enabling bundled sales of air ancillary and third-party products. Investments in technology platforms (SAP and Navitaire launched in Q3 2023) enhance booking and revenue management capabilities. The company’s brand efforts include expanding the Allegiant credit card and loyalty programs, which are recognized in customer awards. This supports Allegiant’s strategy as a profitable leisure-focused carrier (PLFC). [8-K 2023-11-02; 8-K 2024-02-05]

### Labor Insights

11. **Workforce expansion to support new business lines and operations**  
Allegiant added over 1,300 full-time equivalent employees in 2023, including approximately 1,000 new hires for the Sunseeker Resort operation. This labor growth supports the company’s integrated travel company strategy and new resort operations, alongside its airline business. [10-K 2024-02-29]

### Route Network Insights

12. **Extensive and growing route network serving underserved markets**  
As of February 1, 2024, Allegiant operated 126 Airbus A320 series aircraft on 555 routes to 124 cities, including 428 unique nonstop routes without current competition. The network spans 90 origin cities and 33 leisure destinations across 42 states, with 24 operational bases providing flexibility to shift capacity according to demand. The company announced 12 new routes for 2024. The model targets leisure travelers in underserved cities, offering low-frequency, nonstop service connecting small and medium markets to vacation destinations. [10-K 2024-02-29]

### Wrap Up

Allegiant Air’s Q4 2023 financial results reflected a sharp decline in operating income driven by higher operating expenses and special charges related to accelerated fleet depreciation and property damage at its newly opened Sunseeker Resort. While revenues were flat year-over-year in the quarter, the company’s full-year 2023 results showed improved airline profitability excluding these charges, supported by disciplined capacity management, diversified ancillary revenue streams, and steady passenger growth. Liquidity declined and net debt increased due to capital spending, including investments in the Sunseeker Resort and fleet renewal with Boeing 737 MAX aircraft planned to enter service in 2024. The operational model remains focused on leisure travelers from underserved markets, supported by a large and growing route network and direct distribution strategy.

**Guidance for 2024** includes system ASM growth of 2.0% to 6.0%, scheduled service ASM growth in the same range, fuel cost per gallon guidance around \$2.85 to \$2.90, and an airline operating margin target of 8.0% to 10.0% in Q1 2024. Earnings per share guidance for airline-only operations is \$1.00 to \$2.00 in Q1 2024, reflecting expectations of operational improvement and margin recovery. No material regulatory, operational disruptions, or labor disputes were disclosed for the period.

### Commercial Strategy Insights

The company expects the resort to be EBITDA positive in 2024 but acknowledged it will take time to ramp to financial maturity [8-K filed 2024-02-05]. 12. **Staffing challenges persisted in 2023, prompting capacity pullbacks and incremental investments in hiring and retention, which pressured unit costs and irregular operations expenses.**

### Wrap Up

In 2023, Allegiant Air demonstrated a financial recovery with sharply improved earnings and margins driven by higher fares, ancillary revenue growth, and operational improvements, despite a challenging fourth quarter marked by rising costs. The company maintained a cautious approach to capacity growth due to labor and operational constraints, while investing heavily in fleet modernization with the upcoming introduction of Boeing 737 MAX aircraft and capital projects including the new Sunseeker Resort. Elevated fuel costs and staffing challenges pressured unit costs and irregular operations expenses, partially offset by strong demand and brand-driven ancillary revenue streams such as the co-branded credit card and Allegiant Extra product.

Looking ahead, Allegiant’s strategy emphasizes operational reliability, network focus on underserved markets, and diversification into leisure hospitality. The company guided full-year 2024 airline-only earnings per share excluding specials in the range of \$7.75 to \$8.50, with system ASM growth of about 1.8% and fuel costs expected around \$3.12 per gallon [8-K filed 2024-02-05]. No material regulatory or legal risks were disclosed beyond routine operational challenges.

### Wrap Up

Allegiant Air’s Q4 2024 and full-year results reflect a company navigating a sharp earnings loss at the consolidated level due to a substantial impairment charge on its Sunseeker Resort asset, while the airline segment itself showed improved profitability and operational efficiency. However, rising labor costs and a modest decline in passenger volumes pressured full-year margins and unit economics. Cash and liquidity remain solid, supporting planned capital expenditures and debt repayments.

Allegiant Air's 2025 financial and operational results reflect a year of strategic fleet renewal, disciplined cost management, and selective capacity growth focused on leisure travel markets. ### Wrap Up

Sun Country Airlines demonstrated a strong operational and financial rebound in Q2 2021 as leisure travel demand recovered from pandemic lows. Capacity and utilization expanded markedly, with load factors nearing pre-pandemic levels.    Adjusted operating income for Q4 was \$15 million (9% margin), versus a GAAP operating income of \$11 million (6% margin), showing positive earnings conversion after adjustments for stock comp, special items, and other non-cash or one-time costs [8-K 2022-02-07].

The company increased owned aircraft from 14 to 21 in 2021, acquired additional aircraft under finance leases, and reduced operating leases by returning six aircraft. Total passenger fleet grew from 31 to 36 aircraft by year-end [10-K 2022-02-18; 8-K 2022-02-07].  
   The company expects to add eight or more passenger aircraft in 2022 with LOIs signed for five 737-800s and two more deliveries planned, aiming for approximately 50 passenger aircraft by year-end 2023 [8-K 2022-02-07; 8-K 2022-03-08].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

8. **Sun Country’s revenue mix reflects a hybrid model with approximately 64% from leisure scheduled passenger service, 20% from charter, and 15% from cargo, leveraging diversified revenue streams to stabilize performance.**  
   Scheduled service revenue grew strongly in 2021, with ancillary revenues per passenger reaching record levels (\$44.05 in Q4), driven by baggage fees, seat selection, and onboard sales [8-K 2022-02-07; 10-K 2022-02-18].  
   Charter revenues increased sequentially, supported by new contracts including a five-year agreement with Caesars Entertainment and Major League Soccer charters expected to ramp up in early 2022 [8-K 2022-02-07; 8-K 2021-11-01].  
   The company also expanded its network with 7 new nonstop destinations from Minneapolis-Saint Paul (MSP) in 2021, broadening to over 70 airports, a 40% increase from 2019 [8-K 2021-11-01].

### Route Network Insights

9. **Sun Country’s network focuses on seasonal leisure markets with 97% of markets being seasonal, concentrated largely at its MSP hub, where it is the second-largest carrier with 58% passenger share.**  
   The airline continues to grow nonstop markets by over 40% versus 2019, with significant opportunity in unserved markets from MSP. It also focuses on non-MSP markets with high seasonal peaks, such as Dallas-Fort Worth to Cancun and Los Angeles to Honolulu [8-K 2022-03-08].  
   The fleet expansion plan supports this growth with no aircraft order book, acquiring mid-life Boeing 737-800s opportunistically to control capital commitments [8-K 2022-03-08].

### Risks and Other Disclosures

10. **Fuel price volatility remains a material risk; Sun Country had no fuel hedges outstanding as of September 30, 2021, exposing it fully to market price fluctuations.**

Management notes the risk of higher fuel prices impacting results given competitors’ potential advantages with newer, more fuel-efficient aircraft [10-K 2022-02-18; 10-Q 2021-11-01].  
    The company complies with CARES Act restrictions, including prohibitions on share repurchases and dividend payments through September 2022, and restrictions on certain executive compensation through April 2023 [10-Q 2021-11-01].

### Wrap Up

Sun Country Airlines showed a marked recovery in 2021, returning to full-year profitability driven by growth in scheduled passenger, charter, ancillary, and cargo revenues. The fourth quarter reflected operational challenges from the Omicron variant, weather, and technology issues, resulting in a slight GAAP loss but positive adjusted earnings and strong unit revenue performance above pre-pandemic levels. The company maintained cost discipline with adjusted CASM near 2019 levels despite rising fuel prices and increased flying. Balance sheet improvements, including reduced net debt and increased liquidity, underpin an active fleet expansion strategy focused on acquiring mid-life Boeing 737-800 aircraft to support network growth primarily from its MSP hub and seasonal leisure markets.

Looking forward, Sun Country’s 2022 guidance anticipates a 9%-14% revenue increase over Q1 2019, with ASMs up 5%-10%, but adjusted operating margins expected to be lower by 11.5 to 15.5 percentage points versus 2019, reflecting ongoing recovery dynamics and investments including the new pilot labor agreement. The ramp-up of new charter agreements with Caesars Entertainment and Major League Soccer, along with continued fleet additions, are poised to shape the company’s operational and financial trajectory in 2022 and beyond [8-K 2022-02-07].

2022.Q1:
### Financial Insights

1. **Sun Country Airlines achieved a full-year 2021 operating income of \$107 million, a substantial increase from \$17 million in 2020, with adjusted operating income of \$51 million versus a loss of \$40 million in 2020.** The company reported full-year 2021 net income of \$77.5 million compared to a loss of \$3.9 million in 2020. Diluted EPS was \$1.31 in 2021 versus a loss of \$0.08 in 2020 [10-K filed 2022-02-18]. Adjusted net income for 2021 was \$19.8 million, recovering from a \$47.9 million loss in 2020 [8-K filed 2022-02-07]. The adjusted EBITDAR margin improved to 19.8% in 2021 from 9.7% in 2020 [8-K filed 2022-03-08].

2. **Total operating revenue increased 55.2% year-over-year to \$623 million in 2021, driven by recovery across scheduled service, charter, ancillary, and cargo segments.** Scheduled service revenue rose 44.7% to \$279 million, charter service revenue increased 29.8% to \$127 million, ancillary revenue jumped 72.3% to \$117 million, and cargo revenue grew 148.4% to \$91 million [10-K filed 2022-02-18]. Fourth quarter 2021 revenue was \$173 million, 5% higher than Q4 2019, with scheduled service TRASM (total revenue per available seat mile excluding cargo) 5% above Q4 2019 levels [8-K filed 2022-02-07].

3. **Cost recovery was challenged by rising fuel prices and increased operational activity, with aircraft fuel expense up 54.8% in 2021 to \$129 million, reflecting a 39% increase in fuel gallons consumed and a 38% rise in average price per gallon.** Fuel represented approximately 25% of operating expenses in 2021 [10-K filed 2022-02-18]. Adjusted CASM (cost per available seat mile excluding fuel and other costs) improved to 6.44 cents in 2021 from 7.57 cents in 2020 and was slightly higher than the 6.31 cents reported in 2019, despite 18% lower ASMs in 2021 compared to 2019 [8-K filed 2022-02-07].

4. **Liquidity strengthened significantly, with cash and cash equivalents increasing to \$309 million at year-end 2021 from \$62 million at year-end 2020.** Total liquidity (cash plus undrawn revolver) was \$334 million at December 31, 2021, up \$34 million from Q3 2021 [8-K filed 2022-02-07]. Net debt declined to \$236 million at year-end 2021 from \$475 million at the end of 2020, reflecting debt repayments and improved cash flow [8-K filed 2022-02-07].

5. **Sun Country completed a \$188 million financing secured by 13 Boeing 737-800 aircraft in Q1 2022, with proceeds used to refinance five owned aircraft and finance acquisition of others, supporting fleet growth.** The company received \$172.5 million on March 31, 2022, with an additional \$15.8 million expected by mid-September 2022 [8-K filed 2022-04-05].

6. **The company ratified a new four-year pilot labor agreement effective January 2022, offering competitive pay and work rules intended to support growth plans.** This new agreement is expected to enable pilot attraction and retention necessary for expansion [8-K filed 2022-02-07].

### Operations Insights

7. **Sun Country’s total ASMs increased by approximately 40% in 2021 to 4.8 billion from 3.5 billion in 2020, with RPMs up 61%, resulting in a load factor improvement to 74.7% from 64.9%.** Scheduled service block hours increased 40.4% year-over-year, reflecting higher operational activity [10-K filed 2022-02-18]. In Q4 2021, the load factor was 76.6%, up 16.2 points versus Q4 2020 [8-K filed 2022-02-07].

8. **Fleet size expanded to 48 Boeing 737 Next Generation aircraft at year-end 2021, including 36 passenger aircraft and 12 freighters for cargo operations.** The passenger fleet grew by five aircraft during 2021, with additional deliveries planned for 2022, targeting a total of eight or more new passenger aircraft additions this year [8-K filed 2022-02-07; 10-K filed 2022-02-18]. The company owns the majority of its aircraft, having purchased six formerly leased aircraft in 2021 to reduce lease expense [10-K filed 2022-02-18].

9. **Cargo operations under the Amazon Air Transportation Services Agreement (ATSA) contributed \$91 million in revenue in 2021, up 148% from 2020, with 12 freighter aircraft deployed.** Cargo fuel usage and expenses are largely reimbursed by Amazon under a pass-through cost arrangement, enhancing margin stability in this segment [8-K filed 2022-03-08; 10-K filed 2022-02-18].

10. **Charter flying increased, with charter block hours growing 150% since 2019, and charter revenue in Q4 2021 was \$39 million, 15% higher than Q3 2021 but down 21% from Q4 2019 due to military flying weakness.** New charter agreements with Major League Soccer and Caesars Entertainment are expected to ramp up in early 2022 [8-K filed 2022-02-07; 8-K filed 2022-03-08].

### Labor Insights

11. **The ratified four-year pilot agreement effective January 2022 provides competitive pay and work rules, supporting pilot recruitment and retention aligned with growth ambitions.** The new contract is cited as a key enabler of growth plans [8-K filed 2022-02-07].

12. **Employee count increased 28% year-over-year to 2,181 at the end of 2021, reflecting operational recovery and expansion.** The company had previously implemented voluntary leave programs during the pandemic, some costs of which were offset by CARES Act payroll support [8-K filed 2022-02-07].

### Route Network Insights

13. **Sun Country continued expanding its route network, adding 34 new markets in 2021 and focusing on leisure travel with seasonal capacity deployment aligned to peak demand periods.** The airline is the second largest carrier at Minneapolis-St. Paul (MSP) with a 58% passenger share, growing share by 3% in 2021 [8-K filed 2022-03-08; 10-K filed 2022-02-18].

14. **The network strategy integrates scheduled service, charter, and cargo operations to maximize aircraft utilization and profitability, with approximately 97% of markets being seasonal reflecting leisure demand patterns.** The company dynamically shifts capacity to high-demand days and months, optimizing yields [8-K filed 2022-03-08].

### Wrap Up

Sun Country Airlines demonstrated strong financial recovery in 2021, with net income of \$77.5 million and adjusted EBITDAR margin near 20%, supported by a 55% revenue increase driven by growth across scheduled service, charter, ancillary, and cargo segments. The company managed cost pressures from rising fuel prices while improving adjusted CASM versus pandemic levels, supported by fleet ownership and operational efficiencies. Liquidity and net debt improved substantially, positioning the airline for growth.

Operationally, Sun Country expanded its fleet and network, leveraging a flexible model combining scheduled leisure service, charter flying, and contract cargo operations with Amazon. The ratified pilot labor agreement and fleet financing completed in Q1 2022 underpin growth plans. The network remains heavily seasonal and leisure-focused, with continued market additions and share gains at its Minneapolis hub. Risks disclosed include fuel price volatility, pandemic-related demand uncertainty, and labor market dynamics.

Guidance for Q1 2022 projects total revenue of \$215–\$225 million (9–14% above Q1 2019), total system ASMs of 1.9–2.0 billion (5–10% above Q1 2019), an adjusted operating margin of 8–12%, and economic fuel cost per gallon of \$2.79 (24% above Q1 2019) [8-K filed 2022-02-07]. No material operational disruptions or litigation developments were disclosed for the period ending March 31, 2022.
2022.Q2:
### Financial Insights

1. **Sun Country generated a record quarterly revenue of \$227 million in Q1 2022 but saw net income decline 71% year-over-year to \$3.6 million.**  
   Total operating revenue rose 78% to \$226.5 million from \$127.6 million in Q1 2021, driven by a 127% increase in scheduled service revenue to \$124.1 million and a 90% rise in ancillary revenue to \$45.1 million. Despite this growth, net income dropped from \$12.4 million to \$3.6 million due to higher operating expenses and non-operating costs [8-K 2022-05-05; 10-Q 2022-05-06].

2. **Operating income declined 12% to \$21.8 million while adjusted operating income rose to \$22.8 million, reflecting a 10.0% adjusted operating margin.**  
   GAAP operating income fell from \$24.9 million to \$21.8 million, with an operating margin of 9.6%. Adjusted operating income, which excludes special items and stock compensation, improved from \$1.2 million to \$22.8 million, indicating better underlying profitability [8-K 2022-05-05; 8-K 2022-06-22; 10-Q 2022-05-06].

3. **Fuel costs surged 166% to \$64.5 million due to a 45% increase in fuel consumption and a 68% rise in price per gallon to \$3.20.**  
   Fuel expense represented 32% of total operating expense in Q1 2022 versus 24% in Q1 2021. The company highlighted that charter and cargo customers, accounting for about one-third of fuel usage, pay fuel costs directly, providing a natural hedge [10-Q 2022-05-06; 8-K 2022-05-05; 8-K 2022-06-22].

4. **Non-fuel operating expenses nearly doubled to \$140.2 million but operating expense per block hour (excluding fuel and special items) decreased 5.9% from 2019 levels.**  
   Despite a 99% increase in total operating expenses to \$204.7 million, Sun Country achieved cost control with adjusted cost per block hour down 5.9% compared to 2019, reflecting efficiency gains amid growth [8-K 2022-05-05; 8-K 2022-06-22].

5. **Sun Country’s net debt increased modestly to \$309 million as of March 31, 2022, supported by a \$188 million Enhanced Equipment Trust Certificate (EETC) financing secured by 13 Boeing 737-800 aircraft.**  
   The EETC proceeds financed aircraft purchases and lease buyouts, with total liquidity at \$297 million at quarter-end. Finance lease obligations rose 32% quarter-over-quarter due to these transactions [8-K 2022-05-05; 10-Q 2022-05-06].

6. **Free cash flow remains a strength, with Sun Country generating industry-leading free cash flow margins despite the high fuel price environment.**  
   The company’s asset-light model and diversified revenue streams contributed to a 2021 free cash flow yield of 9.3% of revenue, outperforming ULCCs and larger carriers [8-K 2022-06-22].

### Operations Insights

7. **Scheduled service capacity expanded 46% year-over-year to 1.68 billion available seat miles (ASMs), with a 73% increase in revenue passenger miles (RPMs) and load factor rising 12.6 percentage points to 79.5%.**  
   Revenue passengers carried grew 67% to 922,652, supported by 44% more departures and 48% more block hours. Scheduled service TRASM (unit revenue per ASM including ancillary and other revenue) increased 48% to 10.25 cents [10-Q 2022-05-06].

8. **Fleet growth continued with 38 passenger aircraft at quarter-end, up two from December 2021, plus 12 freighters supporting cargo operations.**  
   The company completed purchases of four aircraft in April 2022 and anticipates further lease buyouts financed by the EETC. The fleet strategy focuses on Boeing 737-800s, with no current order book, allowing opportunistic mid-life aircraft acquisitions [8-K 2022-05-05; 8-K 2022-06-22; 10-Q 2022-05-06].

9. **Sun Country’s flexible scheduling targets peak leisure demand, with approximately 97% of markets being seasonal and capacity concentrated on high-yield days.**  
   This approach drives higher unit revenues compared to peers by limiting flying during trough periods and capitalizing on leisure and visiting friends and relatives (VFR) traffic patterns [8-K 2022-06-22].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

10. **Ancillary revenue per passenger nearly doubled to \$48.87, driven by improved merchandising, new product offerings, and pricing optimization.**  
    Management expects ancillary revenue to continue growing through enhanced merchandising on suncountry.com, introduction of new products, pricing technology improvements including machine learning, and expansion of third-party product sales. A \$16 passenger interface fee went into effect in April 2022 [10-Q 2022-05-06; 8-K 2022-06-22].

11. **Sun Country continued to grow market share at its Minneapolis-St. Paul (MSP) hub, now the second largest carrier with 58% of passengers, up from 0% in 2017.**  
    The airline added 17 new MSP markets in 2021 and plans further growth, including 25 new routes planned from 2022 to 2025, leveraging its position as a premier leisure carrier at MSP [8-K 2022-06-22].

12. **Charter and cargo business lines, comprising about 33% of block hours and 32% of revenue, provide contracted, recurring revenue with pass-through fuel costs, supporting margin stability.**  
    Cargo services include a contract with Amazon for Crew, Maintenance and Insurance (CMI) flying, with opportunities to diversify into freight companies. The new pilot contract signed in late 2021 contains provisions facilitating cargo growth [8-K 2022-05-05; 8-K 2022-06-22].

### Labor Insights

13. **Employee headcount increased 31% to 2,316 at quarter-end, reflecting growth in operations and the impact of the new pilot contract effective from Q1 2022.**  
    Salaries, wages, and benefits rose 35% to \$59.6 million, partially due to workforce expansion and contract terms [8-K 2022-05-05; 10-Q 2022-05-06].

### Wrap Up

Sun Country Airlines’ Q1 2022 results reveal strong top-line growth driven by a recovery in scheduled passenger service and ancillary revenues, supported by a flexible, leisure-focused network and a diversified business model including cargo and charter operations. The surge in fuel prices materially increased costs, but the company’s fuel pass-through in charter and cargo and disciplined cost control helped maintain a 10% adjusted operating margin. Fleet expansion and financing through an equipment trust certificate underpin capacity growth, while labor costs rose in line with operational scale and new contracts. Ancillary revenue growth and market share gains at its MSP hub reflect ongoing commercial momentum.

The company’s guidance for Q2 2022 anticipates total revenue of \$210–\$220 million, a 24–30% increase over Q2 2019, with adjusted operating income margin between 5% and 9%, reflecting continued strong demand but margin compression compared to Q1. No material operational disruptions, regulatory actions, or litigation risks were disclosed for this period.
2022.Q3:
### Financial Insights

1. **Sun Country’s Q2 2022 revenue rose 47% year-over-year to \$219 million but posted a net loss of \$3.9 million due to sharply higher fuel and labor costs.** Operating revenues increased from \$149 million in Q2 2021 to \$219 million in Q2 2022, driven primarily by a 56% increase in passenger revenue to \$195 million and a 48% rise in charter revenue to \$42.7 million. However, total operating expenses more than doubled (+117%) to \$215.7 million, propelled by a 159% surge in aircraft fuel costs to \$77 million and a 42% increase in salaries, wages, and benefits to \$60.3 million. The net effect was a decline in operating income from \$49.8 million in Q2 2021 to \$3.4 million in Q2 2022, resulting in a net loss of \$3.9 million versus net income of \$52.2 million a year earlier [10-Q filed 2022-08-10].

2. **Fuel expense doubled year-over-year due to an 89% increase in fuel price per gallon and a 31% rise in fuel consumption linked to higher block hours.** Fuel cost per gallon excluding derivatives rose from \$1.99 to \$3.76 in the first half of 2022 versus 2021, while fuel gallons consumed increased from 28.9 million to 37.8 million gallons. This combination drove a \$87.5 million increase in fuel expense for the six months ended June 30, 2022 [10-Q filed 2022-08-10].

3. **Labor costs rose sharply, reflecting a new pilot collective bargaining agreement effective early 2022 and increased staffing amid operational growth.** Salaries, wages, and benefits increased 39% year-over-year to \$120 million for the first half of 2022, reflecting higher headcount and wage rates [10-Q filed 2022-08-10].

4. **Despite strong revenue growth, operating income declined due to cost inflation; adjusted operating income was \$4 million in Q2 2022, down from \$12 million a year earlier.** Adjusted operating income excludes special items and was positive but down 67% year-over-year [8-K filed 2022-08-08].

5. **The company’s liquidity position remained strong at June 30, 2022, with \$213 million in cash and equivalents, \$70 million in available-for-sale securities, and a \$25 million undrawn revolving credit facility, totaling nearly \$308 million in liquidity.** However, total debt and lease obligations increased to \$645 million from \$546 million at year-end 2021, raising the debt-to-capital ratio to 0.57 from 0.53 [10-Q filed 2022-08-10].

6. **Capital expenditures accelerated, with \$137.6 million spent on property and equipment in the first half of 2022, nearly double the prior year, reflecting fleet growth and transition from operating leases to finance leases.** The fleet grew to 53 Boeing 737 Next Generation aircraft as of June 30, 2022, including 26 owned and 11 finance-leased passenger aircraft, up from 33 total aircraft a year earlier [10-Q filed 2022-08-10].

### Operations Insights

7. **System block hours increased 17% year-over-year to approximately 64,560 hours in H1 2022, driven by cargo growth, while scheduled passenger service block hours remained below 2019 levels due to staffing and training constraints.** Scheduled service block hours were down 9% versus Q2 2019, reflecting ongoing operational challenges, including training throughput issues cited by management [8-K filed 2022-08-08; 10-Q filed 2022-08-10].

8. **Cargo operations faced setbacks with a 4% revenue decline and a swing to an operating loss of \$264,000 in Q2 2022 from a \$15.4 million profit a year earlier, driven by heavy maintenance and reduced block hours.** Cargo block hours fell 5% year-over-year, and departures declined 2%, negatively impacting revenue and profitability [10-Q filed 2022-08-10].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

9. **Scheduled service TRASM (total revenue per available seat mile) improved 29% over Q2 2019 and 13% sequentially from Q1 2022, reflecting strong leisure demand and higher yields despite capacity constraints.** In June 2022, TRASM was 44% higher than June 2019 levels, supporting an 8% GAAP operating margin for scheduled service despite \$4.47 per gallon jet fuel prices [8-K filed 2022-08-08].

10. **Ancillary revenues grew 52% year-over-year to \$44.2 million in Q2 2022, supported by increased passenger volumes and higher fees such as baggage and seat selection.** Ancillary revenue growth contributed to the 56% increase in total passenger revenue [10-Q filed 2022-08-10].

11. **Charter service revenue rose 48% to \$42.7 million in Q2 2022, with plans to add a third aircraft for Caesars Entertainment in October 2022 and new Essential Air Service routes starting December 2022, signaling ongoing expansion in this segment.** New service to Grand Cayman also planned for December 2022 [8-K filed 2022-08-08].

### Labor Insights

12. **Operational capacity was constrained by training throughput issues and staffing shortages, limiting scheduled service flying and increasing unit costs due to underutilized assets and incremental contractor spend.** Management described these as temporary challenges and reported progress in resolving them, but they negatively impacted capacity and margins in Q2 2022 [8-K filed 2022-08-08].

### Wrap Up

Sun Country Airlines’ Q2 2022 financial results show a company recovering strongly in revenue—up nearly 50% year-over-year—driven by passenger and charter growth alongside rising ancillary income. However, these gains were largely offset by sharply higher fuel prices and labor costs, compressing operating income and resulting in a net loss. Cargo operations weakened due to maintenance disruptions, while operational capacity constraints from training bottlenecks limited scheduled service growth and pressured unit costs. The fleet expanded through ownership and finance leases, supporting future growth but increasing capital expenditures and debt levels. Liquidity remains solid, with over \$300 million available including cash and credit facilities. Commercially, TRASM exceeded pre-pandemic levels, reflecting strong leisure demand, but capacity limits curtailed upside.

Management’s guidance for Q3 2022 projects total revenue of \$215–220 million (up 25–28% versus Q3 2019) and an operating margin of 3–5%, with fuel costs expected to moderate to \$3.84 per gallon. The company anticipates easing of training constraints, which should support capacity growth and margin improvement, but remains exposed to fuel price volatility and operational risks. No material litigation, accidents, or regulatory actions were disclosed.
2022.Q4:
### Financial Insights

1. **Sun Country achieved record full-year 2022 revenue of \$894.4 million, up 43.6% from 2021, with Q4 revenue reaching \$227.2 million.**  
   The airline reported a full-year GAAP operating margin of 6.2% and adjusted operating margin of 6.5%, with Q4 margins slightly higher at 6.7% GAAP and 7.0% adjusted. Adjusted diluted EPS for the year was \$0.42, compared to \$0.31 in 2021, while Q4 adjusted EPS was \$0.13. The revenue growth was driven by a 57% year-over-year increase in passenger revenue and significant ancillary revenue growth, reflecting recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic impact [8-K 2023-02-02; 10-K 2023-02-15].

2. **Operating expenses rose sharply, with total operating expenses for 2022 at \$838.7 million (12.39 cents per ASM), up from \$511.1 million (8.77 cents per ASM) in 2021, driven primarily by a 128% increase in aircraft fuel costs.**  
   Aircraft fuel expense was \$268.4 million in 2022 (3.96 cents per ASM), up from \$129.1 million (2.22 cents per ASM) in 2021, reflecting an 83% increase in fuel price per gallon and 20% higher fuel consumption due to increased flying. Salaries, wages, and benefits also increased 38% to \$178.6 million, while aircraft rent declined 45% to \$7.3 million due to fleet ownership changes [10-Q 2022-11-02; 10-K 2023-02-15].

3. **Adjusted CASM (cost per available seat mile) excluding fuel and other non-operating items rose to 7.04 cents in 2022 from 6.48 cents in 2021, indicating cost pressure beyond fuel.**  
   The increase partly reflects higher maintenance, labor, and other operating costs, including incremental contract labor spend and maintenance events for the cargo fleet. The airline expects unit cost pressures related to utilization to ease as pilot hiring and training progress [10-K 2023-02-15; 8-K 2022-11-01].

4. **Cash and liquidity declined significantly during 2022, ending the year with \$92.1 million in cash and \$10.8 million restricted cash, down from \$309.3 million cash and \$8.4 million restricted cash at the end of 2021.**  
   Total liquidity, including available-for-sale securities and revolver availability, was \$285.1 million as of September 30, 2022, down from \$334.3 million a year prior. The company funded operations and capital expenditures primarily through cash from operations, stockholder contributions, debt issuance, and financing arrangements [10-Q 2022-11-02; 10-K 2023-02-15].

5. **The company’s total debt and lease obligations increased to \$653.1 million at September 30, 2022, from \$545.6 million at December 31, 2021, reflecting aircraft purchases and lease reclassifications.**  
   Finance lease obligations rose to \$255.1 million from \$192.2 million, while operating lease obligations declined to \$27.8 million from \$76.0 million due to lease amendments and aircraft acquisitions. Interest expense increased 19% to \$23.1 million in the first nine months of 2022, driven by a larger mix of financed owned aircraft [10-Q 2022-11-02].

6. **During Q4 2022, Sun Country repurchased approximately 1.4 million shares under a \$25 million Accelerated Share Repurchase (ASR) program, at an average price of \$18.23 per share, with \$25 million remaining authorized for repurchases.**  
   The repurchase program is discretionary with no expiration, funded from existing or future cash flows, and is not related to the CARES Act restrictions, which had lapsed by the end of 2022 [8-K 2022-10-31; 8-K 2023-02-02; 10-K 2023-02-15].

### Operations Insights

7. **Sun Country operated a fleet of 54 Boeing 737-NG aircraft as of December 31, 2022, comprising 53 Boeing 737-800s and one 737-700, plus 12 freighter aircraft dedicated to Amazon cargo operations.**  
   The passenger fleet increased by seven aircraft year-over-year, with two aircraft reclassified from operating to finance leases and two previously operating lease aircraft purchased outright. One owned aircraft was retired due to damage beyond economic repair during 2022 [10-K 2023-02-15].

8. **System block hours increased nearly 18% in 2022 compared to 2021, reflecting expanded flying despite training constraints on pilot availability that limited growth in scheduled service block hours in Q3 2022.**  
   Average daily aircraft utilization was 6.4 hours in Q3 2022, down from 7.0 hours in Q3 2021, indicating some inefficiency due to smaller-than-desired scale. The airline hired 91 pilots in 2022 (a 20% increase), aiming to alleviate utilization pressures in 2023 [8-K 2022-11-01].

9. **Completion factor, a key operational reliability metric measuring the percentage of scheduled flights completed, was 98.8% for 2022, an improvement over 96.8% in 2020 and 99.4% in 2021, and was the highest among key competitors during the important holiday season.**  
   This metric reflects operational performance including weather and other disruptions, important for customer experience and cost control [10-K 2023-02-15].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

10. **Passenger revenue growth was supported by a 61% increase in ancillary revenue to \$192.5 million in 2022, with ancillary revenue per passenger rising to \$53.49 from \$42.89 in 2021.**  
    The increase was driven by new ancillary products, the return of onboard food and beverage sales, and higher demand. The airline also expanded its loyalty program, Sun Country Rewards, which accounted for 71% of bookings in 2022, up 21 percentage points from 2018, helping reduce distribution costs [10-Q 2022-11-02; 10-K 2023-02-15].

11. **Sun Country’s revenue mix in 2022 was 79% passenger (scheduled and charter), 10% cargo, and 1.3% other, with scheduled service revenue increasing 57% year-over-year to \$438.3 million and charter service revenue rising 27% to \$161.6 million.**  
    Cargo revenue declined slightly by 1% to \$90.4 million, primarily due to heavy maintenance events reducing block hours and an approximately \$1.7 million revenue benefit recognized in 2021 that did not recur [10-K 2023-02-15; 10-Q 2022-11-02].

### Labor Insights

12. **Salaries, wages, and benefits expenses increased 38% year-over-year to \$178.6 million for the full year 2022, reflecting workforce growth and wage inflation, including costs related to pilot hiring and training efforts.**  
    The company continues to invest in pilot recruitment and training to support growth, with 91 new pilots hired in 2022, but acknowledged ongoing utilization pressures due to smaller-than-desired scale in late 2022 [8-K 2022-11-01; 10-Q 2022-11-02].

### Corporate Insights

13. **Sun Country completed a secondary public offering of 5.25 million shares by a selling stockholder affiliated with Apollo Global Management in February 2023, with no proceeds to the company.**  
    The underwriter has a 30-day option to purchase an additional 787,500 shares. This transaction does not affect Sun Country’s capital but may impact the public float and shareholder composition [8-K 2023-02-15].

14. **The company remains subject to certain CARES Act-related restrictions on executive compensation through April 1, 2023, although prohibitions on share repurchases and dividends had lapsed by the end of 2022.**  
    Sun Country was in compliance with CARES Act provisions as of September 30, 2022, and corrected an immaterial executive compensation excess related to CARES Act limits after year-end, with no accrued liability as of December 31, 2022 [10-Q 2022-11-02; 10-K 2023-02-15].

### Wrap Up

Sun Country Airlines’ fourth quarter and full year 2022 results reflected a substantial recovery from pandemic-impacted 2021, with record revenues driven by strong passenger and ancillary growth and expanded flying hours. However, operating expenses surged, particularly fuel costs which doubled year-over-year, and labor expenses increased significantly amid ongoing pilot hiring and training challenges that constrained utilization. The airline’s fleet expanded modestly with a shift toward owned and finance-leased aircraft, increasing debt and lease obligations. Liquidity declined notably during the year, although the company maintained a sizable cash and securities buffer supported by debt and equity financing.

The company’s commercial strategy emphasized ancillary revenue growth and loyalty program expansion, while operational reliability remained strong, as evidenced by a leading completion factor. The board authorized a \$50 million share repurchase program, with \$25 million executed in Q4 2022, indicating capital return activity alongside operational investments. Corporate developments included a secondary share offering by a major shareholder and ongoing CARES Act-related compliance. The company’s guidance for Q1 2023 projects revenue growth of 24%-28% year-over-year, operating margins improving to 15%-20%, and a modest increase in block hours, reflecting management’s expectation of easing cost pressures as utilization normalizes. No material risks or disruptions beyond those inherent in fuel price volatility, labor availability, and regulatory compliance were disclosed for the period ending December 31, 2022.
2022.FY:
### Financial Insights

1. **Sun Country Airlines grew revenue 44% in 2022 to a record \$894 million but faced margin pressure from higher fuel costs and operational constraints.**  
   Full year 2022 total operating revenue reached \$894.4 million, up 43.6% from 2021 [8-K 2023-02-02]. Scheduled service revenue increased significantly, for example by 127% in Q1 2022 versus Q1 2021 (\$124.1M vs. \$54.6M) [10-Q 2022-05-06]. Despite this growth, full year GAAP operating margin was 6.2% and adjusted operating margin was 6.5%, down from margins above 8% in prior years [8-K 2023-02-02; 8-K 2022-02-07]. Fuel costs represented approximately 33% of operating expenses in the nine months ended September 30, 2022, up from 26% in the prior year, driven by an 83% increase in fuel cost per gallon and 20% higher fuel consumption [10-Q 2022-11-02]. These elevated fuel costs, combined with operational challenges such as training throughput issues and Hurricane Ian’s impact (estimated \$1 million revenue loss in Q3 2022), constrained margins [8-K 2022-11-01; 8-K 2022-08-10].

2. **Adjusted earnings per share improved to \$0.42 for 2022 despite quarterly volatility and a net income of \$77 million for 2021.**  
   For full year 2022, GAAP diluted EPS was \$0.29 and adjusted diluted EPS was \$0.42 [8-K 2023-02-02]. This followed a 2021 net income of \$77.5 million and adjusted net income of \$20 million, with 2021 adjusted EPS of \$0.33 [8-K 2022-02-07; 10-K 2022-02-18]. Quarterly results were mixed, with Q2 2022 reporting a net loss of \$4 million and Q3 showing \$15 million operating income [8-K 2022-08-08; 8-K 2022-11-01].

3. **Operating expenses excluding fuel per block hour declined 6% in Q1 2022 versus Q1 2019, but total operating expenses grew 34% year over year due to higher fuel and volume.**  
   First quarter 2022 GAAP operating expenses increased 36% versus Q1 2019, driven mainly by a 76% increase in aircraft fuel expense [8-K 2022-05-05]. Excluding fuel and special items, operating expenses per block hour declined 6%, reflecting cost control [8-K 2022-05-05]. Sales and marketing expenses rose 69% in Q1 2022 versus Q1 2021, reflecting increased activity [10-Q 2022-05-06]. Depreciation and amortization increased 20% year-over-year in H1 2022 due to more owned aircraft and finance leases [10-Q 2022-08-10].

4. **Liquidity declined from \$318 million at end 2021 to approximately \$103 million at end 2022 amid capital expenditures.**  
   Cash, cash equivalents, and restricted cash totaled \$317.8 million at December 31, 2021, falling to \$102.9 million at December 31, 2022 [10-K 2023-02-15]. Capital expenditures were \$123 million in 2022, largely for aircraft acquisitions and related investments [10-K 2023-02-15]. The company’s liquidity sources included cash from operations, stockholder contributions, and debt financing [10-Q 2022-08-10; 10-Q 2022-11-02].

5. **Sun Country’s board authorized a \$50 million share repurchase program with an initial \$25 million accelerated repurchase agreement in late 2022.**  
   In November 2022, the board approved repurchasing up to \$50 million of common stock, with intent to initiate a \$25 million accelerated share repurchase (ASR) [8-K 2022-11-01]. Subsequently, a secondary public offering by the Apollo-affiliated selling stockholder occurred in February 2023, but Sun Country itself did not sell shares or receive proceeds [8-K 2023-02-15].

### Operations Insights

6. **Capacity grew modestly in 2022 with 42 passenger aircraft and 12 freighters, but training and staffing issues limited utilization and pressured unit costs.**  
   Passenger fleet grew from 36 aircraft at end 2021 to 42 at end 2022, with 12 cargo freighters maintained [8-K 2022-11-01; 10-K 2023-02-15]. System block hours increased 2% year-over-year in Q3 2022 but scheduled service block hours declined 2% due to training throughput constraints [8-K 2022-11-01]. Staffing challenges also kept scheduled service and charter block hours below 2019 levels in Q2 2022, despite 10% overall system block hour growth fueled by cargo expansion [8-K 2022-08-08; 8-K 2022-06-22]. Management noted that increasing utilization toward historical levels in 2023 is expected to ease unit cost pressures [8-K 2022-11-01].

7. **Revenue passenger miles (RPMs) and available seat miles (ASMs) surged in 2022 as demand recovered, with load factors improving significantly.**  
   For Q1 2022, scheduled service RPMs increased 72.7% and ASMs rose 45.5% versus Q1 2021, lifting load factor to 79.5% from 66.9% [8-K 2022-05-05]. Nine-month 2022 scheduled service revenues increased 66% year-over-year [10-Q 2022-11-02]. Ancillary revenue per passenger grew due to new products and pricing initiatives, reaching \$55.29 in Q3 2022, up 29% year-over-year [10-Q 2022-11-02]. Cargo block hours and departures declined slightly year-over-year due to maintenance events, with cargo revenue down 3% in Q3 2022 [10-Q 2022-11-02].

8. **Sun Country’s hybrid model leverages shared assets across scheduled, charter, and cargo operations to mitigate seasonality and improve returns.**  
   Approximately one-third of revenue comes from cargo and charter businesses, which have long-term contracts with fuel pass-through provisions, partially hedging fuel cost volatility [8-K 2022-06-22]. The company shares aircraft and pilots across business lines, enhancing operating leverage and flexibility [8-K 2022-06-22; 10-K 2023-02-15]. Scheduled service focuses on leisure and visiting friends and relatives (VFR) passengers, primarily from Minneapolis-St. Paul (MSP) and other regional markets [10-K 2023-02-15].

### Route Network Insights

9. **Sun Country expanded its Florida network with new nonstop destinations in early 2023 and increased service from Wisconsin to Orlando.**  
   The airline announced new service to Destin-Fort Walton Beach and Melbourne, Florida, beginning February 2023, marking its 11th and 12th nonstop Florida destinations [8-K 2022-11-01]. Additionally, service expansions from Eau Claire, Green Bay, and Madison, Wisconsin to Orlando were scheduled for April 2023 [8-K 2022-11-01]. These network expansions align with the leisure focus and seasonal demand patterns.

10. **Sun Country continues to grow market share at MSP, the airline’s primary hub, and plans fleet growth to approximately 50 passenger aircraft by year-end 2023.**  
    The airline is the second largest carrier at MSP with a 58% passenger share, growing steadily since 2017 [8-K 2022-06-22]. The fleet strategy focuses on owning Boeing 737-800 aircraft acquired opportunistically, with no active order book, targeting approximately 50 passenger aircraft by the end of 2023 [8-K 2022-06-22; 10-K 2023-02-15]. Cargo freighters remain at 12 aircraft [10-K 2023-02-15].

### Labor Insights

11. **Sun Country ratified a new pilot labor agreement in late 2021, improving pay and work rules to support growth despite increased costs.**  
    The new pilot contract, ratified at the end of 2021, offers competitive compensation and benefits, facilitating pilot recruitment and retention [8-K 2022-02-07]. The agreement contributed to higher labor costs but is expected to support future capacity increases [8-K 2022-05-05]. Staffing and training throughput challenges persisted in 2022, limiting scheduled service capacity growth and pressuring unit costs [8-K 2022-11-01].

### Wrap Up

In 2022, Sun Country Airlines demonstrated significant revenue growth driven by recovery in passenger demand and ancillary revenue expansion, reaching a record \$894 million. The airline's hybrid business model combining scheduled leisure service, charter, and cargo operations supported resilience amid ongoing operational challenges, including training bottlenecks and elevated fuel prices. These cost pressures, particularly fuel which rose sharply in price and consumption, compressed operating margins despite strong revenue growth. The fleet grew modestly to 42 passenger and 12 cargo aircraft, while the company maintained a disciplined capital approach with \$123 million in property and equipment investments and liquidity declining from \$318 million to \$103 million over the year. The board authorized a \$50 million share repurchase program late in 2022, signaling a return of capital focus.

Network expansions in Florida and Wisconsin, along with continued market share gains at Minneapolis-St. Paul, underpin Sun Country’s growth strategy supported by a new pilot labor agreement aimed at securing capacity growth. Operational constraints from staffing and training limited utilization and pressured unit costs, but management expects these to ease as utilization returns to historical levels in 2023.

**Guidance Overview:** For Q1 2023, Sun Country projected total revenues of \$280 to \$290 million (24%-28% above Q1 2022), an economic fuel cost per gallon of \$3.58, and an improved operating income margin of 15% to 20%, reflecting expected easing of cost pressures and higher utilization [8-K 2023-02-02]. The company planned 35,000 to 36,000 system block hours, a 3.5% to 6.5% increase over Q1 2022. This guidance suggests management anticipates operational improvements and margin recovery in the near term.

Total operating expenses were \$238.3 million, up from \$204.7 million in Q1 2022. Salaries, wages, and benefits increased 27% to \$75.4 million, reflecting higher headcount and increased pilot unit costs. Aircraft fuel expense rose 12% to \$72.3 million, consistent with a 12% increase in fuel cost per gallon guidance and higher block hours. Adjusted CASM, which excludes fuel, stock compensation, cargo-related costs, and other non-cash or non-recurring items, increased to 7.10 cents from 6.21 cents, indicating inflationary and operational cost pressures beyond fuel [10-Q 2023-04-28; 8-K 2023-02-02].

5. **Operating cash flow improved sharply, but capital expenditures doubled**  
Operating activities generated \$47.9 million in cash, up 163% from \$18.2 million in Q1 2022. However, purchases of property and equipment rose 111% to \$105.0 million, reflecting aircraft acquisitions including two aircraft held for operating lease purchased for \$63 million partially financed with term loans. The net effect was a \$8.6 million decrease in cash, a substantial improvement from a \$37.3 million cash reduction in the prior year period [10-Q 2023-04-28].

7. **Share repurchases continued with 1.37 million shares bought at \$18.23 average price in Q1**  
Sun Country repurchased 750,000 shares at \$19.75 per share from underwriters of a secondary offering by Apollo Global Management affiliates and completed a \$25 million accelerated share repurchase program begun in late 2022, acquiring 480,932 shares. Sun Country's fleet as of March 31, 2023, consisted of 57 Boeing 737 Next Generation aircraft: 53 Boeing 737-800s, 3 Boeing 737-900ERs (a new variant for the airline), and 1 Boeing 737-700. The three 737-900ERs were acquired in early 2023 but remain leased to Oman Air until late 2024 and 2025, with delivery to Sun Country scheduled thereafter. Total system block hours (a measure of aircraft utilization) for Q1 2023 were guided at 35 to 36 thousand, reflecting a 3.5% to 6.5% increase versus Q1 2022. ### Commercial Strategy Insights

The average total fare per passenger increased \$38.14 or 21% to \$221.48 in Q1 2023 compared to Q1 2022. The company attributes this to resilient demand and a higher load factor, with the business mix including leisure and visiting friends and relatives (VFR) passengers, charter customers, and cargo services. Ancillary revenue growth of 52% also contributed to total passenger revenue gains [10-Q 2023-04-28; 8-K 2023-04-27].

### Labor Insights

11. **Labor costs increased significantly due to higher headcount and pilot unit costs**  
Salaries, wages, and benefits rose 27% year-over-year to \$75.4 million, driven by increased staffing levels and higher per-unit labor costs for pilots. In February 2023, an affiliate of Apollo Global Management sold 5.25 million shares in a secondary offering, with underwriters granted a 30-day option for an additional 787,500 shares. The offering closed in February 2023 [8-K 2023-02-15; 8-K 2023-02-22].

### Wrap Up

Sun Country Airlines delivered record revenue and earnings in Q1 2023, driven by a 21% increase in average fares and an 8.6-point load factor gain, with passenger revenue up 32% year-over-year. Operating income more than doubled to \$55.8 million, supporting a 19% margin despite rising labor and fuel costs that pushed adjusted CASM higher. The airline’s fleet grew modestly with the addition of new aircraft types, and capacity increased alongside operational challenges from severe winter weather at its Minneapolis hub. Cash flow from operations improved significantly, though capital expenditures doubled due to aircraft acquisitions, including purchases of aircraft previously on operating lease. Liquidity remained robust at \$261.5 million, though net debt and lease obligations increased. The company continued share repurchases following a secondary offering by Apollo affiliates.

For Q2 2023, Sun Country guides revenue of \$255 million to \$265 million (16% to 21% growth versus Q2 2022), an operating margin of 11% to 16%, and economic fuel cost per gallon of \$2.85 (35% lower than Q2 2022). Total system block hours are expected to rise 11% to 14%. The airline does not currently plan to enter into fuel hedges and maintains exposure to fuel price volatility and interest rate risk. No material labor disputes or regulatory actions were disclosed.

### Wrap Up

Sun Country Airlines reported record revenues in Q4 and full year 2023, supported by capacity growth, diversified revenue streams from scheduled, charter, cargo, and ancillary sources, and disciplined cost management that led to modestly improved adjusted operating margins despite fare pressures. The airline expanded its fleet and network while continuing significant share repurchases funded by cash flow. Fuel price declines and operational scale partially offset rising interest and stock-based compensation expenses. The company’s hybrid low-cost model and peak demand scheduling underpin its strategy to manage seasonality and volatility.

Guidance for Q1 2024 projects total revenue of \$310 million to \$320 million (5% to 9% growth vs. Q1 2023), an operating margin between 17% and 21%, and economic fuel cost per gallon of \$3.00. ### Wrap Up

Sun Country Airlines reported a record third-quarter revenue of \$249 million in 2024, maintaining profitability with a 5.0% GAAP operating margin despite a 3% drop in passenger revenue caused by fare pressure from increased industry capacity. The company’s diversified business model, including cargo and aircraft leasing, helped offset softness in scheduled passenger revenue and fuel price volatility. Operating expenses grew modestly, driven by higher labor and ground handling costs, while fuel expenses declined due to lower prices and consumption efficiency. Adjusted CASM rose slightly, reflecting non-fuel cost pressures amid capacity growth.

Operationally, Sun Country grew passenger capacity moderately, maintained a stable fleet of 63 passenger aircraft and 12 cargo freighters, and plans to add eight new freighters under an extended Amazon contract through 2030. Liquidity improved with a stronger cash position and reduced net debt compared to year-end 2023, supported by lower capital expenditures and steady operating cash flow. The company also expanded its international leisure network from Milwaukee and extended leases on subleased aircraft, positioning for fleet growth in 2025.

**Guidance for Q4 2024** anticipates total revenue of \$250–260 million (2–6% growth year-over-year), economic fuel cost per gallon of \$2.47 (20% lower), and operating income margin of 7–9%, with scheduled service ASMs growing slightly over 3% [8-K 2024-10-30]. The company expects the first new Amazon freighter aircraft in late March or early April 2025, supporting cargo expansion and a moderate scheduled service capacity reduction to accommodate this growth [8-K 2024-08-01]. No material labor disruptions or regulatory risks were disclosed in the period.

Sun Country Airlines’ fourth quarter and full-year 2025 results highlight a strategic shift emphasizing cargo growth, with eight additional freighter aircraft added and cargo block hours increasing over 50% year-over-year in Q4. Despite higher unit costs driven by cargo expenses and labor cost increases, the company maintained profitability and improved liquidity, supported by a new term loan facility and share repurchases. The launch of a new co-branded credit card program in Q3 2025 supports the loyalty strategy focused on leisure travelers.

The announced merger with Allegiant in early 2026 represents a major corporate development, expected to close in the second half of 2026, and is positioned to combine complementary route networks and fleets. Operationally, Sun Country is expanding cargo infrastructure with a new base and additional aircraft planned in 2026, while continuing to optimize its passenger and charter service through dynamic fleet and crew deployment.

   These special items comprised approximately \$20.4 million of equity-related compensation, \$1.0 million of airport exit costs, and \$2.8 million of mark-to-market adjustments on fuel hedges not qualifying for hedge accounting [8-K 2015-02-18; 8-K 2015-01-22].

### Operations Insights

7. **Capacity remained essentially flat in 2014, with a slight Q4 decrease, while traffic and load factors improved, reflecting higher efficiency in seat utilization.**  
   Available Seat Miles (ASMs) for Q4 2014 slightly decreased by 0.3% to 3.044 billion compared to Q4 2013, with 53 Airbus A320-family aircraft in service [8-K 2015-02-18; 10-K 2015-03-03]. For the full year, ASMs were stable at approximately 12.24 billion [10-K 2015-03-03]. Revenue Passenger Miles (RPMs) increased 3.1% in Q4 and 2.6% for the full year, driving a 2.7 and 2.1 point increase in load factor to 81.2% and 82.3%, respectively [8-K 2015-02-18; 10-K 2015-03-03].

8. **Passenger volumes grew modestly, with a 2.7% increase in Q4 and 2.8% for the full year, while average stage length remained stable.**  
   Q4 onboard passengers rose to 1.62 million from 1.58 million in Q4 2013, with an average stage length of approximately 1,451 miles [8-K 2015-02-18]. For the full year, passengers increased to 6.51 million from 6.33 million in 2013, with an average stage length of 1,466 miles [10-K 2015-03-03].

9. **Operational reliability remained high, with on-time performance at 81.5% and a completion factor of 99.4% for 2014, consistent with top rankings in industry quality ratings.**  
   Virgin America was the top-ranked airline in the Airline Quality Rating for 2014, reflecting strong operational performance metrics such as low mishandled baggage rates (0.95 per 1,000 passengers) [10-K 2015-03-03].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

10. **Virgin America expanded ancillary revenue streams, notably through a new co-branded credit card launched in early 2014, contributing to a 25.5% increase in other revenue in Q4 and 18.7% for the year.**  
    The airline also increased seat selection and change fee revenues due to higher passenger volumes and fee adjustments [8-K 2015-02-18; 10-K 2015-03-03].

11. **The frequent flyer program grew by 16.2% in 2014 to over 3.4 million members, supported by campaigns incentivizing travelers to switch from legacy carriers.**  
    Virgin America also expanded its commercial partnerships, ending 2014 with four codeshare and 32 interline agreements, enhancing connectivity [8-K 2015-02-18].

### Route Network Insights

12. **Virgin America expanded its network presence in key business markets, notably launching a mid-continent focus city at Dallas Love Field (DAL) and adding service to New York LaGuardia (LGA) and Washington National (DCA).**  
    The airline became the only carrier at DAL offering three classes of service and introduced a dedicated First Class check-in lounge there [8-K 2015-02-18]. The network served 21 airports in the U.S. and Mexico as of December 31, 2014, with a fleet of 53 narrow-body Airbus aircraft [10-K 2015-03-03].

### Wrap Up

Virgin America's Q4 2014 and full year results reflect a steady improvement in financial performance, highlighted by record profitability and margin expansion. Revenue growth was supported by higher load factors and a significant increase in ancillary revenue, particularly from a new co-branded credit card. Modest capacity growth and operational reliability sustained improved unit revenues. Cost pressures arose mainly from increased salaries and profit sharing, partly offset by lower fuel and aircraft rent expenses. The November 2014 IPO and recapitalization substantially strengthened the balance sheet, reducing debt and interest expense, which contributed to net income growth.

Looking ahead, the company’s 2015 guidance anticipates modest capacity growth of 2-3% in Q1, with PRASM expected to be stable to slightly positive (-1% to +1%) and CASM excluding fuel and profit sharing forecasted to increase by 1-3%. Fuel costs are expected to average \$2.45 to \$2.55 per gallon in Q1 2015, reflecting continued hedging and market conditions [8-K 2015-02-18; 8-K 2015-01-22]. No material operational disruptions, labor issues, or regulatory risks were disclosed for this period.

The net income increase was supported by a 4.6% rise in total revenue per available seat mile (RASM) to 12.17 cents and a decrease in interest expense by \$33.8 million, primarily due to debt reduction following the 2013 and 2014 recapitalizations [10-K filed 2015-03-03; 8-K filed 2015-02-18].

Other revenue increased to \$160.8 million from \$135.4 million, driven primarily by advertising, brand revenues, and ancillary fees such as seat selection and change fees, boosted by the launch of Virgin America Visa Signature and Premium Visa Signature credit cards in early 2014 [8-K filed 2015-02-18; 10-K filed 2015-03-03].

Aircraft rent declined 8.8% to \$184.4 million due to lease renegotiations and fleet management. Fuel expense decreased 1.6% to \$499.1 million, reflecting a 3.1% reduction in average price per gallon to \$3.08, offsetting a 1.5% increase in fuel consumption [10-K filed 2015-03-03]. CASM excluding fuel and profit sharing increased 2.9% to 7.02 cents, indicating underlying cost pressures beyond fuel [8-K filed 2015-02-18; 10-K filed 2015-03-03].

   Virgin America completed its initial public offering (IPO) in November 2014, issuing 13.1 million shares at \$23 per share, raising net proceeds of \$277.6 million after fees [10-K filed 2015-03-03]. The IPO proceeds were used to reduce outstanding debt substantially, lowering interest expenses by \$33.8 million year-over-year and improving liquidity [8-K filed 2015-02-18].

   Fourth quarter total operating revenue rose 3.4% to \$372.2 million, with RASM increasing 3.7% to 12.23 cents, driven by a 2.7 point load factor increase and 25.5% growth in other revenue from ancillary products and the co-branded credit card [8-K filed 2015-02-18]. CASM excluding special items rose modestly by 0.7% to 11.10 cents. Special items, including \$20.4 million in IPO-related equity compensation and \$2.8 million in mark-to-market fuel hedge losses, were excluded from these income figures [8-K filed 2015-02-18].

   The single fleet type supports operational efficiency and cost control [10-K filed 2015-03-03]. The airline installed GoGo’s next-generation ATG4 WiFi fleetwide by December 2014, maintaining its position as the first U.S. airline to offer fleetwide inflight WiFi [8-K filed 2015-02-18].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

11. **Ancillary revenue growth of 18.7% was driven by new co-branded credit cards and increased fees for seat selection and change fees, supported by a 16.2% growth in the frequent flyer program membership to over 3.4 million.**

12. **The airline expanded its commercial partnerships, ending 2014 with four codeshare and 32 interline agreements, supporting revenue growth and network connectivity.**

### Labor Insights

13. **Salaries, wages, and benefits rose 31% to \$257.4 million, reflecting competitive market pressures for pilots and inflight staff, increased seniority, profit sharing, and \$19.6 million in IPO-related equity compensation.**

### Wrap Up

Virgin America’s 2014 fiscal year was marked by record profitability supported by stable capacity, improved load factors, and growth in ancillary revenues, especially from a new co-branded credit card program. The company’s IPO in November 2014 materially strengthened its balance sheet, providing \$394.6 million in unrestricted cash and enabling significant debt reduction that lowered interest expenses. Despite rising salaries and benefits, the airline managed to partially offset these cost pressures through reduced aircraft rent and fuel expenses aided by a declining fuel price environment, though fuel hedge losses limited some benefits. Operationally, Virgin America maintained a modern single-type fleet, high reliability, and expanded its network strategically into major business markets including Dallas Love Field and New York area airports. Commercially, the airline enhanced its premium brand positioning through frequent flyer growth, partnerships, and digital innovation.

For the first quarter of 2015, Virgin America guided for a 2.0% to 3.0% capacity increase, flat to slightly positive passenger revenue per available seat mile (PRASM), and a 1.0% to 3.0% increase in CASM excluding fuel and profit sharing. The company expects economic fuel costs between \$2.45 and \$2.55 per gallon, reflecting hedges and market prices as of early 2015 [8-K filed 2015-02-18]. No material operational disruptions, labor disputes, or regulatory risks were disclosed for 2014.

2015.Q1:
### Financial Insights

1. **Virgin America achieved first quarter 2015 net income of \$10.5 million excluding special items, reversing a loss of \$22.4 million in the same period of 2014.**

Fully diluted earnings per share excluding special items were \$0.24, compared to a loss per share of \$(31.86) in 2014Q1, reflecting the impact of the November 2014 IPO and related balance sheet restructuring [8-K 2015-04-30; 10-Q 2015-04-30].

2. **Operating revenue grew 4.1% year-over-year to \$326.4 million in 2015Q1, driven by a 4.1% increase in passenger revenue and a 4.6% increase in other revenue.**  
   Passenger revenue rose to \$289.4 million from \$278.0 million, supported by a 2.6% increase in passenger revenue per available seat mile (PRASM) to 10.27 cents, which resulted from a 1.4% yield increase and a 0.9 point rise in load factor to 80.1% [8-K 2015-04-30; 10-Q 2015-04-30]. Other revenue growth was attributed mainly to increased advertising and brand revenues via the co-branded credit card program and higher Express fee revenue [10-Q 2015-04-30].

Salaries, wages, and benefits rose by \$10.9 million, reflecting increased accrued profit sharing (\$2.1 million), equity-based compensation (\$1.3 million), and compensation alignment with industry averages [10-Q 2015-04-30]. Aircraft maintenance expense decreased 27.4% due to lower scheduled heavy maintenance activity [8-K 2015-04-30].

4. **Operating income turned positive to \$15.4 million with a 4.7% operating margin, compared to a loss of \$13.1 million and -4.2% margin in 2014Q1.**

Net interest and other expenses declined by \$6.9 million year-over-year due to reduced related-party debt following the IPO and recapitalization [10-Q 2015-04-30].

2015.Q2:
### Financial Insights

   When excluding fuel and profit sharing, CASM increased 7.1% to 7.27 cents, reflecting wage inflation and other non-fuel cost pressures. Fuel expense declined 29.3% year-over-year to an average economic fuel cost per gallon of \$2.20 including taxes and hedging effects [8-K 2015-07-30].

3. **Operating revenue growth was modest at 0.5% compared to Q2 2014, with passenger revenue per available seat mile (PRASM) up 0.5% to 11.24 cents, driven by a 0.2 point load factor increase and a 0.3% yield rise, plus a \$3.2 million positive Elevate loyalty revenue adjustment.**  
   Total RASM rose 0.6%. The loyalty program contributed to revenue enhancement, increasing PRASM by 0.9% [8-K 2015-07-30].

   The company also terminated a \$100 million letter of credit facility, saving approximately \$5.5 million annually in financing costs, and arranged financing for five Airbus A320 deliveries at interest rates below 5% [8-K 2015-07-30].

5. **Capacity measured by Available Seat Miles (ASMs) remained flat year-over-year at 53 Airbus A320-family aircraft as of June 30, 2015, with no retirements and no growth in Q2 2015 capacity compared to Q2 2014.**

   Revenue Passenger Miles (RPMs) were down 1.9% in June on 1.3% lower capacity, but year-to-date RPMs increased 1.2% [8-K 2015-07-08].

8. **Salaries, wages, and benefits increased 26.0% year-over-year in Q2 2015 to \$74.8 million, reflecting wage inflation and a \$6.7 million accrual for teammate profit sharing and related payroll taxes.**

9. **Virgin America expanded its loyalty program, Elevate, growing membership by over 114,000 in Q1 2015, which contributed \$3.2 million to PRASM in Q2, indicating increasing ancillary revenue from loyalty-related sources.**

10. **The airline launched new service announcements for Hawaii routes starting November and December 2015 from San Francisco, and expanded point-to-point operations including Dallas Love Field to Austin Bergstrom, reflecting targeted network growth within its premium low-cost model.**

### Route Network Insights

11. **Virgin America operated a stable fleet of 53 Airbus A320-family aircraft serving 21 U.S. and Mexico airports at June 30, 2015, with no aircraft retirements planned in 2015 and 2016 fleet growth targeted to 63 aircraft by year-end 2016.**  
    The company planned 10 new A320 deliveries in 2015-2016 and projected 13-15% capacity growth in 2016, indicating a return to network expansion after a flat Q2 2015 [8-K 2015-07-30].

12. **Capacity growth in 2016 is expected to be accompanied by a targeted 1-2% decrease in CASM excluding fuel and profit sharing, suggesting anticipated operating efficiencies from fleet expansion and network optimization.**  
    However, the company expects CASM excluding fuel and profit sharing to increase 2-3% in Q4 2015 due to pay and benefit initiatives and lower average stage length from Dallas Love Field capacity deployment [8-K 2015-07-30].

### Wrap Up

Virgin America's 2015 second quarter showcased record profitability with net income excluding special items rising 75% year-over-year to \$64.4 million on stable capacity and moderate revenue growth. The earnings improvement primarily reflected significantly lower fuel costs, partially offset by higher labor expenses, including profit sharing, and reduced maintenance costs. Operationally, the fleet remained steady at 53 Airbus A320-family aircraft, with plans for fleet and capacity growth resuming in late 2015 and into 2016. The company improved liquidity and reduced financing costs through strategic debt management and cash flow generation. Commercially, Virgin America enhanced its premium product offering, loyalty program revenue, and network reach, particularly with new Hawaii services and Dallas Love Field expansion.

Looking ahead, Virgin America expects moderate capacity growth of 2-3% in Q3 2015 with PRASM declines of 2-4% and CASM excluding fuel and profit sharing rising over 10%, driven by wage increases and maintenance costs. The airline anticipates a 9-10% capacity increase in Q4 2015 with a 2-3% rise in CASM excluding fuel and profit sharing, and significant 2016 capacity growth of 13-15% with targeted unit cost reductions excluding fuel. Fuel prices remain a material risk, with hedges covering approximately 46% of near-term requirements. No major operational disruptions, labor disputes, or regulatory issues were disclosed for the quarter.

### Wrap Up

Virgin America’s third quarter 2015 results show strong profitability growth driven mainly by lower fuel costs and disciplined capacity expansion with a modest 3.0% ASM increase supported by fleet growth to 55 aircraft. Despite a 2.7% decline in PRASM due to lower load factor and yield, ancillary revenue growth and operational efficiency improvements contributed to record operating margins of 18.2%.
