### Financial Insights

1. **Virgin America achieved record full-year net income of \$201.5 million excluding special items, a 138.8% increase over 2014, driven by higher operating income and improved margins.**  
   Operating income excluding special items rose to \$211.7 million in 2015 from \$96.4 million in 2014, reflecting an 83.8% increase. The operating margin excluding special items improved to approximately 13.9% for the full year (calculated from operating income and revenue), up from about 6.5% in 2014. On a GAAP basis, net income was \$340.5 million, and operating income was \$177.2 million, both substantially higher than 2014 levels. Fully diluted earnings per share excluding special items were \$4.53 for 2015, compared to a pro forma \$1.69 in 2014. This performance included a 2.7% increase in total operating revenue to \$1.53 billion, with passenger revenue up 2.2% to \$1.36 billion and other revenue up 7.0% to \$166.7 million [8-K 2016-02-18; 10-K 2016-02-29; 10-K 2015-03-03].

2. **Revenue per available seat mile (RASM) declined 1.0% in 2015 compared to 2014, despite a PRASM premium in competitive markets and growth in ancillary revenue.**  
   Full-year RASM was 12.05 cents, down from 12.17 cents in 2014. Passenger revenue per available seat mile (PRASM) showed mixed trends: it increased in early 2015 quarters but declined in the second half, with a 5.1% decrease in Q4 2015 due to weaker demand in December and a low fare environment at Dallas Love Field. Ancillary revenue growth contributed to total operating revenue growth, supported by expanded partnerships and new customer service solutions [8-K 2016-02-18; 8-K 2015-04-30; 8-K 2015-10-29].

3. **Operating costs excluding special items increased modestly, with significant fuel cost savings offset by higher salaries, wages, and benefits.**  
   Total operating expenses excluding special items grew by 2.5% in 2015 compared to 2014, reflecting a 30.3% reduction in aircraft fuel expense from \$499.1 million to \$347.7 million due to lower average fuel prices and hedging. However, salaries, wages, and benefits increased 21.8% to \$289.6 million, influenced by pay and benefit initiatives implemented during 2015. Aircraft rent rose 19.3% to \$219.8 million, partly due to new aircraft deliveries. Other operating expenses, including sales and marketing (+10.2%) and landing fees (+8.9%), also increased [10-K 2016-02-29; 8-K 2015-04-30; 8-K 2015-07-30].

4. **Cost per available seat mile (CASM) excluding fuel and profit sharing increased by approximately 7-9% in 2015 due to higher labor and maintenance costs, partially offset by capacity growth and fleet efficiency.**  
   CASM excluding special items decreased overall due to fuel savings, but CASM excluding fuel and profit sharing rose 7-9% year-over-year, driven by wage increases and maintenance expenses. The company targeted a 7-9% increase in this CASM component for 2015 and expected it to remain flat in 2016. CASM excluding special items decreased 7.7% in Q3 2015 and 5.5% in Q1 2015 compared to the respective prior-year quarters, reflecting fuel cost declines [8-K 2015-07-30; 8-K 2015-04-30; 8-K 2015-10-29].

5. **Virgin America generated positive operating cash flow each quarter, ending 2015 with \$496.3 million in unrestricted cash, up from \$394.6 million at the end of 2014, supporting fleet acquisitions and debt reduction.**  
   Operating cash flow was \$23.8 million in Q4 2015. The company financed approximately 80% of the purchase price for five 2015 Airbus A320 deliveries at interest rates under 5%, with similar arrangements for five 2016 deliveries. The strong cash position and debt management allowed the company to terminate a \$100 million letter of credit facility, saving approximately \$5.5 million annually in financing costs [8-K 2016-02-18; 8-K 2015-07-30; 8-K 2015-04-30].

### Operations Insights

6. **Virgin America expanded its fleet from 53 to 58 Airbus A320-family aircraft in 2015, increasing capacity by 3.7% year-over-year, with a 10.3% ASM increase in Q4 2015.**  
   The airline took delivery of five A320 aircraft in 2015 and planned five more for 2016. Capacity growth was constrained in early 2015 by severe winter weather but accelerated in the second half. Load factor was stable at 82.2% for the full year, slightly down 0.1 points from 2014, with monthly fluctuations including a 2.2-point decline in December 2015 due to higher capacity growth relative to traffic. The company planned to increase capacity by 13-15% in 2016, ending the year with 63 aircraft [8-K 2016-02-18; 8-K 2015-04-30; 8-K 2016-02-05].

7. **Traffic (revenue passenger miles) grew 3.6% in 2015, with passenger counts up 8.1% to 7.0 million, reflecting network expansion including new service to Hawai'i and Dallas Love Field.**  
   Virgin America launched flights from San Francisco to Honolulu and Kahului, Maui in late 2015 and initiated service between Dallas Love Field and Austin Bergstrom International Airport. However, the airline ended service between Dallas Love Field and Austin effective November 30, 2015, and added new service between Dallas Love Field and Las Vegas starting December 1, 2015. Load factors in developing markets were generally lower, contributing to PRASM pressure [8-K 2016-02-18; 8-K 2015-04-30; 8-K 2015-10-29].

8. **Operational reliability and customer experience remained strong, with Virgin America ranked number one in the Airline Quality Report for the third consecutive year and receiving multiple industry awards.**  
   The airline was recognized as ‘Best U.S. Airline’ in Condé Nast Traveler’s Readers’ Choice Awards for the eighth consecutive year and received top rankings for in-flight service, product quality, and staff service in multiple surveys. The company also upgraded its in-flight entertainment system and WiFi connectivity in 2015, including partnerships with Netflix, Spotify, and The New York Times to enhance ancillary revenue opportunities [8-K 2016-02-18; 8-K 2015-07-30; 8-K 2015-10-29].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

9. **Virgin America maintained a premium-branded, low-cost carrier (LCC) model, achieving a PRASM premium over other LCCs and some legacy carriers in key markets through product differentiation and ancillary revenue growth.**

Ancillary revenue growth was supported by the introduction of new customer service solutions and the ability to sell ancillaries via Global Distribution Systems (GDS) [8-K 2015-09-09; 8-K 2016-02-18; 8-K 2015-04-30].

10. **Virgin America’s network strategy focused on high-yield business and leisure destinations, with a point-to-point route structure centered on San Francisco and Los Angeles, and selective expansion into new markets meeting return on invested capital (ROIC) criteria.**  
    The airline served 23 airports in the U.S. and Mexico by year-end 2015, including expansion into Hawai'i and new service from Dallas Love Field. Capacity was concentrated primarily on domestic routes (97%), with significant exposure on transcontinental routes (64% combined NY transcon and other transcon). The company avoided exceeding 10% of capacity in new or developing markets to limit cannibalization and maintain profitability thresholds [8-K 2015-09-09; 8-K 2016-03-08].

### Labor Insights

11. **Salaries, wages, and benefits costs increased significantly in 2015, reflecting pay and benefit initiatives implemented during the year, including profit-sharing accruals.**  
    Labor costs rose 21.8% year-over-year to \$289.6 million, with notable quarterly increases including a \$7.1 million accrual for profit sharing and related payroll taxes in Q3 2015 and similar accruals in other quarters. ### Route Network Insights

12. **Virgin America’s fleet plan included the acquisition of ten Airbus A321neo aircraft for delivery in 2017-2018, expected to deliver up to 20% better fuel and carbon efficiency, supporting cost reduction and revenue growth opportunities.**

The airline’s network continued to evolve with new routes to Hawai'i and adjustments at Dallas Love Field, including discontinuation of the DAL-AUS route and addition of DAL-LAS service [8-K 2016-02-18; 8-K 2015-10-29].

### Wrap Up

Virgin America’s 2015 fiscal year was marked by record profitability driven by strong operating income growth and significant fuel cost savings, despite modest declines in unit revenues and rising labor costs. Capacity grew moderately with fleet expansion, enabling network growth into new markets like Hawai'i and Dallas Love Field, though some route adjustments were made. The company maintained a premium LCC positioning with a PRASM premium over peers and continued to invest in customer experience enhancements and ancillary revenue streams. Labor cost increases and maintenance expenses exerted upward pressure on unit costs, partially offsetting fuel savings. The airline ended 2015 with a strong cash position and manageable debt levels, supporting planned fleet growth including more fuel-efficient aircraft deliveries in coming years.

**Guidance for early 2016** indicated expected capacity growth of 14-16% in Q1, with PRASM anticipated to decline 3-5% and CASM excluding fuel and profit sharing rising 2-3%, due primarily to ongoing labor cost initiatives. Economic fuel costs were projected between \$1.55 and \$1.65 per gallon in Q1 2016, lower than 2015 levels. The company expected full-year 2016 CASM excluding fuel and profit sharing to decrease 1-2%, reflecting operational efficiencies from fleet modernization and resumed growth [8-K 2016-02-18; 8-K 2016-02-05]. No material litigation, accidents, or labor disruptions were disclosed for 2015.

### Wrap Up

Virgin America’s 2016 first quarter showed robust capacity and traffic growth with a 15.8% increase in ASMs and 16.0% more passengers, maintaining a stable load factor of 80.1%. Despite a 3.7% decline in unit revenues driven by lower yields and fares, the airline achieved significant financial improvement, with operating income more than doubling to \$31.9 million and net income rising 36.5% to \$17.5 million. 10. **Merger agreement with Alaska Air Group announced post-2016Q1, with regulatory review ongoing**  
    On April 1, 2016, Virgin America entered a definitive merger agreement to be acquired by Alaska Air Group for approximately \$4 billion including debt. The transaction was unanimously approved by both boards and expected to close by January 1, 2017, subject to regulatory approvals and shareholder vote. As of May 16, 2016, the Department of Justice issued a second request for information, extending the review process [8-K filed 2016-04-04; 8-K filed 2016-05-17].

    Virgin America incurred \$1.6 million in merger-related professional fees during 2016Q1, included in operating expenses. These costs partially offset the benefits from lower fuel prices and contributed to the increase in non-fuel CASM [10-Q filed 2016-04-28].

12. **Risk disclosures highlighted typical merger-related uncertainties and operational risks**  
    Virgin America’s filings emphasized risks related to merger integration, regulatory approval, labor relations, fuel price volatility, and general economic conditions. The company also noted the potential impact of the merger announcement on key personnel retention and supplier relationships [10-Q filed 2016-04-28; 8-K filed 2016-04-22].

### Wrap Up

Virgin America’s 2016Q2 operational and financial results reflect continued capacity growth, fleet expansion, and network development primarily from its California hubs. Despite a modest decline in unit revenues driven by lower yields and average fares, the airline achieved a significant improvement in profitability and operating margins, largely due to sharply lower fuel costs. Non-fuel cost pressures, including merger-related fees and increased labor and marketing expenses, partially offset these gains but did not prevent a 36.5% rise in net income for 2016Q1.

Operationally, load factors improved in the spring months, with traffic growth outpacing capacity expansion by a small margin, suggesting better utilization of added seats. Commercial initiatives such as new routes to Denver and Hawai’i and a loyalty partnership with Starwood aimed to diversify and strengthen revenue streams. The announced merger with Alaska Air Group, pending regulatory approval, introduced new costs and risks but also defined a strategic turning point for the company.

**Guidance and Forward-Looking Notes:**  
No explicit guidance for 2016Q2 or beyond was disclosed in the filings. The merger review process was active as of mid-2016, with no set completion date beyond an expectation to close by January 1, 2017. Virgin America maintained an active fuel hedging program covering about 40% of expected 2016 fuel needs, with all contracts expected to settle by year-end, mitigating some fuel price volatility risk. There were no disclosed operational disruptions, labor disputes, or material litigation affecting the company during the period.

### Wrap Up

Virgin America’s 2016 Q3 and year-to-date SEC filings depict a company expanding capacity and network while facing pressure on yields and passenger revenue per seat mile amid a competitive domestic fare environment. Despite higher operating income and margins, net income declined due to increased income tax provisions and merger-related expenses.

The pending Alaska Air Group acquisition influenced legal costs and risk considerations. Liquidity and debt levels rose to fund fleet expansion, while labor costs grew with workforce increases. Fuel hedging mitigated some price volatility risks, but all contracts were set to expire by year-end 2016. Network additions in Hawaii and Denver supported traffic growth and higher departures. Ancillary revenue initiatives partially offset lower passenger yields.

No material operational disruptions, litigation outcomes, or labor disputes were disclosed for this period. The company’s financial and operational profile reflects an airline scaling up while navigating margin pressures and the uncertainties of an acquisition process.

The company faces risks from pilot supply constraints that could reduce utilization and trigger penalties. ### Wrap Up

Republic Airways’ Q3 2018 results show a marked shift from prior-year profitability to a slight operating loss driven by one-time lease termination costs, higher labor-related flight operations expenses, and increased general and administrative charges related to stock compensation accounting changes. Contract revenues grew modestly due to expansion of the E-175 fleet, partially offset by lower CRJ flying. Operational metrics such as block hours, ASMs, and passengers increased modestly, reflecting growth in United contract flying. However, pilot training and retention challenges elevated flight operations costs and constrained utilization, posing a risk to contract performance and financial results. The company increased capital spending to purchase previously leased CRJ-900 aircraft, raising debt levels but also reducing future lease expenses. Liquidity remains supported by positive operating cash flow and proceeds from the August 2018 IPO.

Guidance for Q4 2018 anticipates an increase in fleet count to 145 aircraft and block hours rising to approximately 112,000, with a forecasted reduction in non-pass-through engine expenses to \$3.0 million. The company is negotiating further aircraft purchases and refinancing of high-cost debt to reduce interest expense. Negotiations on expiring capacity purchase agreements, especially with United for CRJ-700 aircraft, remain a material operational and financial risk. No major operational disruptions or litigation were disclosed for the period.

2019.Q3:
### Financial Insights

1. **Contract revenue growth and improved earnings in Q3 2019 versus Q3 2018**  
   Republic's contract revenue increased 6.5% to \$170.4 million in Q3 2019 from \$159.9 million in Q3 2018, driven by increased flying on E-175, CRJ-900, and CRJ-700 fleets and higher performance incentive pay. Total operating revenue rose 4.9% to \$180.2 million. Net income improved to \$3.0 million (\$0.09 per diluted share) from a net loss of \$11.1 million (\$0.48 loss per diluted share) in Q3 2018. Adjusted net income, excluding non-cash lease termination expenses, was \$10.4 million versus \$8.8 million in Q3 2018. Adjusted EBITDA rose to \$45.9 million from \$41.7 million year-over-year [8-K 2019-08-09; 10-Q 2019-08-14].

2. **Year-to-date contract revenue and profit increased with higher flying activity**  
   For the nine months ended June 30, 2019, contract revenue increased 8.4% to \$510.6 million, reflecting more block hours (+14.3%) and flying on the E-175, CRJ-900, and CRJ-700 fleets. Operating income was \$90.7 million compared to \$30.9 million in the prior year period, and net income rose to \$35.3 million from \$13.9 million. Adjusted EBITDA for the nine months was \$157.8 million, up from \$105.5 million [10-Q 2019-08-14].

3. **Lease termination expenses declined due to aircraft purchases, boosting earnings**  
   Lease termination expenses decreased 36.9% to \$9.5 million in the nine months ended June 30, 2019, primarily because of the June 2019 purchase of 10 CRJ-700 aircraft previously leased from GECAS, compared to higher lease termination costs related to the June 2018 purchase of nine CRJ-900 aircraft. This non-cash expense reduction contributed to improved pre-tax income [10-Q 2019-08-14; 8-K 2019-08-09].

4. **Aircraft rent expense declined as purchases replaced leases, but depreciation increased**  
   Aircraft rent expense fell 24.7% year-to-date to \$41.1 million due to the purchase of 19 aircraft (9 CRJ-900s in 2018, 10 CRJ-700s in 2019) previously leased under GECAS. However, depreciation and amortization rose 20.8% to \$57.5 million, reflecting the capitalization of these purchases and spare engines, partially offsetting rent savings [10-Q 2019-08-14].

5. **Maintenance expense decreased year-to-date but increased sequentially in Q3**  
   Maintenance costs declined 9.4% year-to-date to \$139.5 million, mainly due to fewer engine overhauls and C-checks and reduced pass-through maintenance reimbursed by partners. However, in Q3 alone, maintenance expense rose 12.5% to \$54.3 million due to higher labor and outside labor support, partially offset by lower pass-through maintenance [10-Q 2019-08-14].

6. **Interest expense rose moderately reflecting new debt for aircraft purchases**  
   Interest expense increased slightly to \$42.1 million year-to-date, driven by new financing for the nine CRJ-900 aircraft purchased in June 2018 and the ten CRJ-700 aircraft purchased in June 2019. The \$70 million loan for the CRJ-700s bears interest at LIBOR plus 5.25% with monthly payments through fiscal 2023 [10-Q 2019-08-14; 8-K 2019-08-09].

7. **Liquidity and capital expenditures reflect aircraft acquisitions and spare engines**  
   Capital expenditures for the nine months ended June 30, 2019 were \$116.7 million, primarily for the purchase of 10 CRJ-700 aircraft and seven spare engines. Cash, cash equivalents, and restricted cash totaled \$83.6 million as of June 30, 2019 [10-Q 2019-08-14].

### Operations Insights

8. **Block hours and capacity increased substantially with fleet growth and utilization gains**  
   Block hours increased 10.8% in Q3 2019 to 114,042 hours and 14.3% year-to-date to 341,071 hours compared to 2018, reflecting more flying on E-175, CRJ-900, and CRJ-700 aircraft. Available seat miles (ASMs) rose 11.7% in Q3 and 14.5% year-to-date, while revenue passenger miles (RPMs) increased 12.7% in Q3 and 14.3% year-to-date. The average stage length increased modestly (4.5% in Q3) [10-Q 2019-08-14].

9. **Operational challenges in Q3 included aircraft downtime and industry-wide CRJ-900 avionics failure**  
   Three aircraft were unavailable for nearly all of Q3 2019 due to a ground damage incident and extended C-check turn times caused by Bombardier labor shortages. This shortage of spare aircraft, combined with a CRJ-900 avionics failure affecting the industry, caused Republic to miss new performance criteria under its American Airlines capacity purchase agreement (CPA), leading to American removing two aircraft from the CPA effective November 2, 2019 [8-K 2019-08-09].

10. **Controllable completion factor remained high despite Q3 operational disruptions**  
    The controllable completion factor (flights completed excluding weather and other uncontrollable cancellations) was 99.4% in Q3 2019, and total completion factor was 95.9%, indicating generally reliable operations aside from noted disruptions [8-K 2019-08-09].

### Labor Insights

11. **Increased pilot staffing drove higher flying but raised pilot and training costs**  
    The increase in block hours and contract revenue was supported by higher pilot staffing levels. However, pilot and pilot training expenses rose in Q3 2019 due to expectations of needing additional pilots going forward and increased line maintenance expenses. Improved staffing helped reduce pilot premium pay compared to prior periods [8-K 2019-08-09; 10-Q 2019-08-14].

12. **General and administrative expenses decreased due to lower stock-based compensation costs**  
    G&A expenses fell 43.6% in Q3 2019 to \$12.4 million, mainly driven by an \$11.1 million decrease in compensation expense related to stock appreciation rights (SARs) that had increased in value in 2018 [10-Q 2019-08-14].

### Route Network Insights

13. **Fleet composition and CPA aircraft counts stable with purchases reducing leased aircraft**  
    As of June 30, 2019, Republic operated 145 aircraft: 62 CRJ-900s under American CPA, 20 CRJ-700s and 60 E-175s under United CPA, with 18 aircraft leased from third parties after purchasing 10 CRJ-700s in June 2019. The total fleet count remained steady versus prior quarters, but leased aircraft declined due to purchases [8-K 2019-08-09; 10-Q 2019-08-14].

### Wrap Up

Republic Airways' third quarter 2019 results showed revenue growth driven by increased flying across its E-175, CRJ-900, and CRJ-700 fleets, supported by higher pilot staffing. Operating income and net income turned positive compared to losses in the prior year, aided by lower lease termination and aircraft rent expenses following the purchase of 19 aircraft previously leased from GECAS. However, depreciation and maintenance costs increased, reflecting capitalized assets and higher labor expenses. Operational reliability was generally high, but specific challenges in Q3, including aircraft downtime and a CRJ-900 avionics failure, led to capacity reductions by American Airlines under their CPA. Interest expense rose modestly due to new debt financing for purchased aircraft.

For the full fiscal year 2019 Q4, Republic guided continued fleet and block hour activity, with the fleet count forecast stable at 142 CPA aircraft. The company also disclosed ongoing investments in pilot training and maintenance capabilities, reflecting strategic priorities amid operational challenges. No material litigation, regulatory actions, or labor disputes were reported for the period.

### Financial Insights

   For the three months ended December 31, 2019, Republic Airways reported contract revenues of \$171.8 million, up 0.8% from \$170.4 million in 2018Q4, driven primarily by increased flying on the E-175 fleet and a reduction in credits given to major airline partners per contractual utilization levels [10-Q filed 2020-02-10]. Total operating revenues increased 3.3% to \$184.0 million due to a 58.8% increase in pass-through and other revenues to \$12.2 million, largely from maintenance pass-through related to the E-175 fleet. Despite revenue growth, net income for 2019Q4 was \$10.8 million, down 43.5% from \$19.1 million in 2018Q4, and operating income declined from \$39.2 million to \$27.2 million [10-Q filed 2020-02-10]. The decline in profitability reflects higher operating expenses, particularly maintenance and depreciation.

2. **Maintenance costs surged in 2019Q4, raising total operating expenses by nearly 13%**  
   Maintenance expense increased by \$18.3 million (46.0%) to \$58.1 million in 2019Q4 compared to 2018Q4, primarily due to increased engine overhaul, C-check expenses, and labor costs [10-Q filed 2020-02-10]. Pass-through maintenance expenses reimbursed by major airline partners also rose by \$3.5 million. This maintenance cost surge was a key driver of the 12.9% increase in total operating expenses to \$156.8 million in 2019Q4 [10-Q filed 2020-02-10].

3. **Aircraft rent expense fell significantly in 2019Q4 following fleet purchases, partially offset by higher engine rent**  
   Aircraft rent declined by \$2.8 million (19.8%) to \$11.3 million in 2019Q4 due to purchasing ten CRJ-700 aircraft previously leased under the GECAS Lease Facility in June 2019 [10-Q filed 2020-02-10]. This reduced lease expense was offset partially by a \$1.1 million increase in engine rent from leasing additional engines [10-Q filed 2020-02-10].

4. **Depreciation and amortization increased by 11.1% in 2019Q4 due to fleet purchases and spare engine acquisitions**  
   Depreciation and amortization expense rose \$2.1 million to \$20.6 million in 2019Q4 compared to 2018Q4. The increase was mainly attributable to depreciation on the ten CRJ-700 aircraft purchased in June 2019 and the purchase of spare engines and rotable inventory, partially offset by a decrease in aircraft enhancement depreciation [10-Q filed 2020-02-10].

   Adjusted EBITDA for 2019Q4 was \$50.8 million, down from \$59.3 million in 2018Q4, and Adjusted EBITDAR decreased from \$73.6 million to \$61.9 million [8-K filed 2019-12-13; 10-Q filed 2020-02-10]. This reflects the impact of higher maintenance, depreciation, and other expenses on earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization, and rent.

6. **Long-term debt increased due to financing fleet purchases, with \$807 million net debt excluding current maturities at December 31, 2019**  
   Republic Airways financed the purchase of ten CRJ-700 aircraft for \$70 million in June 2019, increasing debt with notes bearing LIBOR plus 5.25% interest [10-K filed 2019-12-17; 10-Q filed 2020-02-10]. 7. **Capital expenditures in 2019 increased substantially, mainly for fleet purchases and spare engines, raising capital intensity**  
   For the fiscal year ended September 30, 2019, Republic Airways spent \$125.4 million on capital expenditures primarily related to purchasing ten CRJ-700 aircraft previously leased and eight spare engines [10-K filed 2019-12-17]. Departures increased 1.9% to 62,725 flights [10-Q filed 2020-02-10].

9. **Fleet composition remained stable at 145 aircraft, with approximately equal split between American and United flying**  
   As of December 31, 2019, Republic operated 145 aircraft with approximately 742 daily departures. The fleet included 60 E-175s and 20 CRJ-700s under United contracts, and 60 CRJ-900s under American contracts [10-Q filed 2020-02-10]. Approximately 55% of the scheduled service aircraft were operated for United and 45% for American [10-Q filed 2020-02-10]. The CRJ-200 remained an operational spare, and two CRJ-900s were unassigned [10-K filed 2019-12-17].

10. **Block hours increased 11.0% year-over-year for the fiscal year ended September 30, 2019, driven by expanded flying on E-175, CRJ-900, and CRJ-700 fleets**  
    For the fiscal year ended September 30, 2019, block hours rose to 456,247 from 410,974 in 2018, an increase of 11.0% [10-K filed 2019-12-17]. This was primarily due to increased flying on the E-175, CRJ-900, and CRJ-700 fleets enabled by higher pilot staffing levels [10-K filed 2019-12-17].

### Labor Insights

11. **Flight operations expenses increased slightly in 2019Q4 despite a decline in pilot training costs, reflecting improved staffing and wage increases**  
    Flight operations expense decreased \$0.6 million (1.1%) to \$52.6 million in 2019Q4 compared to 2018Q4, primarily due to lower pilot training wages and related costs. This was partially offset by higher pilot and flight attendant wages as staffing levels improved [10-Q filed 2020-02-10]. For fiscal 2019, flight operations expense rose modestly by \$1.8 million (0.9%) to \$210.9 million, driven by increased wages from additional flying [10-K filed 2019-12-17].

### Commercial Strategy Insights

12. **Capacity purchase agreements with American and United remain the sole revenue source, providing revenue stability but limiting exposure to ticket price and fuel volatility**  
    All operating revenues in 2019Q4 and fiscal 2019 derived from capacity purchase agreements with American and United [10-Q filed 2020-02-10; 10-K filed 2019-12-17]. These agreements guarantee monthly revenue per aircraft, fixed fees per block hour, and reimburse certain direct operating expenses. The major airline partners control route selection, pricing, and marketing, reducing Republic's exposure to fluctuations in ticket prices, passenger volumes, and fuel prices, which are paid directly by the partners [10-K filed 2019-12-17; 10-Q filed 2020-02-10].

### Route Network Insights

13. **The fleet is aligned with capacity purchase agreements, with aircraft lease terms generally shorter than contract terms, exposing the company to some tail risk**  
    As of September 30, 2019, 17 aircraft leases extended beyond their respective capacity purchase agreement terms, creating aggregate exposure to aircraft without guaranteed flying contracts [10-K filed 2019-12-17]. The company intends to align lease and contract terms to mitigate this risk. The fleet consists mainly of E-175, CRJ-900, and CRJ-700 regional jets deployed under American and United agreements [10-K filed 2019-12-17].

### Corporate Insights

14. **No unresolved SEC staff comments or material litigation disclosed; the company maintains compliance with capacity purchase agreements**  
    The filing reports no unresolved SEC staff comments [10-K filed 2019-12-17]. Republic believes it is in material compliance with its capacity purchase agreements and maintains good relationships with its major airline partners [10-K filed 2019-12-17].

15. **Risks include potential loss or non-renewal of capacity purchase agreements and competition from major airlines’ captive regional carriers**  
    The company discloses that American and United could reduce or terminate capacity purchase agreements or shift flying to their captive regional carriers, which would materially harm Republic’s business, financial condition, and results [10-K filed 2019-12-17]. The company also notes exposure to operational risks and pilot availability constraints.

### Wrap Up

In 2019Q4, Republic Airways experienced modest revenue growth primarily from increased flying on its E-175 fleet under capacity purchase agreements with American and United. However, net income declined significantly due to a sharp rise in maintenance expenses and higher depreciation from fleet purchases. The company reduced aircraft rent expenses by acquiring previously leased CRJ-700 aircraft, which helped offset some cost increases. Operational metrics showed slight growth in capacity, block hours, and passengers, with a stable fleet aligned to its major airline partners. Labor costs were mixed, with lower pilot training expenses but higher wages from increased staffing.

The company's financial structure reflects increased debt from financing fleet acquisitions, and capital spending rose above historical levels due to aircraft and spare engine purchases. Capacity purchase agreements continue to provide revenue stability and shelter Republic from fuel and fare volatility but also concentrate risk in reliance on American and United. Tail risk remains from aircraft leases extending beyond contract terms. No material litigation or regulatory issues were disclosed. The company’s outlook for 2020 was provided but later withdrawn due to COVID-19 uncertainties [8-K filed 2020-03-18].

This summary is based solely on disclosures through December 31, 2019, and early 2020 filings, with no forward-looking statements or projections included beyond those explicitly stated in the excerpts.

### Financial Insights

### Commercial Strategy Insights

All operating revenue was derived from CPAs with American and United, providing fixed monthly fees per aircraft, block hour fees, and reimbursements of certain expenses. ### Corporate Insights

13. **COVID-19 outbreak introduced significant demand uncertainty, prompting suspension of 2020 guidance and expectation of material block hour reductions**  
Due to the evolving COVID-19 pandemic and its impact on air travel demand, the company withdrew prior 2020 and 2021 guidance and reported that major partners American and United requested a 55% block hour reduction in April 2020, with further cuts anticipated. ### Wrap Up

In Q1 2020, Republic Airways operated a stable but slightly expanded regional flying program under capacity purchase agreements with American and United, with modest revenue growth driven by increased E-175 flying and pass-through maintenance revenues. However, net income declined sharply due to a substantial rise in heavy maintenance costs, partially offset by reduced aircraft rent expense following the purchase of leased aircraft. Operational reliability improved, and the fleet was poised for growth with 20 new E-175 deliveries scheduled from May 2020. The company maintained liquidity through cash from operations and a revolving credit facility.

The onset of the COVID-19 pandemic introduced unprecedented demand uncertainty, leading the company to suspend financial guidance and anticipate significant block hour reductions imposed by its major partners. These developments materially affect near-term capacity and cash flow expectations but were not reflected in Q1 results. Republic’s revenue model under capacity purchase agreements limits exposure to fuel and fare volatility but does not shield it from partner-driven schedule changes. The company’s forthcoming operational and financial performance will depend heavily on the evolving pandemic situation and partner decisions.

### Wrap Up

Republic Airways’ second quarter fiscal 2020 results show the initial material impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, manifesting as modest revenue growth offset by sharply increased maintenance costs and reduced flying activity. The firm’s capacity purchase agreement model limited its exposure to passenger traffic declines but exposed it to significant block hour reductions mandated by major airline partners, which caused steep drops in utilization and variable revenue in April. Maintenance expenses surged due to the timing of heavy airframe and engine work, pressuring margins. Flight operations costs rose due to labor wage increases and training. Liquidity was supported by \$52 million cash on hand, credit facility draws, CARES Act payroll support, and debt deferrals, but the company carried significant debt with ongoing principal and interest obligations. Fleet adjustments included purchasing previously leased aircraft to reduce rent expense and delaying new aircraft deliveries. The company acknowledged uncertainty around the pandemic’s duration and recovery timing, with planned capacity reductions likely to continue into late 2020 and possibly 2021.

**Guidance:** Republic Airways did not provide formal guidance for the remainder of 2020 due to COVID-19 uncertainty but planned modest demand recovery beginning in the September 2020 quarter. The company is actively managing expenses, deferring maintenance and capital expenditures, and pursuing additional financing and government assistance to maintain liquidity [10-Q 2020-05-11].

### Wrap Up

Republic Airways’ Q3 2020 results were heavily shaped by the COVID-19 pandemic, which caused a steep decline in flying activity and related contract revenue, down nearly 60% year-over-year. Operating expenses fell even more sharply, driven by reduced flight operations and maintenance costs and a significant \$43 million CARES Act payroll support grant, allowing the company to maintain positive net income despite the revenue drop. Capacity and passenger volumes collapsed over 70%, reflecting major cuts by American and United Airlines, Republic’s principal partners under capacity purchase agreements that provide fixed revenue components insulating the company from some demand volatility. Maintenance costs showed divergent trends, with Q3 expenses down sharply but nine-month costs up due to timing and fleet ownership changes. Republic maintained a stable fleet under its contracts and is preparing for new E175 deliveries for United, with financing arrangements in progress. Liquidity improved to \$65 million unrestricted cash, supported by CARES Act funding and available collateral, while debt levels decreased modestly with refinancing benefits lowering interest expense. Labor costs declined in line with reduced flying, aided by government tax credits.

It anticipates continued schedule reductions into Q4 2020 and possibly beyond, with ongoing monitoring of pandemic impacts and customer demand. The deferred revenue of \$16 million will be recognized over the remaining contract terms as flights resume, representing a timing rather than a permanent revenue loss. ### Wrap Up

Republic Airways’ 2020Q4 and full fiscal year reflected the severe impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on flying activity and revenues, with block hours down over 40% in Q4 and 31% for the year. The company’s revenue decline was partially offset by pass-through maintenance revenues and government support under the CARES Act, which enabled it to remain profitable and cash flow positive despite the downturn. Operating expenses declined in line with reduced flying, driven by lower labor and maintenance costs, while aircraft rent fell due to fleet ownership changes. Liquidity was bolstered by a \$195 million CARES Act loan and repayment of several aircraft financing loans, resulting in a year-end cash balance of \$181 million.

Republic’s operations continued under capacity purchase agreements with American and United Airlines, which provided fixed monthly payments and expense reimbursements, sheltering the company from some market volatility but limiting growth opportunities. The fleet remained stable at 146 aircraft, with cargo operations initiated via DHL. Labor cost reductions aligned with lower flying helped preserve margins, and the company avoided furloughs through 2020. Risks remain from pandemic uncertainty, debt obligations, and the potential for partner contract changes or reductions, with the timing of demand recovery unclear.

**Forward Guidance:**  
For FY2021, Republic plans gradual block hour increases from 68,000 in Q1 to 89,000 in Q4, reflecting modest demand recovery assumptions [8-K filed 2021-02-09]. Pass-through maintenance expense is forecasted to decline sequentially after early 2021 peaks. No further borrowings are available under the CARES Act loan facility, and the company expects to manage capital expenditures prudently under uncertain market conditions [10-Q filed 2021-02-09]. The company continues to monitor pandemic impacts, partner agreements, and financial covenants closely.

### Financial Insights

2. **Net income decreased to \$27.5 million (\$0.78 per diluted share) from \$47.6 million (\$1.36 per diluted share) in 2019.** Operating income was \$80.2 million versus \$121.1 million in 2019. Other expense declined \$14.7 million to \$43.2 million, reflecting lower interest expense and the absence of a \$3.6 million loss on extinguishment of debt recorded in 2019 [10-K 2020-12-14].

3. **Operating expenses fell 22.8% to \$464.9 million, led by a \$41.6 million (19.7%) reduction in flight operations costs due to decreased pilot and flight attendant wages and training from less flying.** Maintenance expenses decreased 2.2% to \$192.1 million, aircraft rent fell 6.5% to \$48.8 million mainly from purchasing ten CRJ-700 aircraft previously leased (reducing lease expense by \$9.9 million), partially offset by increased engine rent [10-K 2020-12-14]. General and administrative expenses increased 3.4% to \$52.2 million, driven by higher pass-through property tax [10-K 2020-12-14].

4. **Depreciation and amortization rose 5.5% to \$82.3 million, primarily due to depreciation on the ten CRJ-700 aircraft purchased in June 2019, which were previously leased under the GECAS Lease Facility [10-K 2020-12-14].** Lease termination expenses dropped from \$9.5 million in 2019 to zero in 2020, reflecting no new lease terminations after the 2019 purchase of the CRJ-700 aircraft [10-K 2020-12-14].

5. **Liquidity was supported by CARES Act funding, with \$95.2 million in payroll support received April–September 2020, of which \$83.8 million was recognized in 2020.** The company drew \$23.0 million from its revolving credit facility to cover operational needs and had \$65 million in unrestricted liquidity as of June 30, 2020 [10-Q 2020-08-10]. Five unencumbered CRJ-700 aircraft were available as collateral for financing if needed [10-Q 2020-08-10]. Capital expenditures, net of rotable spare parts and financing, were about 5.7% of annual revenue in 2020, elevated from historical 1.2–1.5% levels, reflecting aircraft enhancements and revenue declines [10-K 2020-12-14].

### Operations Insights

7. **Block hours flown declined 31.4% year-over-year to 313,110 hours, reflecting reduced flying on CRJ-900, CRJ-700, and E-175 fleets due to COVID-19.** Available seat miles (ASMs) decreased 30.2% to 7.58 billion, and revenue passenger miles (RPMs) fell 40.3% to 5.13 billion, resulting in a lower passenger count of 8.5 million (down 42.0%) [10-K 2020-12-14]. Fuel and certain other expenses are paid directly by the major airline partners [10-K 2020-12-14].

12. **Flight operations expense declined \$41.6 million (19.7%) in 2020 due to lower pilot and flight attendant wages and pilot training expenses from reduced flying.** Flight operations expense in Q4 2020 decreased 29.8% versus Q4 2019, primarily due to lower wages and training costs [10-K 2020-12-14; 10-Q 2021-02-09].

### Route Network Insights

13. **Fleet transition plans included United electing to lease out 20 CRJ-700 aircraft to another United Express carrier with transition planned in 2022; RJET will continue to operate these until then.** United also has termination rights with 90+ days’ notice for the CPA or aircraft removal [10-K 2020-12-14].

### Wrap Up

Republic Airways’ 2020 fiscal year was marked by a substantial decline in flying activity and revenues due to the COVID-19 pandemic, with block hours down 31.4% and total operating revenue falling 24.6%. The company’s reliance on capacity purchase agreements with American and United Airlines provided revenue stability through fixed monthly payments, though contract revenue still fell 25.8% due to fewer flights. Operating expenses decreased 22.8%, driven largely by lower flight operations costs from reduced flying and wage savings, while depreciation increased due to prior aircraft purchases that replaced leases. CARES Act payroll grants and liquidity measures, including credit facility draws and available collateral aircraft, supported financial stability amid disrupted demand. Fleet size remained steady at 146 aircraft, with ongoing fleet transitions including CRJ-700 aircraft phased out by 2022 and new E-175 deliveries delayed but expected to resume in 2021.

The company’s 2020 results reflect the operational and financial stresses of the pandemic, with deferred revenues recognized as flights resume and cost savings partially offsetting revenue declines. United’s rights to modify or terminate capacity agreements and the timing of new aircraft deliveries represent ongoing operational uncertainties. RJET’s capital expenditures increased as a percentage of revenue due to lower top-line, reflecting investments in aircraft enhancements despite the downturn. The company’s debt was reduced through scheduled repayments and loan payoffs, aided by lower interest expense. Overall, the filings depict a business navigating significant COVID-19 impacts with structural revenue protections under CPAs, cost controls, and government support, while facing risks from partner contract terms and fleet transition timing.

Republic Airways’ Q2 2021 results reflect a significant contraction in flying and contract revenues driven by the ongoing impact of COVID-19, offset by government payroll support grants and cost reductions that supported improved profitability despite lower volumes. Labor costs fell in line with reduced block hours, constrained by PSP2 grant conditions that limited layoffs.    Mesa ended the fiscal year with \$57.7 million unrestricted cash. ### Wrap Up

Mesa Air Group’s 2022 financial results reflect a challenging operating environment marked by an industry-wide pilot shortage and elevated pilot wages, which pressured block hour production and increased flight operations costs. These factors contributed to significant non-cash impairment charges on CRJ fleet assets, culminating in large GAAP net losses despite modest revenue growth driven by higher contract rates. The company responded with fleet rationalization through sales of CRJ-700, CRJ-900, and CRJ-200 aircraft, and spare engines, generating liquidity to reduce debt and interest expense. Operationally, Mesa is consolidating its network by exiting American CPA flying and expanding its United CPA operations, accompanied by new pilot pay agreements and development programs to address labor shortages.

Guidance beyond the period was not detailed in the excerpts, but the company disclosed that the transition of American CPA flying to United is expected in early 2023, with liquidity initiatives and pilot pipeline improvements aimed at stabilizing operations. Risks remain related to pilot availability, contract renewals, and the successful execution of restructuring plans.

Depreciation and amortization dropped 27.7% to \$15.2 million, reflecting impaired CRJ-900 assets and 20 aircraft classified as non-depreciable assets held for sale. Flight operations expense rose 22.5% to \$58.3 million, driven by pilot wage increases and higher training costs. General and administrative expenses increased 11.2% to \$14.0 million due to higher outside services [10-Q 2023-02-09].

5. **Interest expense increased to \$11.3 million driven by higher interest rates and greater outstanding finance lease principal balances**  
   Interest expense rose from \$7.9 million to \$11.3 million year over year, reflecting both higher interest rates and increased finance lease liabilities, partially offset by a small increase in interest income [10-Q 2023-02-09].

6. **Liquidity at quarter end was \$56.1 million in unrestricted cash with total debt of \$701.3 million, including \$64.2 million reclassified to finance leases**  
   Mesa ended Q1 2023 with \$56.1 million in unrestricted cash and equivalents. Total debt stood at \$701.3 million, primarily secured by aircraft and engines. This includes \$64.2 million reclassified from operating leases to finance leases on 15 CRJ-900 aircraft due to a lease amendment with RASPRO Trust [8-K 2023-02-09; 10-Q 2023-02-09].

7. **Significant capital raising and debt reduction transactions executed or planned involving aircraft and engine sales and new credit facilities**  
   During fiscal 2022 and into Q1 2023, Mesa sold 18 CRJ-700 aircraft to United, with 10 sold in 2022 and the remaining 8 closing in January 2023 for net proceeds of \$44.8 million after debt retirement. The company also agreed to sell 11 CRJ-900 and 1 CRJ-200 aircraft to a third party, expected to generate \$8.2 million net proceeds after debt retirement. Additionally, an agreement to sell 30 spare engines to United is expected to generate \$80 million gross proceeds, retiring \$26.4 million of debt. Mesa established and drew a \$25.5 million line of credit with United. Agreements with Export Development Bank of Canada and junior noteholders reduced debt and interest payments, providing up to \$14 million in liquidity, and lease buyout pricing on 15 CRJ-900 aircraft was reduced by \$25 million [10-Q 2023-02-09].

8. **Capital expenditures were modest at 0.9% of revenue, focused on flight equipment and spare engines to support operations and pilot development**  
   Capital expenditures net of purchases and financing were approximately 0.9% of revenue for Q1 2023. The company is investing in aircraft and spare engines, including a pilot development program involving the purchase of up to 29 Pipistrel Alpha Trainer 2 aircraft to accelerate pilot hour accumulation [10-Q 2023-02-09].

### Operations Insights

9. **Capacity and traffic sharply reduced as block hours declined 40.8% and available seat miles fell 44.1%, with consequential drops in passengers and departures**  
   Available seat miles (ASMs) dropped from 2.1 billion to 1.18 billion, a 44.1% decline. Block hours decreased from 86,079 to 50,940 (40.8%), departures fell 36.1% to 27,776, and passengers carried declined 35.2% to 1.75 million. Average stage length decreased 12.3% to 565 miles, reflecting changes in route structure or fleet deployment [10-Q 2023-02-09; 8-K 2023-02-09].

10. **Operational reliability improved with controllable completion factors rising to 99.4% for American and 99.9% for United**  
    The controllable completion factor, which excludes cancellations due to weather or air traffic control, increased year over year for American (from 97.7% to 99.4%) and United (from 98.3% to 99.9%). 11. **Pilot shortage and attrition materially constrained capacity, causing penalties under CPAs and reduced block hours**  
    The company reported that pilot shortages and elevated attrition, driven by accelerated hiring at major carriers, reduced block hour production and caused operational shortfall penalties under CPAs. About 64% of scheduled service aircraft were operated for United, 34% for American, and 2% for DHL. Several CRJ-700 and CRJ-900 aircraft were classified as assets held for sale [10-Q 2023-02-09].

### Route Network Insights

    In December 2022, Mesa entered into an amendment with American Airlines to terminate and wind down the American CPA by April 3, 2023. ### Labor Insights

14. **Pilot wage increases and training costs rose materially, reflecting new pay scales and pilot development investments**

### Wrap Up

Mesa Air Group’s Q1 2023 results reveal a delicate balance between sharply reduced flying capacity and improved operational reliability amid a persistent pilot shortage. Contract revenues declined due to a 40.8% drop in block hours, but higher pilot pay rates partially offset revenue loss. Operating expenses fell, driven by lower maintenance, depreciation, and aircraft rent, but were offset by rising flight operations costs linked to wage increases and training. The company’s net loss narrowed, with adjusted EBITDA improving, though interest expense rose. Mesa pursued significant asset sales and credit arrangements to bolster liquidity and reduce debt, while preparing for the April 2023 wind-down of its American CPA and transition of aircraft to United CPA. Pilot shortages remain a key operational constraint, influencing capacity and financial performance.

**Guidance and forward-looking context:** While explicit guidance was not included in these excerpts, management disclosed the upcoming operational transition from American CPA to United CPA by April 3, 2023, and ongoing efforts to restore capacity through pilot development and improved pay scales. Mesa Air Group’s Q2 2023 results reflect a continuing strategic transition of its CRJ-900 fleet from American Airlines to United Airlines, which reshaped its revenue base and operational footprint. Republic Airways’ Q3 2023 results reflect a continuing transformation driven by fleet downsizing, contract transitions, and pilot labor challenges.     The controllable completion factor (CCF), a metric measuring the percentage of flights completed excluding weather and air traffic control cancellations, was 99.5% in Q4 2023 versus 99.7% in Q4 2022 [8-K filed 2024-01-26].     Flight operations expense rose by \$39.7 million (22.4%) in fiscal 2023 compared to 2022, primarily reflecting the implementation of a new pilot pay scale and higher pilot training costs [10-K filed 2024-01-26]. ### Wrap Up

In fiscal 2023, Republic Airways (Mesa Air Group) faced a substantial reduction in flying activity and fleet size, driven by pilot shortages and strategic fleet rationalization, leading to a 6.2% revenue decline and a net loss of \$120.1 million despite improved operating leverage from lower impairment charges and aircraft rent expenses. Flight operations costs rose significantly due to higher pilot pay and training, while maintenance spending was deferred to match reduced flying. The company generated significant liquidity by selling CRJ-900 aircraft and engines, reducing debt by over \$160 million during the year, but still faces sizeable debt maturities in the coming twelve months. Operational reliability remained high, supporting the primary revenue relationship with United Airlines, which accounted for approximately 95% of Q4 2023 revenue.

Management’s efforts to stabilize liquidity include agreements with United Airlines to increase block-hour rates (expected to add approximately \$63.5 million in revenue over the next twelve months), continued asset sales, and amendments to credit agreements. The company’s ability to maintain financial stability depends on executing its sales and financing plans and managing operational constraints such as pilot availability. To address liquidity, the company implemented asset sales, including CRJ-700 and CRJ-900 aircraft, engine sales, and secured new credit lines with United Airlines [10-K filed 2024-01-26; 10-Q filed 2023-08-14].

### Operations Insights

7. **Block hours declined 30.4% to 188,947 hours in fiscal 2023, reflecting operational impacts from pilot shortages and a strategic reduction in CRJ flying.** Revenue Passenger Miles (RPMs) and Available Seat Miles (ASMs) also fell significantly, with ASMs down 36.5% to 4.24 billion and RPMs down 51.2% to 2.71 billion for the year ended September 30, 2023. ### Labor Insights

11. **Pilot shortages and attrition below pre-pandemic levels materially constrained flight operations, reducing block hours flown and revenues while increasing pilot training costs.** The company established the Mesa Pilot Development Program to increase pilot supply, including purchasing 29 Pipistrel Alpha Trainer 2 aircraft to accelerate pilot training hours [10-Q filed 2023-05-09; 10-Q filed 2023-02-09].

### Route Network Insights

### Wrap Up

Republic Airways experienced a challenging 2023 fiscal year marked by a significant reduction in flying activity and revenues, primarily due to pilot shortages, fleet downsizing, and contract transitions. Despite a 6.2% decline in total operating revenue to \$498.1 million, the company reduced its net loss from \$182.7 million in 2022 to \$120.1 million in 2023, helped by lower impairment charges and reduced rent and depreciation expenses following the reclassification of aircraft leases and asset sales. However, higher pilot pay scales and training costs increased flight operations expenses, offsetting some cost savings.

Operationally, block hours fell over 30%, with capacity and traffic metrics declining sharply, reflecting both pilot supply constraints and strategic fleet reductions, including the sale of all CRJ-700 aircraft and ongoing sales of CRJ-900s. The company remains focused on liquidity management through asset sales, new credit facilities with United Airlines, and cost control measures, while also investing in pilot training to address workforce challenges. The transition of CRJ flying from American to United was completed, consolidating the network under United’s CPA. The company’s liquidity and debt position remain under pressure but are supported by ongoing asset dispositions and financing arrangements.

**Guidance and Forward-Looking Details:** The company expects to complete CRJ-900 and engine sales by March 2024, generating proceeds to retire debt and improve liquidity. United Airlines has agreed to higher block-hour rates retroactive to October 1, 2023, projected to add approximately \$63.5 million in revenue over the next twelve months. The company has secured a \$25.5 million line of credit with United, with potential forgiveness tied to operational performance milestones through December 2024. Scheduled principal repayments and asset sales are expected to reduce debt by \$225 million in fiscal 2024, targeting a year-end debt balance near \$310 million. The company continues to monitor covenant compliance and may adjust capital spending in response to market conditions [10-K filed 2024-01-26; 8-K filed 2024-01-18].

No material operational disruptions, strikes, regulatory actions, or litigation affecting financial results were disclosed for 2023.
